sections.text: Abortiporus biennis (Bull.) Singer is a species of fungus in the family Podoscyphaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Two different forms of Abortiporus biennis can be found: a "normal"-looking one, with a brown cap 5–15 cm in diameter and a white hymenophore that, when damaged, turns reddish to reddish-brown; and a form with an irregular, "interrupted" shape, made up of irregular white pores (1–3 per mm) that exude a reddish fluid (guttation) and turn reddish-brown when damaged. In this second form, as the fungus grows it often engulfs sticks and blades of grass, as some species of the genus Hydnellum do. The fruiting bodies overlap one another; the surface is rough and hairy. Microscopic features: The flesh is tough, white to pinkish, sometimes light brown, and a pinkish fluid appears when it is squeezed. It produces hyaline, smooth, ellipsoid, slightly thick-walled spores measuring 4–7 × 3.5 µm, as well as asexual chlamydospores.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It grows mainly on buried hardwood, most often in artificial habitats, e.g. on remains of stumps in lawns, rarely on trunks in more natural conditions. Rather rare, it occurs from June to January. The species is rarely recorded in Poland. Two localities are reported from Gryfino County and one from Kołobrzeg County. There is a single locality in the Źródliskowa Buczyna reserve. In the Białowieża Forest it has been recorded twice (Jaroszewicz 1996, Niemelä 2013). Threat category E (Endangered – critically threatened).

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: Daedaleopsis confragosa also turns red, but it is tougher, its fruiting body has a more regular shape, and it grows on branches and trunks. Abortiporus biennis may resemble a small Grifola frondosa or Meripilus giganteus, but neither of these species turns red (the latter turns from grey to black). Loweomyces fractipes is very similar, with a single cap and a lateral stem, but it does not redden, and the pores are well defined and smaller (4–5 per mm).
Agaricus arvensis Schaeff. is a species of fungus in the family Agaricaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Ovoid when young, later hemispherical, convex, and flat in the mature fruiting body. The surface is bare, silky-shiny, white to cream in colour. It turns yellow when pressed. Gills: Free, crowded. White in young fruiting bodies and they remain white for quite a long time. Later greyish-brown with a fleshy tinge, finally chocolate-brown or even blackish-brown. They never have a pink tinge. Stem: Height 5–15 cm, thickness 1–3 cm. Cylindrical, thickened at the base, first solid, then hollow, easily breaking away from the cap, with a large hanging ring at the top. It turns yellow when pressed. Flesh: Soft and elastic, white, sometimes yellowish in old fruiting bodies. Taste insignificant, smell of anise. Spore print: Blackish-brown or purple-brown. Spores 6–8 × 4–5 µm. Similar species: There are many similar species of Agaricus. Among those with an aniseed smell, Agaricus silvicola is similar, but its gills remain reddish-pink for a long time. Agaricus xanthodermus turns yellow when pressed (like A. arvensis), but smells of carbolic acid.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North and South America, Europe, Asia and Australia. In Poland it is common. A saprotrophic fungus. It grows on the ground in coniferous, deciduous and mixed forests, in forest nurseries, in gardens, on meadows and pastures, in forest litter and on various kinds of organic waste. It produces fruiting bodies from May to October. The fruiting bodies grow singly or in small groups.
Agaricus augustus Fr. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Agaricaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 10–25, initially almost spherical, then successively ovoid, hemispherical, convex-flattened, and finally expanded. The surface is light ochre, covered with adpressed scales ranging in colour from rusty-brown to reddish-brown. Gills: Crowded, initially whitish, then salmon-pink, finally chocolate-brown. The edges are lighter. Stem: Height 10–20 cm, thickness 2–3 cm, cylindrical, with a bulb at the base, usually hidden in the ground, firm, breaking off cleanly, initially solid, then hollow. The surface is white to ochre-yellow, yellow-brown when pressed. The ring is large, pendulous, whitish-yellowish on the upper side, yellowish-rusty and fibrillose on the lower side. Flesh: Thick, soft, initially whitish, then yellowish-rusty, with a pleasant smell of anise or almonds. Microscopic features: Basidiospores dark brown to black, ellipsoid, 5.6–9 × 3.7–6.5 μm, Q = 1.47 ± 0.13, slightly thick-walled. Cheilocystidia numerous, club-shaped, 17.5 × 5 μm. The cap skin consists of groups of hyphae emerging outward and forming scales. Specimens occurring in America have spores without a germ pore, whereas European specimens have distinct germ pores. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America, Europe and Asia (here localities are given only in Japan). In Poland, numerous localities of this species have been reported in the scientific literature. A terrestrial saprotrophic fungus. It grows in forests and at their edges, on sandy and calcareous soils. It produces fruiting bodies from August (sometimes from July) to October.
Agaricus bitorquis (Quél.) Sacc. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Agaricaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 4–10, even 15 cm, hemispherical when young, flat in older specimens, even with a sunken centre. The margin extends beyond the gills and stays inrolled for a long time. The surface is smooth and dry, sometimes cracking into patches. It is whitish and does not change colour when rubbed. Sometimes remnants of the veil are found on its margin. Gills: Crowded, narrow and free. Initially light pink, then chocolate-brown, finally blackish-brown. The edges are white and flocculose. Stem: Short and thick, cylindrical with a narrowed base, solid and firm. The surface is smooth or woolly, whitish. It has a massive, double ring, white to light ochre in colour. Flesh: Firm and very compact, white, does not change colour when damaged, or turns slightly pink. It has a pleasant almond smell and a nutty taste. Similar species: Agaricus bisporus, found mainly in cultivation and sold in shops. In natural habitats it is quite rare, and its wild-growing form is darker, brownish and has a tight ring.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Agaricus bitorquis is fairly common in Poland. In the scientific literature up to 2003, 8 localities were described. A terrestrial fungus occurring mainly in towns. It can be found in gardens, on roadsides, in city parks and in thickets with elder, sometimes in cracks in pavements and even in old, damaged plaster.
Agaricus campestris L. is a species of fungus in the family Agaricaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 5–11 cm, closed and almost spherical in young specimens, later hemispherical, finally flatly expanded. The margin is cracked into scales, the surface is silky-fibrous, and at the top there are sparse, adpressed brown scales. When pressed it turns yellowish or brownish (older specimens). The cap is initially white, later greyish-ochre. In mature fungi, especially in dry weather, the upper surface of the cap cracks, forming deep grooves and patches. The skin can be easily peeled from the whole cap. Gills: Crowded, free at the stem. Only in very young, still closed fruiting bodies are they white; then they become pink and darker with age; chocolate-brown to blackish-brown. In old fruiting bodies they become violet-black from the spores. Stem: Height 4–8 cm, thickness 1–2 cm, cylindrical, solid, easily breaking away from the cap, with a white membranous ring at the top. The surface is smooth, white, brownish in older specimens. The ring is not very durable and disappears in older specimens. The upper part of the stem is often pinkish from the flesh showing through.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The species is distributed across the whole globe: apart from Antarctica it occurs on all continents, also on many islands. In Central Europe it is widespread and fairly common, but because of excessive fertilisation of meadows and pastures its numbers in Europe are declining. The fruiting bodies grow very fast; after abundant summer rains they sometimes sprout within a single day. It is this species of fungus that gave rise to the saying "to grow like mushrooms after rain".
Agaricus xanthodermus Genev. is a species of fungus in the family Agaricaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 4–12(15) cm, entirely white and convex, the skin silky, often radially cracked, sometimes covered with delicate scales, and it may be light beige at the top. The skin of the cap turns yellow under pressure. Gills: Rather thin, at first pink, whitish-pink and shades thereof, with time turning chocolate-brown. Stem: Up to 10–12 cm high, entirely white, slender, passing in the lower part into a bulb; under pressure it turns chrome yellow. The stem is sometimes hollow inside (see photo). The ring is pendulous, with a characteristic edge running all around its underside. Flesh: White, turning intense yellow when cut, chrome yellow when rubbed at the base. The smell resembles carbolic acid or ink, and this smell intensifies when cooked. The taste is very unpleasant. Spore print: Dark. Spores elliptical, 5.5–6.5 × 3.5–4.5 µm. The spore-shedding period falls in the months from July to October. Similar species: This fungus is most easily confused with Agaricus arvensis. The feature that distinguishes them is the smell of the flesh.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Localities of this species have been described in North, Central and South America, Europe and Australia. In Poland it is fairly common. A terrestrial saprotrophic fungus. Fruiting bodies from May to October. It occurs in deciduous and coniferous forests, in areas near roads and in roadside thickets, in parks, gardens and meadows, sometimes forming larger clusters.
Agrocybe pediades (Fr.) Fayod is a species of fungus in the family Agrocybaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 1–4 cm, shape hemispherical in young fruiting bodies, later convex, almost flat in older ones. Colour yellowish to yellow-brown, the surface smooth, slightly sticky when moist, sometimes with whitish veil remnants on the margin. Gills: Adnate or slightly decurrent, medium broad, initially cream, then brown, sometimes rusty-brown. In young fruiting bodies often completely covered by the veil. Stem: Height 2–4 cm, thickness 1–2 mm, cylindrical or slightly tapering toward the base, straight, sometimes curved. The surface is dry, smooth below the cap, otherwise finely fibrillose, the same colour as the cap. Flesh: Without taste or with a mealy taste, without smell. Microscopic features: Spores 9–13 × 6.5–8 µm, smooth, elliptical, with slightly truncated tips. Cystidia 30–70 × 8–15 µm, club-shaped and swollen, with pointed or slightly swollen ends. Similar species: Species of Agrocybe are difficult to distinguish. Agrocybe pediades shows variation in colouring and spore morphology.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In the Northern Hemisphere it is widely distributed. In the Southern Hemisphere its occurrence has been reported in Australia, New Zealand and one place in Chile. In Poland it is common. A saprotroph. It rarely occurs in coniferous forests; it mostly grows on meadows, pastures, in parks, gardens, cultivated fields, on roadsides, among moss and grass. It produces fruiting bodies from May to October. Like many other species of fungi, it appears en masse after prolonged rain.
Agrocybe praecox (Pers.) Fayod is a species of fungus in the family Agrocybaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 2–8 cm, hemispherical in young fruiting bodies, then arched, finally almost flat, sometimes with a depressed centre. It is hygrophanous. The surface is smooth, yellowish, creamy-white, ochre or brownish. On the margin there are usually remnants of a whitish veil. Gills: Notched, crowded, initially whitish, then greyish-white, clay-brownish or dirty brown. Stem: Height 4–9 cm, thickness 4–9 mm, cylindrical, hollow inside. The surface is bare, whitish to ochre-cream. The base has white rhizomorphs. The ring is membranous, pendulous, disappearing only in older fruiting bodies. Flesh: Soft and whitish in the cap, brown in the stem. It does not change colour when damaged. It has a faint mealy smell and a mealy-bitter taste. Microscopic features: Spore print brown. Spores ellipsoid to ovoid, smooth, 7.5–10 × 5–6 μm, with distinct germ pores. Similar species: Agrocybe praecox is morphologically variable and difficult to distinguish from similar species. Agrocybe dura also grows in spring. It is paler and has an umbonate, fleshier, non-hygrophanous cap, which usually cracks in dry weather.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Agrocybe praecox occurs on all continents except Antarctica and Australia and on many islands. In Europe it is widely distributed. In Poland it is common. A saprotrophic fungus. It grows on wood remains, bark, sawdust and forest litter. It occurs in peat bogs, grassy forest edges, thickets, clearings and pastures, in parks, gardens, orchards, road verges and field boundaries. It usually produces fruiting bodies from May to July.
Aleuria aurantia (Pers.) Fuckel is a species of fungus in the family Pyronemataceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Diameter 2–10 cm. In young individuals almost spherical, later cup-shaped with bent margins, in older ones almost flat, roundish, lobed and with wavy margins. No stem. The inner spore-bearing layer, in which the spores are formed, is smooth, coloured from yellow-red through orange to cinnabar-brown-red; the outer side is delicately velvety, coloured from whitish to pale yellow-ochre. Flesh: Very thin, brittle and watery. It is white-grey, with faint taste and smell; when crushed the smell is pleasant. Spores: Colourless, oblong-elliptical, covered with reticulate ornamentation. Size: 16–24 × 8–12 μm. Similar species: Sarcoscypha austriaca has a more intense colour (scarlet red) and grows only in early spring. Melastiza chateri is smaller and has a black-speckled margin of the fruiting body. Caloscypha fulgens has an orange-yellow fruiting body, with the inside of the cup grey when young, later orange, and delicately granular on the outside. It grows in early spring in mountain coniferous forests.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Aleuria aurantia is distributed worldwide. It occurs on all continents except Antarctica, but it is present on the Antarctic islands of the South Shetlands and South Orkneys. It also occurs on many islands of all oceans. In Europe in the north it reaches Iceland and the Svalbard archipelago and is common. A terrestrial saprotrophic fungus. Fruiting bodies appear from late summer to autumn, usually in groups, often very numerous, on the ground, mainly in open, sunny places.
Amanita citrina Pers. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Amanitaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Fleshy, 5–10 cm in diameter, pale yellowish, less often yellow-greenish, at first hemispherical, later flat. On its surface there are a few patches of various sizes. When young, the whole cap is enclosed in a veil. As the fruiting body grows it tears apart. From its lower part the ring on the stem forms, from the upper part the patches on the cap, which are often washed off by rain. Gills: White on young fruiting bodies, yellowish-white on older ones, crowded, not attached to the stem. Stem: Thin (1–2 cm) and tall (5–15 cm), cylindrical, easily separating from the cap. It is white or yellowish-white, tapering upward. On the bulbous base of the stem there is a short volva up to 4 cm thick, with ragged, uneven edges. On the stem there is a yellowish ring, pendulous in mature specimens. Flesh: White, brittle, with a mild taste and a smell of raw potatoes. It does not change colour when broken. Spore print: White. Spores smooth, 7–10 μm in diameter.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in temperate-climate areas of Asia, North America and Europe, and in Australia. In Poland it is very common. It grows in various types of forests, especially on sandy areas and acidic soils. Fruiting bodies appear from July to November.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: It is very similar to Amanita virosa and to Amanita phalloides. Specimens of Amanita citrina from whose caps the rain has washed off the patches can be especially easily mistaken.
Amanita crocea (Quél.) Singer is a species of fungus belonging to the family Amanitaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Ochre-orange to yellow-orange, 6–15 cm in diameter, initially hemispherical-ovoid-bell-shaped, with age convex to expanded and with an umbo; the surface is sticky when moist, smooth and velvety when dry, usually without veil remnants, the margin distinctly striate to 1/3 of the radius. Gills: Cream, fairly crowded, broad, free. Stem: Cylindrical, height 10–15 cm, thickness 1–2.5 cm, slightly tapering upward; the surface has yellow-orange flocks on a white background. At the base of the stem there is a persistent and sturdy volva, membranous, white on the outside, yellowish inside. Flesh: White, thin, without smell, the taste mild, indefinite. Spore print: White. Spores spherical or almost spherical, size: 11–12.5 × 9–10 µm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in Europe and North America. Since the 1980s it has been increasingly rare in Europe. In the scientific literature for Poland, 6 localities were reported up to 2003. The fruiting bodies grow singly or in groups, in deciduous forests, at their edges, in grass, in warm, sunny places; it prefers mineral soils. It tolerates nitrogen compounds in the soil poorly.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: It may be confused with Amanita caesarea, which also has a similar yellow-orange colour, but that species does not occur in Poland. It can also be confused with Amanita fulva, which forms smaller fruiting bodies and has a cap of a pale orange colour.
Amanita fulva Fr. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Amanitaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 3 to 10 cm, initially bell-shaped conical, later arched with a small umbo, finally flatly expanded without an umbo. It is distinctly striate at the margin, bare, smooth, usually without veil remains, slimy-sticky in wet conditions, light brown, orange-brown, finally red-brown. Sometimes there are greyish veil remnants on the surface. The skin can be peeled from the whole cap. Gills: Moderately crowded, not attached to the stem, white or light grey. Stem: Height 8–15 cm, diameter 0.8–1.2 cm, cylindrical, tapering upward, smooth, without a ring, hollow in older specimens, white to ochre-brown. The base of the stem is surrounded by a membranous, loose volva with features characteristic of this species; it is membranous, attached at the bottom, free at the top, loose, reaching up to 1/4 of the height of the fruiting body. Its colour ranges from white to ochre-brown. Flesh: The flesh is watery and whitish, brittle, thin, the smell indistinct, the taste sweetish. Spore print: White or cream. Spores spherical, non-amyloid, measuring 9.7–12.5 × 9.7–12.5 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America, Europe, Asia and Africa. In Poland it is common. It grows in deciduous and coniferous forests from lowlands to mountains, on the ground, especially under spruces, but also under pines, oaks, beeches and birches.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: Amanita crocea, which forms larger fruiting bodies and has a cap of a vivid orange colour. Amanita vaginata. It usually has greyish shades, but there are varieties with colouring very similar to Amanita fulva. They differ in the volva.

Amanita muscaria (L.) Lam. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Amanitaceae. It is probably the most characteristic species of Amanita. It is a large, spotted, usually red fungus and is one of the most recognisable and widely encountered in popular culture; it inspired the creators of, for example, the Mario game series (after eating a mushroom Mario became bigger) and the houses of the Smurfs in comics and cartoons. All varieties of Amanita muscaria, in particular A. muscaria var. muscaria, are known for their hallucinogenic properties, the main psychoactive constituents being ibotenic acid (a neurotoxin) and muscimol.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter up to 20 cm. In very young specimens spherical, then hemispherical, with time low-arched, and in older specimens flat and slightly depressed in the centre. The surface is smooth, delicately scalloped near the margin in older specimens. Initially it is covered with a whitish veil. After it tears, white or whitish-yellow patches remain on the cap. In wet weather it is sticky. Gills: White or pale yellowish, ventricose, crowded, free. Stem: Height up to 20 cm, thickness up to 3 cm. It is cylindrical, easily breaking off, solid when young, then hollow. The colour is white or yellow; it has a pendulous, white (sometimes yellowish) ring. The base is bulbous, surrounded by several rows of roll-like thickenings and without a distinct volva. Flesh: White, brittle, does not change colour when damaged, without smell and with a mild taste. Spore print: White. Spores smooth, ellipsoid, measuring 9–11 × 6–9 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A cosmopolitan species widely distributed in the temperate climate zone across the whole Northern Hemisphere, but it also occurs in some regions with a warm climate, e.g. in Central America, in the Hindu Kush, or around the Mediterranean Sea. With pine seedlings, its spores and mycelium have been carried to various other regions of the world and it now also appears in Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and South America. In Central Europe, including Poland, it is very common.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: Amanita regalis – has a brownish cap skin, yellow dots and ring edge, and grows only under spruces. Russula xerampelina and other red russulas – have a straight stem without a ring or other decoration and a smooth cap. Amanita junquillea – is sometimes confused with the yellow varieties of Amanita muscaria, but it is smaller and has a different stem structure.
Amanita pantherina (DC.) Krombh. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Amanitaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 4–12 cm in diameter, spherical when young, then becomes convex and flat. Colour: brown-grey, brownish or brown-yellow; in mountain areas it may be blackish-brown. The surface is covered with white patches. The skin on the surface is easily removable. A characteristic feature distinguishing it from similar species of Amanita (A. excelsa and A. rubescens) is that the margins of the cap are distinctly striate. Gills: Crowded, white, free at the stem, not fusing with it. Stem: 5–15 cm high and 1–2 cm thick, white, initially thick and massive, later slender, cylindrical, hollow inside. It is wider at the bottom and has a bulbous, relatively small swelling with several rows of rolls (a characteristic feature distinguishing it from similar species of Amanita). Under the cap there is a smooth, membranous ring that disappears in older fungi. Flesh: Entirely white, brittle, does not change colour when damaged. Mild, sweetish-insipid in taste, with a faint smell resembling radish or raw potato. Spore print: White. Spores smooth, broadly ellipsoid, measuring 9–12 × 7–9 μm. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs across the whole Northern Hemisphere in the temperate climate zone. In the Southern Hemisphere it is known only in Australia. In Poland it is common. It can be found mainly from June to October in deciduous forests, less often in coniferous ones. It occurs singly or in small groups of a few specimens, both in the lowlands and in the mountains.
Amanita phalloides (Vaill. ex Fr.) Link is a species of fungus belonging to the family Amanitaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 5–15 cm, hemispherical when young, then bell-shaped-arched, finally expanded. The skin is smooth, not striate at the margin, and consists of adpressed, radially arranged fibres. The colour is whitish-greenish, olive-greenish, grey-green, brownish-green, usually lighter at the margin, sometimes yellowish. In the sun, and in older specimens, the colour is faded. The skin is easily peeled and there are often white veil remnants on it. Stem: Height up to 15 cm, thickness up to 2 cm. It is cylindrical, ending at the base in a bulb up to 4 cm in diameter. The bulb is surrounded by a tall, whitish, spreading volva. The colour of the stem is whitish with a yellowish-greenish tinge. It has a distinct, hanging ring of a colour from white to yellowish. Above the ring the stem is smooth; below the ring there are delicate scales, sometimes forming a zigzag pattern. Flesh: White, does not change colour when broken. In young specimens the flesh has a mild smell; in old ones it smells somewhat of potatoes. The taste is pleasant. Gills: Crowded, white, with a slight yellowish-greenish tinge in old specimens. In young specimens they are not visible, as they are covered by a whitish veil. Spore print: White

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It originates from Europe, from where it has spread as an invasive species. Today it occurs on all continents except Antarctica. In Central Europe, including all of Poland, it is common. It occurs most often in deciduous forests, also in mixed ones; it grows singly or in small groups. It most often grows under oaks, but also under many other tree species: beeches, horse chestnuts, birches, hazels, hornbeams, pines and spruces. It most often occurs on soils with a neutral or alkaline reaction, but can also grow on acidic soils.
Amanita porphyria Alb. & Schwein. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Amanitaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 4–9 cm in diameter, bell-shaped-arched in young individuals, then quickly flattening. The margin is blunt, without striations; the surface of the cap is smooth, bare with delicate, embedded fibres, usually with patch-like veil remnants. The colour is grey-brown or grey-violet. In dry weather it is shiny, in wet weather slippery. Gills: White, of unequal length, crowded and free at the stem. Stem: Height 8–13 cm, thickness 1–2 cm, cylindrical, narrowed in the upper part. Solid in young fruiting bodies, later hollow inside; in older ones grey-brown with a violet tinge. The ring is hanging and disappears in older specimens. The base is bulbous with a large volva, standing away from the stem and torn, which is usually darker than the stem. Flesh: Brittle, white, rather thin. It has an unpleasant smell of rotting potatoes and the taste of radish. Spore print: White. Spores spherical, smooth, 8–10 μm in diameter. Similar species: Sometimes Amanita excelsa is similar, but it does not have a protruding bulb, and is also larger and fleshier.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs across the whole Northern Hemisphere. Its localities have been described in North America, Europe and Japan. In Poland it is common. In the scientific literature for Poland, numerous localities have been reported. It grows mainly in coniferous forests on acidic soils; in the lowlands in pine forests, in the mountains under spruces. The fruiting bodies grow from July to October.
Amanita regalis (Fr.) Michael is a species of fungus belonging to the family Amanitaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter , initially bulbous and enclosed in a veil, later hemispherical, then increasingly expanded. The surface is dry, shiny, liver-brown in colour, darker at the top, covered with fairly regular, concentrically arranged ochre-yellow patches. In older specimens the margin of the cap is striate. Gills: Free, crowded, white, later creamy-yellowish. In young specimens covered by a yellowish veil. Stem: 8–20 cm in height, diameter , cylindrical, fragile. At the base it has a bulb with several rows of rings covered with warts (veil remnants). The surface is smooth, white or yellow-white, with a distinct yellowish ring. Flesh: Yellowish-brown under the skin of the cap, with a mild and faint taste. It does not change colour when damaged. Spore print: White.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs only in some countries of Europe. In Poland the species is rare. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status V – vulnerable. It is also on lists of threatened species in Germany and Lithuania. It occurs more often in mountain areas and can be found in coniferous forests. It grows on the ground among grasses, especially under firs. The fruiting bodies appear from June to September.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: Amanita excelsa. It has a grey-brown cap without yellow patches, white gills, and a scalloped, white ring.
Amanita rubescens Pers. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Amanitaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Flesh-reddish, pale reddish, brown-reddish or light brown with a reddish tinge, up to 15 cm in diameter. The surface is dry, covered with brown-pink patches of various sizes; hemispherical in young specimens, then flatly expanded. Gills: White when young, later with a pinkish bloom, up to 12 mm wide, adnate or decurrent, fairly crowded. When damaged they change colour to brown-reddish. Stem: Initially whitish, later brown-reddish, thickened and bulbous at the base, up to 15 cm high, surrounded by remains of the volva in the form of irregular rolls. It has a striate ring. Flesh: White, fleshy, turns reddish when damaged, brittle, without smell, with a mild taste. Spore print: White. Spores smooth, broadly ellipsoid, measuring 6–7 × 8–10 μm. Similar species: Characteristic of Amanita rubescens are the pinkish tinge, the reddening of the flesh after damage and the lack of distinct striations on the cap. Moreover, in Amanita pantherina there is a folded volva at the base of the stem.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is widely distributed in the Northern Hemisphere. The most numerous described localities are in North America and Europe. It has also been recorded in Africa. In Poland it is very common. It occurs in deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests. It grows on the ground, among moss, especially under birches, beeches, pines and oaks. It produces fruiting bodies from June to November.
Amanita strobiliformis (Paulet ex Vittad.) Bertill. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Amanitaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter up to 20 cm, initially convex, later expanded, depressed in the centre, with a sharp margin. The surface is cream-white to light grey, covered with flaky patches of the same colour or darker. They are soft and delicate, hanging from the margin of the cap. This Amanita can reach very large sizes, so that in cap size it resembles Macrolepiota procera, but it exceeds it 2–3 times in mass. Gills: White-cream, crowded, bulging. Stem: Height up to 15 cm, thickness up to 5 cm, base bulbous-thickened, deeply embedded in the substrate, slightly widening toward the base, firm, the stem solid. The ring is cream, thick. Flesh: White, thick in the fruiting body, smell faint, resembling old ham. Spore print: White. Similar species: It is easy to confuse with Amanita species that have a bulbous base, e.g. Amanita virosa. The most similar is Amanita echinocephala.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In Poland the species is rare. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. It is also on lists of threatened species in Belgium, the Czech Republic, Germany, Denmark, Estonia, the Netherlands, Sweden and Slovakia. It grows in deciduous and mixed forests, also under dwarf mountain pine, on the ground, especially under trees and shrubs such as maple, dwarf mountain pine, linden and arborvitae. It can also be found outside forests, in open areas under single trees and at the edge of roads.
Amanita virosa Bertill. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Amanitaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 6–10 cm, initially oval, later conical-bell-shaped, finally slightly convex. The surface of the cap is smooth, dry and silky, sticky in wet weather. The colour is white and only at the top pale yellow. With age it may turn yellow. On the surface it sometimes has irregular large patches, sometimes it is without patches. Gills: White, crowded, sometimes with ragged edges. Free at the stem. Stem: Height: 8–12 cm, thickness 1–2 cm, cylindrical, narrowed at the top, with a bulbous base. With age it becomes slender. The surface has large fibrous scales. On the stem there is a ring, which, however, may disappear in old specimens. The bulbous base of the stem has a distinct, ragged volva. Flesh: White, brittle, does not change colour when broken. The taste is mild, the smell unpleasant, stifling. Spore print: White. Spores smooth, spherical, measuring 7–10 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Amanita virosa, as described by Elias Fries, came from Sweden. It is known from Europe and East Asia, where its occurrence has been confirmed by genetic tests (e.g. in Jilin Province, China). Nevertheless, the name Amanita virosa has often been wrongly applied to various species occurring in that area, such as Amanita subjunquillea var. alba and Amanita exitialis. The situation is similar in North and Central America, where Amanita virosa does not occur, and most white species of Amanita, such as e.g.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: It can be confused with Agaricus. In very young Agaricus the gills are white, but later they become pink, and in older ones they are chocolate-coloured, which distinguishes these fungi from each other. Thus the danger of confusion concerns only very young Agaricus. Moreover, Amanita virosa has a loose volva on the bulb of the stem, which Agaricus do not have. Amanita verna is very similar, but it has a pure white cap and a smooth stem. There is also a very similar white (albino) form of Amanita phalloides.
Ampulloclitocybe clavipes (Pers.) Redhead, Lutzoni, Moncalvo & Vilgalys is a species of fungus in the family Hygrophoraceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 4–7 cm. Young fruiting bodies are arched with a clearly visible, blunt umbo, with time they become flat, finally concave in the centre. The margin is initially inrolled, later straightened, sharp and thin. The surface is smooth, bare. It is hygrophanous; in dry weather it is light ochre, in wet weather it is coloured from grey-brown to olive-grey. Gills: Crowded and decurrent on the stem, first white, then yellowish. Stem: Height 4–9 cm, thickness 8–18 mm, cottony and soft inside. The base is club-shaped widened and connected to the substrate by white mycelium. The surface is smooth, fibrous, white-grey, cream or light brown. Flesh: White, soft and watery. It does not change colour when damaged. Without distinct taste and without smell, at most with a faint smell of stale flour. Microscopic features: Spore print white. Spores measuring 6–8.5 × 3.5–5 μm, ovoid, elliptical or irregular. The spore surface is smooth, but delicately sculptured under the electron microscope, non-amyloid. No cystidia. Clamp connections occur in the hyphae of the mycelium. Similar species: A characteristic feature of this species is the bulbous-thickened base of the stem.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been described most often in Europe and North America, but it is also known in Korea, Japan and Australia. In Europe it is widely distributed, occurring from Spain to the northern edges of the Scandinavian Peninsula and Iceland. In Poland it is common. It grows on the ground in coniferous, deciduous and mixed forests, in juniper thickets, on wasteland. Fruiting bodies appear from May to November among grasses and fallen leaves. On old specimens of Ampulloclitocybe clavipes another fungus growing on fungi sometimes occurs – Volvariella surrecta.
Apioperdon pyriforme (Schaeff.) Vizzini is a species of fungus in the family Lycoperdaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Height 2–7 cm, diameter up to 3 cm, pear-shaped or club-shaped. The surface is rough, mealy, very finely warty. At the top there are small, low spines that persist for a long time. The colour ranges from white-ochre through grey-nut to grey-ochre, the upper part of the fruiting body usually brownish. The endoperidium is rough, as if mealy, brittle, with very fine warts. It ranges in colour from white-cream to light brown, with a copper tinge in young fruiting bodies, and in old ones it becomes matt, paper-like. Only very young fruiting bodies are white; they quickly change to a darker colour. At the top there is a mound on which, in mature fruiting bodies, a small opening forms through which the spores escape. Initially this opening is round, later its edges become increasingly ragged. At the base of the fruiting body there are whitish, fairly thick rhizomorphs penetrating the substrate. Flesh: Divided into gleba and subgleba. The subgleba is fine-celled, white in young fruiting bodies, grey-brown in older ones. The gleba is of a similar colour, in older fruiting bodies it becomes olive-brown and gradually passes into a clearly visible, elongated columella. Spores:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Except for Antarctica and Africa, it occurs commonly on all continents, also on many islands. In Poland it is also common. A terrestrial saprotrophic fungus. It grows on dead wood, both coniferous and deciduous, on lying trunks and stumps, sometimes seemingly on the ground, in reality on buried wood. It usually grows in large, dense groups. It produces fruiting bodies from June to October.
Armillaria gallica Marxm. & Romagn. is a species of fungus in the family Physalacriaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 2.5–10 cm, conical in young specimens, later convex, finally flat. The margin of the cap is translucent, inrolled in young specimens. It is hygrophanous; when moist it ranges in colour from pink-brown to flesh-brown, when dry it is lighter. On the surface it has concentrically arranged scales and flocks of a colour similar to the cap. They are 1–1.5 mm long and usually persist for a long time on the surface of the cap. Gills: Adnate or shortly decurrent, whitish in young specimens, then light pink with rusty-red spots. Stem: Height 4–10 cm, thickness up to 1.8 cm. It is cylindrical with a bulb-like widened base from which numerous rhizomorphs grow. It has a woolly ring, sometimes fairly thick and persistent, with yellowish flocks on the underside, but sometimes it disappears. The surface of the stem is the same colour as the cap. Below the ring there are numerous flocculose veil remnants of a colour from yellowish to orange-yellow. Flesh: White, turning pink with age, with a mushroomy smell. The taste is initially mild, then acrid and unpleasant.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been described in North America, Europe and Japan. In the Polish scientific literature up to 2003, only 3 localities were reported. It is, however, more common – more localities are given by the online "Atlas grzybów". It grows on stumps, trunks and roots of deciduous trees, rarely of coniferous ones. The fruiting bodies grow singly or in small groups; those growing on roots are usually at a greater distance from the trees.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: Armillaria gallica is confused with Armillaria mellea, Armillaria ostoyae or Armillaria tabescens. In mushroom atlases until the 1980s the yellow honey fungus was not distinguished, and all these species were referred to by the name Armillaria mellea. Distinguishing the individual species of Armillaria is difficult, and on the basis of mature fruiting bodies alone often impossible.

Armillaria mellea (Vahl) P. Kumm. is a species of fungus in the family Physalacriaceae, and also a collective name for a complex of small species (the "Armillaria complex", Armillaria mellea sensu lato) separated out in the 1970s from a previously broadly defined species.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 3–13 cm. At first hemispherical, convex, later flattened. When young it is honey-yellow, honey-brown, olive-yellow, then olive-brown, dark red-brown. It is covered with small red-brown, brown or blackish scales, which are darkest and densest in the middle. In old specimens the scales often disappear and the cap is bare. Gills: Initially whitish, later beige-pinkish, yellowish with brownish spots, decurrent, thin. Stem: Height 8–18 cm, thickness 0.5–2.5 cm; yellowish, honey-brown, red-brown, black-brown, paler at the top, slender, cylindrical, curved, with a widened, rough and darker base. The stems of neighbouring fungi are often fused together. It has a broad membranous ring of golden-yellow colour, which in its lower part is covered with yellow fibrils. Flesh: Whitish, pale flesh-coloured, does not change colour when cut, soft and fleshy in young fruiting bodies, tough and fibrous in old ones (especially in the stem). Spore print: White. Spores ellipsoid, smooth, measuring 7–9 × 5–6 µm. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs on all continents except Antarctica and South America. In Central Europe it is common{, in Poland as well. It occurs most often in autumn from September to November, but sometimes it can appear even at the beginning of August. It usually occurs in groups, sometimes very numerous. It grows on wood (trunks, stumps, branches, roots) of various deciduous tree species in forests, gardens, parks and orchards. Sometimes, when growing on tree roots or on pieces of wood buried in the ground, it gives the impression of growing on the ground.
Armillaria ostoyae (Romagn.) Herink is a species of fungus in the family Physalacriaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 3–8 cm, convex in young specimens, but quickly becomes expanded, and in older specimens concave. The colour is flesh-coloured or red-brown. A characteristic feature is the presence on the cap of blackish-brown, fairly large scales reaching to its margin. Gills: Fairly crowded, initially cream-white, then brown. Stem: Height 4–12 cm, thickness up to 2 cm. It is cylindrical, fibrous, club-shaped, solid and often curved. In older specimens it becomes cottony and hollow inside. In the upper part whitish, lower down rusty and usually with remnants of a whitish sheath and brown fibrils. The ring is fairly thick, white, with dark-coloured scales on the underside and at the edges. Flesh: White, with a pinkish tinge with age, with a mushroomy smell and mild taste. Spore print: White. Spores ellipsoid, smooth, with droplets, measuring 7.5–10 × 5–7 µm. Basidia with clamp connections. Similar species: Mushroom pickers often confuse Armillaria ostoyae with Armillaria mellea or Armillaria tabescens.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been described in North America, Europe and Japan. In Central Europe Armillaria ostoyae is very common, in Poland as well. It grows on coniferous and deciduous trees, mainly on spruce, less often on fir, also on pine and beech. It is common throughout Poland, especially in spruce forests on acidic soil. Sometimes it occurs in such numbers that tree stumps overgrown by Armillaria ostoyae are white from its spores. Armillaria ostoyae is the most frequently occurring species of Armillaria in Poland.
Artomyces pyxidatus (Pers.) Jülich is a species of fungus belonging to the family Auriscalpiaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Bushy, 2–4 cm high, exceptionally up to 8 cm. The bush grows from a single thick trunk, which branches repeatedly upward into ever thinner twigs (as in a candelabrum). The last branching is widened in a cup-like manner, and several small projections grow from the edges of the cup. The twigs are raised upward and fairly dense, so that the bush is compact. The colour ranges from pale flesh-coloured through pale yellow to ochre-yellow. In North America the fruiting body reaches sizes of 4–13 cm in height and 2–10 cm in width. Flesh: Elastic, coloured from whitish to light yellow. When rubbed or damaged it turns brown. The taste is mild or slightly peppery, the smell indistinct, sometimes resembling baked potatoes. Microscopic features: Spore print white. Spores elliptical with a tiny droplet and very finely warted, measuring 4–5 × 2–2.5 μm. Cystidia measuring 50 × 9 μm and of various shapes, sometimes barely protruding.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America, Asia and Europe. In Poland the species is fairly rare. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status V – vulnerable. It is also on lists of threatened species in England, Sweden and Germany. A saprotrophic fungus growing on trees. It grows in forests, on rotting trunks and stumps of deciduous trees (on downy birch, aspen and others), but also on coniferous ones (on Scots pine, on spruce). It produces fruiting bodies from June to October.
Athelia arachnoidea (Berk.) Jülich is a species of fungus in the family Atheliaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Thallus: It forms a thin, membranous, white, spread-out thallus with an indistinct margin and a smooth hymenophore. It does not form fibres. It forms sclerotia. Microscopic features: Hyphal system monomitic. Hyphae colourless, thin-walled, with scattered clamp connections. Hyphae in the subhymenium are 3–5 μm wide and have no clamp connections. No cystidia. Basidia measuring 20–30 × 5–7 μm. Basidiospores ellipsoid to narrowly ovoid, thickened, measuring 10–8(11) × 4.5–5.5 μm, smooth, thin-walled, colourless. However, it produces basidiospores only rarely.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is widely distributed in North America and Europe, and also recorded in Puerto Rico in Central America and in Morocco in North Africa. In Europe it is widely distributed and fairly common; in Poland it is common. Athelia arachnoidea occurs in forests and parks on the bark of deciduous and coniferous trees, both dead and living. It also develops as a parasite on the thallus of lichens and algae growing on tree trunks (for this reason it is classed among lichenicolous fungi). It also causes rhizoctoniosis of carrot. Sometimes it occupies the entire surface of the trunk.
Aureoboletus projectellus (Murrill) Halling is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae. It occurs in North America, and in Europe as an alien species.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Initially convex, never flattening completely, it reaches a diameter of 4–20 cm. The surface is dry, matt, reddish with a characteristic "frill" on the edge of the cap. In young fruiting bodies the colour of the cap is dark brown to cinnamon. Stem: The stem reaches 7–15 cm, relatively long, resembling a Leccinum more than a bolete, yellow or peach-coloured, strongly furrowed with a ribbed surface. Flesh: It has a pinkish tinge, and this colour does not change under the influence of oxygen (oxidation). Tubes: They range in colour from bright yellow to yellow-green. The taste is slightly sour. Spore print: Olive-brown.

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: Aureoboletus projectellus occurs naturally in North America. The first reports of its presence in Europe come from Lithuania. According to reports from local mushroom pickers it was found as early as the 1980s, but these reports were officially confirmed only on the basis of specimens found in 2007–2009. Its migration northward and westward was subsequently observed.
Auricularia auricula-judae (Bull.) Quél. is a species of fungus in the family Auriculariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Diameter 2–10 cm, shape initially goblet-like, later cup-shaped, finally disc-shaped and expanded. Sometimes it resembles an ear in shape. The fruiting body is bent and veined-ribbed. The upper surface is brown, matt, delicately suede-like, and sometimes frosted. The spores are formed on the lower surface, which is red-brown and shiny, smooth, and whitish from spores in mature fruiting bodies. In wet weather the fruiting body is gelatinous and translucent. In dry weather the fruiting bodies may dry out and are then cork-like or horn-like, and their inner side takes on a colour from blackish-brown through brown-violet to blackish-grey. However, after prolonged rain they soak up water again and regain their gelatinous consistency and resilience. Flesh: Thin, gelatinous-elastic, without smell, with a mild taste. Spore print: White, non-amyloid. Spores measuring 16–23 × 6–7 µm. Similar species: Auricularia auricula-judae can be confused with Auricularia mesenterica, which has a hairy-zoned upper surface.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A cosmopolitan species. Apart from Antarctica it occurs on all continents, and also on many islands. In Poland it is common. A parasitic or saprotrophic fungus growing on trees. It develops on weakened or dead wood in forests, thickets, parks, gardens and by roads. It is most often found on elder, but also on many other deciduous tree species (especially on maples and alders), and exceptionally on coniferous ones. It grows throughout the year, also during a mild winter, and occurs from late spring onward on stumps and trunks.
Auricularia mesenterica (Dicks.) Pers. is a species of fungus in the family Auriculariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Gelatinous, soft, somewhat leathery, when dry hard and cartilaginous, attached flat; the margin is mostly spreading, pale, grey-brown and coarsely hairy, on the underside grey to purple-brown; somewhat folded, furrowed and ribbed.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In Poland the species is rare. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. It is also on lists of threatened species in Germany. Sometimes it covers a large area throughout the year, but it mostly develops in late autumn and in winter on living deciduous trees, and after their death it continues to grow for some time.
Auriscalpium vulgare Gray is a species of fungus in the family Auriscalpiaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter up to 5 cm, shape flattened, kidney-shaped or semicircular. It is hairy or felty and slightly zoned. The margin of the cap is lighter. The colour is grey-brown to black. Specimens that have overwintered have a rather inconspicuous blackish-brown colouring and are often covered with green algae. Stem: Lateral or eccentric, up to about 8 cm long. Sometimes branched, brown-black in colour, hairy, thin. Spines: Up to 3 mm long, pale and after a short time grey-brown, ending on the stem. Flesh: From grey-brown to whitish, fibrous-elastic, without a distinct smell. Spore print: White, amyloid. Spores elliptical or ovoid-spherical, warted, colourless, measuring 4–5.5 × 4–4.5 µm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A species widely distributed in North and Central America, Europe and Asia, in areas with a temperate climate. In Poland fruiting bodies appear from January to December, in pine and mixed forests. It grows almost exclusively on fallen pine cones, especially those that are at least partly buried in the ground. Only rarely can it be found on spruce cones. A commonly occurring species, though because of its small size not very often noticed.
Baeospora myosura (Fr.) Singer is a species of fungus in the order Agaricales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: A small fungus with a cap diameter usually 8–22 mm. In young specimens the cap is hemispherical, then convex, finally flat, sometimes with a small bump in the centre. The surface is smooth, matt; when moist the gills show through slightly to half of the cap diameter. The margin is straight, sharp and delicately, radially fibrillose. Gills: Narrowly adnate to the stem or almost free, very crowded. Whitish in colour, with brown spots in older ones. They are 1–2 mm wide and have smooth edges. Stem: Height 1.5–5 cm, thickness 1–2 mm, equal in thickness, solid. The surface is densely and finely dusted with white granules. In the upper part it ranges in colour from pale cream to pale brown, in the lower part it is darker – pinkish-brown or yellowish-brown. The stem is often rooting at the base with white rhizomorphs and overgrown with white hairs. Flesh: The same colour as the surface of the cap. It has a faint mushroomy smell and taste. Microscopic features: Spore print white. Spores smooth, elliptical and almost cylindrical, amyloid, measuring 3–4 × 1.5–2 μm. Pleurocystidia and cheilocystidia thickened, spindle-shaped, up to 40 μm long and up to 10 μm wide.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been described in North America, Europe and Korea and Japan. In Poland it is rare. It occurs in coniferous and mixed forests. It grows on fallen pine cones, less often spruce cones, often buried in the substrate. It produces fruiting bodies from August to November.
Xylodon radula (Fr.) Ţura, Zmitr., Wasser & Spirin is a species of fungus belonging to the family Schizoporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Annual. It is flatly spread out, initially round in shape, thin and tightly adhering to the substrate. The consistency is fairly woody, the surface initially white, then light yellow, finally yellow. The margin remains white; through a lens one can see that it is fringed. The hymenophore is spiny. The spines are conical, blunt, up to 5 mm long and 1–2 mm wide, of the same colour as the fruiting body. They have a rough, lumpy surface. Microscopic features: Hyphal system monomitic. Hyphae thin-walled, only in the middle part of the spines slightly thickened. They are 3–4 μm wide, densely branched and tangled in the subhymenium, otherwise rather straight. Septa few, all with clamp connections. Cystidia few, more often found in mature fruiting bodies. They are cylindrical with constrictions, with homogeneous contents, measuring 50–70 × 5 μm. Basidia almost club-shaped or cylindrical, with 4 sterigmata and a clamp connection at the base. They measure 20–25 × 4–6 μm. Spores hyaline, sausage-shaped, thin-walled, smooth, non-amyloid, usually measuring 9–11 × 3–3.5 μm. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in Asia (India, Japan, Korea), Australasia, Europe, and North and South America. In Poland it is moderately common, recorded mainly in the mountains. It occurs in forests, parks and gardens on dead branches, twigs and on wood, mainly of deciduous trees, but also on fir. It develops mainly on bark, but sometimes also on wood. It causes white rot of wood.
Bjerkandera adusta (Willd.) P. Karst. is a species of fungus in the family Phanerochaetaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting bodies: Annual. A single fruiting body is semicircular in shape, but also spread out or spread out and reflexed. Fruiting bodies often occur in large clusters, covering a surface up to 5 m long. A single fruiting body is 2–10 cm wide and about 1 cm thick. It attaches to the substrate by its side. The fruiting bodies usually grow in groups, one above another like roof tiles. The surface is delicately velvety and wrinkled. The colour ranges from ochre-brown to grey-brown. The marginal zone is distinctly lighter, whitish, and only in older fruiting bodies becomes grey-black. Hymenophore: Tubular. Tubes 4–6 mm long, clearly contrasting with the light colour of the flesh. They are separated from the flesh by a grey-blackish line visible on a cross-section of the fruiting body. When pressed the tubes darken. Pores rounded and small; there are 4–6 per mm. The hymenophore ranges in colour from whitish to grey-dark-brown. Flesh: Whitish or cream, thin, leathery and elastic. It has a faint, slightly sour smell. Spore print: Straw-yellow, non-amyloid. Spores ellipsoid, flattened and narrowed on one side. Size 4–5.5 × 2–3 µm. Similar species: Bjerkandera fumosa is similar.

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: It occurs commonly in various types of deciduous and mixed forests. It grows on rotting trunks and stumps, mainly of deciduous trees, particularly often on beech, and very rarely on coniferous trees. The fruiting bodies grow throughout the year.
Bolbitius titubans (Bull.) Fr. is a species of fungus in the family Bolbitiaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: A morphologically variable species. Fruiting bodies developing on a substrate rich in organic compounds are thick and fleshy; fruiting bodies developing on a poorer substrate are thin and delicate. Cap: Diameter 2–5 cm, initially closed, conical, later ovoid, finally flatly expanded. In young fruiting bodies the margin is inrolled, the surface smooth, coloured from golden to egg-yolk-golden. In older fruiting bodies the surface is slippery, light yellow or olive-yellow. In older specimens the cap fades and becomes whitish, brownish only in the centre. Older specimens have a distinctly striate cap margin. Gills: Thin, moderately crowded. In young fruiting bodies they range in colour from whitish to clay-yellow, in older ones ochre-rusty. Stem: Relatively long compared with the diameter of the cap. It is 5–10 cm long and 3–7 mm thick. It is cylindrical, hollow inside, brittle. The surface is smooth, pale yellow, covered with a whitish bloom. Flesh: Thin, yellowish, watery, without distinct smell and taste. Microscopic features: Spore print rusty-brown. Spores elliptical with truncated ends, smooth, with a germ pore. Size: 10–16 × 6–9 μm. Basidia abruptly thickened.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America, Europe, Africa and Australia. In Poland it is common. It grows in places with a large amount of organic compounds (especially nitrogen), usually outside forests in cultivated fields, in gardens, on fertilised meadows, lawns, roadsides, dung heaps. It develops on animal droppings, especially of horses, and on decomposing grass, hay and straw. It produces fruiting bodies from May to November. The development of the fruiting bodies is very fast – their lifespan is 1–2 days, after which they decompose.
Boletus aereus Bull. is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: It is thick and sometimes wrinkled, and its diameter reaches 30 cm. In young specimens it is hemispherical, later convex-flattened, finally flat. The surface is dry, initially suede-like, later smooth and bare, sometimes cracked. The colour ranges from dark brown through chestnut-brown to dark brown. Tubes: They are up to 3 cm long and can be easily separated from the flesh of the cap. In young fruiting bodies they are white, cream, in older ones yellowish-olive, yellow-green, olive-green. Stem: Height 5–12 cm, thickness 2–4 cm. In young specimens the stem is usually swollen, thick, then club-shaped, cylindrical. The surface is pale brown-red with a characteristic reticulation in dark brown. Flesh: White, only brownish under the skin of the cap. Initially it is very firm, later it becomes softer. It does not change colour in the air. It has a mushroomy smell and taste. Spore print: Olive to olive-brown. Spores smooth, spindle-shaped, measuring 13–16 × 4–5 µm. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America, Europe, Korea and Japan. In Europe it occurs mainly in the Mediterranean basin and south-eastern regions of Europe. Outside these regions it is rare. In Poland the species is very rare. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status E – endangered, critically threatened. It is also on red lists of threatened species in the Czech Republic, Germany, Denmark, Lithuania, Norway and the Netherlands. A thermophilic species. The fruiting bodies grow from May to September.
Boletus edulis Bull. is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: It has a diameter from 6 to 25 centimetres. In young individuals it is usually white, later sandy. With time it becomes light brown and dark brown. It is rare for the cap of Boletus edulis to be carmine in colour. The shape of the cap is initially smooth and hemispherical, later more convex; old specimens are cushion-like expanded. The surface of the cap is matt, sometimes wrinkled; during rain and in older individuals it becomes smooth and sticky. Hymenophore: Small tubes, roundish in cross-section, from 8 to 30 millimetres long. They can be easily separated from the flesh of the cap. The pores and tubes in young fruiting bodies are usually white or cream in colour. In older individuals they are yellowish-olive, yellow-green and olive-green. At the base the hymenophore is sinuately notched. Basidia reach sizes of 32–40 × 10–12 µm, club-shaped with 4 spores. Stem: It has a height from 5 to 20 centimetres, and a thickness from 1.5 to 10 centimetres. It is white, greyish-white or sandy in colour. In young individuals of Boletus edulis the stem is swollen and deeply embedded in the ground, later it elongates, becomes club-shaped and barrel-shaped.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America (mainly west of the Rocky Mountains, less often in the central and eastern part of the continent) and in Europe. It has also been introduced to New Zealand and southern Africa. Boletus edulis occurs in coniferous, deciduous and mixed forests. This fungus forms mycorrhiza with numerous tree species, but mainly with spruces, and therefore it occurs most abundantly in mountain spruce stands. It prefers stands of medium age; in older coniferous stands it gives way to the podgrzyb brunatny.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: Boletus edulis is confused with other species of bolete, until recently regarded rather as its varieties. In Central Europe it is easiest to confuse it with Boletus aereus, which looks almost identical to Boletus edulis. The only feature that differs between these two species is the colour of the cap, which in Boletus aereus is much darker than in Boletus edulis. The similar Boletus reticulatus usually has a cracked cap skin and a darker stem with a more distinct net.
Boletus pinophilus Pilát & Dermek is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 5–30 cm, shape initially hemispherical, then convex-flattened, finally expanded. The surface is delicately felty, usually uneven, bumpy or wrinkled, matt, sticky during rain. It is red-brown in colour, sometimes with a purple or violet tinge. Hymenophore: Tubular. The tubes on young fruiting bodies are pale, on older ones they gradually darken to an olive-yellow colour. Stem: Height 6–16 cm, thickness 3–7 cm, shape initially barrel-shaped, then ovoid, finally club-shaped, covered with a moderately distinct net, whitish at the top, usually reaching the base where it is more brownish. Flesh: White in young fungi (only red-brown under the skin), cream-white with a yellow tinge in older ones. Spore print: Olive. Spores smooth, 14–18 × 5–6 μm, without a germ pore. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in Europe, North America and on the island of Holmvassdalen in the Indian Ocean. It grows mostly under pines, but also under beeches, on acidic soils. Fruiting bodies often appear as early as May and occur until October, most abundantly at the beginning of the season.
Boletus reticulatus Schaeff. is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter up to 25 cm, hemispherical, smooth and dark brown in young specimens, to expanded, cushion-like and lighter in older ones. When it is dry for a longer period, small cracks can be observed on some older specimens. Tubes: Up to 35–40 mm long. White to greyish-white in young fruiting bodies, yellow-green to olive-green in older ones. Sinuately notched at the stem. Pores small, the colour of the tubes. They do not change colour when pressed. Stem: Thickness from 2 to 7 centimetres, height 8–25 cm. Light brown or grey-brown. Covered entirely with a raised net, white when young to brownish in old fruiting bodies, always lighter than the stem. In young specimens the stem is usually barrel-shaped, swollen, then club-shaped. It is also sometimes cylindrical. The mycelium at the base of the stem is white. Flesh: White to cream, brownish under the skin, sometimes slightly yellowish above the tubes; does not change colour in the air. Compact when young, spongy in older individuals. The taste is mild, nutty, the smell pleasant. Spore print: Olive to olive-brown.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Boletus reticulatus occurs in North America, Europe and Asia, and its localities have also been reported in the Republic of South Africa. It is one of the earliest-appearing pored mushrooms. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus. Fruiting bodies mostly from May to early October, even to mid-November. It can be found in deciduous and mixed forests, rarely coniferous ones, and even outside the forest on pond shores, in parks, etc. It forms ectomycorrhiza mainly with oaks (Quercus), beeches (Fagus), hornbeams (Carpinus) and lindens (Tilia).
Byssomerulius corium (Pers.) Parmasto is a species of fungus in the family Irpicaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: It is morphologically variable, but fairly easy to distinguish from similar species because of its parchment-like appearance. It is flat, spread out on the substrate and closely adhering to it, but with margins that bend away. It is thin – 0.2–1 mm thick, but reaches a width and length of even several tens of centimetres. The surface of young fruiting bodies is white, smooth; later the margins bend away from the substrate more and more, and the surface of the fruiting bodies becomes cream, pale yellowish, yellow-ochre, slightly reddish or greyish, irregularly reticulate or porose-pitted. The wrinkles on the surface take on a labyrinthine shape. Microscopic features: Hyphae thin-walled or slightly thick-walled, 2–6 (8) μm wide, straight with septa on which double clamp connections rarely occur. They are weakly encrusted and branch regularly at an acute angle. No cystidia, but basidioles sometimes occur. Basidia long and thickened, narrowed, 4-sterigmate, straight, with septa at the base. They measure 17–40 × 4–6 μm. Spores ellipsoid, cylindrical, straight, sometimes slightly curved.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in Europe, Asia, Africa, Australia, and North, South and Central America. The species is widely distributed in the Northern Hemisphere, but decidedly more often in areas with a temperate climate. In Poland it is very common. It grows on dead, fallen branches of deciduous trees and shrubs. It occurs in forests, parks, thickets, most often in riparian forests, on the banks of rivers and streams. The fruiting bodies are annual. A saprotroph causing white rot of wood.
Caloboletus calopus (Pers.) Vizzini is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 3–15 cm, hemispherical in young specimens, then arched. The margin remains inrolled for a long time. The colour is light brown or grey-olive. The surface is suede-like. Tubes: Long, sinuately notched at the stem; in young specimens they are lemon-yellow, in older ones darker – olive. The pores of the tubes are round, small, and turn blue when crushed. Stem: Height 7–14 cm, thickness 2–4.5 cm. Strong and thick, initially barrel-shaped, then becoming cylindrical or club-shaped. Yellow at the top, carmine-red below. It is entirely covered with a net of delicate lines. Under the cap it is white, in the middle red, at the bottom brown. Flesh: Cream, pinkish near the base of the stem. When cut it changes colour to blue-green. The taste is bitter, the smell faint, sour. Spore print: Ochre-olive. Spores smooth, measuring 12–14 × 4–6 μm. Similar species: Suillellus luridus is similar, but it has orange-red tubes and does not have a red stem. Rubroboletus satanas and Caloboletus radicans have similarly coloured caps.

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: It occurs in North America, Europe and Japan. In Central Europe it is fairly rare. Recently, however, its numbers have increased, probably thanks to a decrease in the amount of sulphur compounds in the air. It occurs mostly in mountain spruce forests and deciduous forests, on acidic soils, mainly under spruces, oaks and beeches. The fruiting bodies appear in summer and autumn. It occurs unevenly; in some areas it is rare, in others common. In Poland it occurs more often in the south, especially at lower mountain elevations.
Caloboletus radicans (Pers.) Vizzini is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 8–15 (up to 30) cm. Hemispherical when young, then somewhat flattened, of a pale, whitish-grey, grey-beige colour. The skin of the cap is suede-like, often cracked. Tubes: Long, up to 15–30 mm, notched. Light yellow when young, later lemon-yellow, olive-yellow with age, turning strongly blue when damaged. Stem: Length up to 13 cm, diameter up to 18 cm. Thickened in the middle part, narrowed at the bottom and ending in a point. Fawn-yellow, lemon-yellow, distinctly turning blue in damaged places. Coloured in the upper part, somewhat paler in the lower. Covered with a delicate net visible only in its upper part. Flesh: Firm, pale yellow, distinctly turning blue on a cross-section. The smell is unpleasant, initially mild, later distinctly bitterish. Spores: Smooth, ellipsoid-spindle-shaped. Spore print: olive-brown. Similar species: Boletus calopus. It differs in its red-coloured stem without a rooting end and its more weakly bluing flesh.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is most widely distributed in Europe, mainly in its southern part. Outside it, its occurrence has been described in China and in a few places in North America and Africa. In Poland the species is rare. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status V – vulnerable species. It is also on the red list of endangered species in Norway. In Poland it is under strict species protection. In Poland up to 2020, 4 historical (old) and 31 contemporary localities were reported. Current localities are also given by the online mushroom atlas. A terrestrial fungus.
Calocybe gambosa (Fr.) Donk is a species of fungus in the family Lyophyllaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 6–12 cm, in young specimens bell-shaped to conical, in older ones arched, finally flatly expanded. The cap is non-hygrophanous, thick-fleshed, usually with a small, blunt umbo; its margin remains inrolled for a long time and is often wavy. The surface is smooth, matt, coloured from whitish to cream. Gills: Thin and crowded, notched with a small tooth at the stem and adnate. Whitish or cream in young specimens, pale ochre in older ones. Stem: Height 4–9 cm, thickness 1.5–4 cm, barrel-shaped in young specimens, cylindrical in older ones. It is firm and solid, the surface smooth, coloured from white to cream, often pale ochre in the lower part. Flesh: Whitish, thick. The taste is mild, the smell of fresh flour. It does not change colour when damaged. Spore print: White. Spores ellipsoid, smooth, measuring 4–7 × 2–3.5 μm. Similar species: It is more pinkish; the danger of confusion exists especially in the case of young specimens, since the gills of both these species are white when young. In older specimens of the wieruszka the gills become pink, and the spore print is also pink, Inosperma erubescens.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs mainly in Europe, but localities have also been reported from the USA and Japan. In Poland the species is common, sometimes forming fairy rings. It grows on the ground on meadows, pastures, forest edges, in gardens, thickets, on grassy slopes, in the lowlands, uplands and foothills. The fruiting bodies appear in spring (from April to June), but exceptionally also in July, and in some years even in late autumn.
Caloscypha fulgens (Pers.) Boud. is a species of fungus in the family Caloscyphaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Of the apothecium (cup) type, initially spherical, but then it splits unevenly, forming a cup with wavy margins. It has a diameter of up to 5 cm. Fruiting bodies often grow close together and as a result of pressure their natural round shape is distorted; moreover, as it develops the cup flattens more and more. Its inner surface is smooth, coloured from yellow to yellow-orange. The outer surface is fibrillose-rough and darker, dark blue in colour with a greenish-blue bloom. Similar discolourations, but to a lesser extent, also occur on the inner surface and on the mycelium growing from the apothecium into the soil. The flesh is brittle, cream, with a mild taste and without smell. Microscopic features: The outer part of the excipulum, about 0.1 mm thick, is made up of swollen hyphae barrel-shaped to spherical in shape, up to 20(–30) µm in diameter and usually covered with resin. The inner part is made up of hyaline, thin-walled hyphae, sometimes branched, with septa, 4–10(–15) µm in diameter.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America (USA, Canada), Europe, Northern Asia and on the Japanese islands. In Poland, M.A. Chmiel cites 7 localities in 2006. More up-to-date and numerous localities are cited by the online mushroom atlas. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status R – a rare species which will probably move to the endangered category in the near future if the threat factors continue to operate. A terrestrial saprotrophic fungus. It occurs in deciduous and mixed forests, mainly in damp places on calcareous substrate.
Calvatia gigantea (Batsch) Lloyd is a species of fungus belonging to the family Lycoperdaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: It is among the fungi forming the largest fruiting bodies. It produces impressive fruiting bodies reaching 10–60 cm in diameter, with a circumference of up to 135 cm, sometimes even more. They are spherical or somewhat flattened, with a cord of white mycelium at the base. The peridium is thin. The exoperidium of young fruiting bodies is white and covered with a mealy bloom; with time it darkens and changes colour to light ochre, finally to leathery-brown. The endoperidium is white, paper-like and during ripening also becomes darker and darker: grey-yellowish, nut-coloured and dirty brown. After ripening the peridium splits in various places over the whole surface and the gleba is exposed. At the base of the fruiting body the gleba is poorly developed and mainly subgleba occurs here; this is also where the fruiting body splits last. The gleba is cottony, compact, denser at the bottom. In young fruiting bodies it is white, as they mature it becomes golden-yellow, grey-yellow, finally olive-brown. After the peridium splits and falls away, the gleba keeps its consistency for a short time, soon becoming powdery. The subgleba is compact, difficult to distinguish from the gleba. Microscopic features:

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: Calvatia gigantea occurs mainly in North America and Europe – on these continents it is widely distributed and its occurrence has been confirmed at many localities. Apart from that it occurs in Taiwan, New Zealand and Singapore. In Poland it is more widespread in the northern part of the country, rarely encountered in the south. The fruiting bodies appear on meadows, pastures, in parks and gardens, on fertile soils rich in nitrogen, as well as on acidic ones. In Poland it was a strictly protected species; since 9 October 2014 it has been removed from the list of protected fungus species.
Cantharellula umbonata (J.F. Gmel.) Singer is a species of fungus in the family Cantharellulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 1.5–4.5 cm, arched when young, later flat, finally funnel-shaped. Sometimes it has a warty umbo in the centre. The surface is matt when dry with adpressed scales, and turns black when moist. The colour is grey-brown or grey, to violet. Gills: Broad and broadly adnate, slightly decurrent on the stem. The colour is white to cream-white. When damaged they turn black after a while. They are crowded and forked at the ends. Stem: Height 3–10 cm, thickness 2–6 mm, cylindrical, solid and brittle. The surface is light grey-brown, covered with longitudinal white fibrils, darker in the upper part, felty at the base. Flesh: Thin, whitish, without distinct taste and smell. When damaged it changes colour to light reddish. Microscopic features: Hyphae in the trama 3.5–5.5 μm in diameter, tangled. The subhymenium is well developed, with hyphae similar to those in the trama, but mostly oriented perpendicular to the hyphae of the trama. Basidia elongated, thickened, smooth, colourless, often containing oil bodies. They have 4 sterigmata and measure 28–35 × 5–6.5 μm. The thin-walled spores measure (7.8-) 8.5–10 (-11.1) × (2.5-) 3–3.5 (-4.2) μm and are narrowly cylindrical to spindle-shaped.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In Europe and North America it is widely distributed. The occurrence of this species has also been reported in Japan. In Germany and the Netherlands it is on lists of threatened species. In Poland it is not common, but it is not threatened. In the scientific literature numerous localities have been described across the whole country. It grows in coniferous and mixed forests, on acidic soil, among moss, especially under spruces. It produces fruiting bodies from August to November.
Cantharellus amethysteus (Quél.) Sacc. is a species of fungus in the family Hydnaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 2–8 cm. In young specimens arched, cushion-like, with time flat, in older specimens it becomes funnel-shaped. At first it has inrolled margins, later it is wavy-bent and lobed. The skin is yellow, but with a violet tomentum, which in older specimens dries and takes the form of small, adpressed scales, especially in the middle of the cap.
