sections.text: Localities have been reported in Europe, North America and Asia. In Europe it is widely distributed. In Poland it was first recorded in 2005. Current localities are given by the online mushroom atlas. It is included there in the list of threatened species worthy of protection.
Exidia nigricans (With.) P. Roberts is a species of fungus in the family Auriculariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Grey when young, spherical or cup-shaped, later brain-like and folded; the upper surface delicately dotted, dark, grey-brown to black. When moist it is soft and translucently gelatinous inside; when dried it becomes hard, crust-like. After rehydration it swells again and becomes gelatinous again. Each individual fruiting body is attached to the substrate. Neighbouring fruiting bodies merge with one another, sometimes forming large packets of gelatinous mass. Spores: Cylindrical, curved, with a smooth surface. Size: 9.5–23 × 3.5–7 μm. Flesh: Blackish to brownish, translucent, gelatinous, odourless. Similar species: Exidia pithya. It also has black, gelatinous fruiting bodies, but smaller, flat, and it grows almost exclusively on coniferous trees. Exidia glandulosa. It has single, barrel-shaped or saucer-shaped fruiting bodies, covered with spines on the outer side.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Its occurrence has been reported in Europe and New Zealand. In Europe in the north it reaches the 55.7th parallel of latitude (in the south of the Scandinavian Peninsula). In Central Europe it is common, in Poland as well. The fruiting bodies appear throughout the year, especially in wet weather. It occurs in various types of forests, on dead wood of deciduous trees. It is more common in the lowlands; in the Polish mountains it reaches a maximum height of about 1000 m a.s.l.
Exidia recisa (Ditm.) Fr. is a species of fungus in the family Auriculariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: The fruiting body is spherical, often pitted-folded at the base, gelatinous-soft; young – yellow-brown, old – dark, red-brown, dried – black. From 2 cm in height and width.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In Poland the species is rare. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status V – threatened with extinction. A saprotrophic fungus growing on trees. It occurs in deciduous and mixed forests, in thickets, especially along rivers and streams, on fallen branches of trees and shrubs. It has been observed on grey alder, black alder, bird cherry, aspen, white willow, osier, grey willow, crack willow and linden. The fruiting bodies appear throughout the year.
Exidia glandulosa (Bull.) Fr. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Auriculariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Diameter 2–9 cm, disc-shaped, cup-shaped or goblet-shaped. It has a short, conical stem. The sides of the fruiting body do not stick to the substrate. The surface is matt, black or brown-black, smooth, folded or covered with pits after the fruiting body matures. The flesh is gelatinous and fairly compact, but in rainy weather or at an older age the fruiting bodies become deformed. They may occur singly, or in small clusters (given under the name E. truncata). Microscopic features: Basidia divided transversely, as in jelly fungi (Tremella sp.). Basidiospores cylindrical, curved, 14–17 µm long and 4.5–6 µm in diameter, with a smooth surface, lacking a germ pore. Spore print white, non-amyloid. Similar species: Exidia nigricans is similar; it forms larger fruiting bodies, brain-like folded and without a stem, attached to the substrate by their sides. They quickly become deformed during ripening and form a mass spreading over the substrate. Under the microscope these two species are indistinguishable, but DNA studies have shown that they are different species.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America, Europe, Asia and Australia. In Poland the species is rare. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. It is also on lists of threatened species in Denmark, Norway and Finland. In Poland Exidia glandulosa can be found in deciduous and mixed forests, in parks, on fallen tree branches. It has been observed on fallen branches, stumps and lying trunks of pedunculate oak, sessile oak and linden.
Exidiopsis effusa Bref. is a species of fungus in the family Auriculariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Spread out, closely adhering to the substrate, leathery, thin. The surface is waxy and slightly shiny. Morphologically it is very variable. It takes a shape from circular or oval to irregular. It is hygrophanous; when moist it becomes gelatinous and translucent, when dry it is whitish, pinkish, slightly violet or greyish in colour. The whitish colour comes from spores covering the fruiting body, which are easily rubbed off. After drying it forms a very thin white, red, or grey-white crust. Microscopic features: Hyphae thin (1.5–2.5 μm), all with clamp connections on the septa. Hyphae within the hymenium are branched, and the basidia are embedded in the gelatinous flesh. New hyphae usually grow from the base of the basidia. Hyphidia are 0.5–1.5 μm wide, weakly branched and occur together with the basidia or above them; in older fruiting bodies they become gelatinous and difficult to distinguish. Basidia have an ovoid, elliptical or pear-shaped form, a size of 16.0 × 10.0 μm and four sterigmata. The sterigmata are tubular, winding and very long, so that they can reach the surface. Basidiospores measure 10.5–15 × 3.5–4.5 μm. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is recorded in many countries of Europe and in Taiwan. In Poland it occurs fairly often. It occurs in deciduous and mixed forests on dead wood; on trunks and fallen branches of deciduous trees, especially on common beech, less often on silver birch.
Fistulina hepatica (Schaeff.) With. is a species of fungus in the order Agaricales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Annual, 10–20 cm wide, 2–6 cm thick. Initially knobby, then cushion-shaped, finally spatula-shaped, semicircular, kidney-shaped. The upper surface is slightly radial, striate and warty, pink, orange-red when young, later blood-red to purple-brown. Young caps, secreting abundant blood-like juice, resemble an animal's liver to an illusion. Flesh: 2–6 cm thick, soft and fleshy when young, full of blood-red juice, flesh-red with marbled veins, with a pleasant smell and a sourish taste. Tubes: 10–15 cm long, compact and dense, whitish, yellowish, later rusty-brown. Pores small, spherical, 0.2–0.3 mm in diameter. Stem: Lateral, short, 2–4 cm long, barely noticeable. Spore print: White. Spores ovoid, smooth, colourless, measuring 4–6 × 3–4 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in Australia, North, Central and South America, Asia and Europe. In the scientific literature for Poland, about 250 localities were reported up to 2020. More up-to-date localities are given by the online mushroom atlas. The species is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. It is also on lists of threatened species in Norway, Finland, Sweden and Lithuania.
Fomes fomentarius (L.) Fr. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Polyporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Up to 50 cm wide, initially bulbous, later hoof-shaped. On the upper side it is covered with a hard, non-cracking crust. In young specimens it is velvety, in older ones bare and matt. In young specimens it is clay-coloured or red-brown, in older ones grey or blackish. On the crust concentric rings are visible, which are zones of annual growth. The margin of the cap is whitish and blunt. Tubes: Arranged in many layers, 2–7 cm long. Initially light orange, later orange-brown, finally ochre-brown. They darken when pressed. Flesh: 0.5–3 cm thick. It is rusty-brown, soft, cork-woody, in the cap it has a suede-like structure, at the point of attachment vegetative mycelium. Spore print: In May and June it releases white, dust-like spores. The spore print is non-amyloid. Spores oblong-elliptical, smooth, measuring 15–20(24) × 5.5–6.5 µm. Similar species: Fomitopsis pinicola. It has a brighter growth zone (yellow or orange-red) and red-brown flesh. Older specimens of it are morphologically difficult to distinguish, since they no longer have such a bright margin.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs only in the Northern Hemisphere: in North America, Europe and Asia. From equatorial regions it is known only from Panama in Central America. In Poland it is very common across the whole country. A perennial species. It occurs throughout the year, on trunks of old, weakened deciduous trees, in particular beeches or birches. It is very common. It can be found in all types of forests, also in riparian forests, where it occurs on poplar.
Fomitiporia punctata (P. Karst.) Murrill) is a species of fungus in the family Hymenochaetaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: The fruiting body adheres closely to the substrate, sometimes covers a large area and is coloured to match the tree species on which it occurs. Initially it is flat, but every year it produces a new, cushion-like, dark spore-bearing layer, as a result of which it gradually becomes more and more convex, cushion-shaped. It reaches a width of 2–30 cm and a thickness of up to 2.5 cm. The fruiting bodies usually occur singly, less often in groups of two or three fruiting bodies. They have a surface coloured from cinnamon-reddish to chestnut-brown. The margin of the fruiting body is clearly demarcated from the substrate, downy-felty in young specimens. Hymenophore: Tubular, brown in young individuals, grey-brown in older ones. The tubes are 5–6 mm long and the fruiting body may have up to 10 layers of them, one on top of another. The pores are so small that they are not visible to the naked eye. They have oblique openings, slightly mouldy. In the hymenium there are few and poorly developed setae, sometimes none at all. Flesh: Dark, red-brown; very fibrous and tough. Spores: Roundish, pointed on one side, thick-walled, hyaline. Size 6–8 × 5–7 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is recorded in North, Central and South America, Europe, Asia and New Zealand. In Poland it is common. It is common in deciduous forests and thickets, especially in riparian forests. It attacks fully healthy trees. The fruiting bodies ripen in autumn. In Poland it has been recorded on the following tree species and genera: willow, grey alder, hornbeam, hazel, common ash, aspen, oak, elder, elm.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: Phellinus laevigatus has a cracked surface, covered with bumps and warts, and is grey to grey-black. Phellinus conchatus is dark brown and often overgrown with moss.
Fomitopsis betulina (Bull.) B.K. Cui, M.L. Han & Y.C. Dai is a species of fungus in the family Fomitopsidaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: An annual fruiting body 10–30 cm in diameter, attached by its side to the trunk and narrowed at the point of attachment. On the upper side greyish-white to brownish, covered with a matt, cracking and peeling skin. The shape is hemispherical or cushion-shaped. Tubes: They are 1.5–5 (exceptionally up to 8) mm long, white in young specimens, straw-yellow in older ones. The pores are round. The tubes of mature fruiting bodies can be easily separated from the flesh of the cap. The taste is astringent, slightly bitterish. Flesh: White, uniformly compact on a cross-section, non-fibrous, tough. After drying it becomes cork-like. Spore print: White, non-amyloid. Spores cylindrical and comma-shaped with a sharply ended base, measuring 5–7 × 1.5–2 µm. They have a smooth surface and usually two guttules inside.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs across the whole Northern Hemisphere. In Poland it is common everywhere. Young fruiting bodies grow from August to October, dead specimens can be found throughout the year. It grows exclusively on birches, which makes it easy to distinguish from other species. It can be found in forests, parks, by roads. In the forest it grows on birches, often at a great height. It can also be found outside the forest on utility wood, e.g. on posts, fences etc. made of birch. Sometimes the fungus Hypocrea pulvinata is parasitic on its fruiting bodies.
Fomitopsis pinicola (Sw.) P. Karst. is a species of fungus in the family Fomitopsidaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Habit: A bracket fungus with a perennial fruiting body attached by its side to a tree (living or dead). Fruiting body: The width reaches up to 40 cm, the thickness up to 15 cm. Young specimens have a flattened fruiting body, older ones a thicker, hoof-shaped one. Older fruiting bodies are covered with a hard grey-brown skin with a lighter growth zone. During great heat the skin melts. The growth zone is whitish, orange to cherry-coloured in young ones, darker and narrower in older ones. Tubes: On the lower side of the fruiting body there are several layers of tubes, up to 8 mm long in each layer, cream to yellowish in colour. With age the underside of the fruiting body becomes brown. The pores of the tubes are round, regular. The hymenophore turns cream when crushed, or on old fruiting bodies. However, the age of the fruiting body cannot be determined from the number of tube layers, since in the course of a year it may produce from one to several of these layers. Flesh: Wood-coloured or lemon-yellow to yellow-brown, turns slightly pink when damaged. It tastes bitter. Spore print: White. Spores smooth and colourless, elliptical or oblong-ovoid, measuring 6–8 × 3–4 μm. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs only in the Northern Hemisphere, in North America, Europe and Asia. In Central Europe it is common. In Poland it is also common. It occurs commonly on coniferous trees, most often on Scots pine and Norway spruce, less often on silver fir and European larch.
Rhodofomes roseus (Alb. & Schwein.) P. Karst. is a species of fungus in the family Fomitopsidaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Habit: A bracket fungus with a perennial, persistent fruiting body, usually attached by its side to a tree. Fruiting body: The width reaches up to 8 cm, the thickness up to 3 cm. The fruiting bodies usually occur in groups of several, sometimes fusing with one another. They are hemispherical or hoof-shaped, sometimes bracket-shaped, in which case their hymenophore runs down the substrate. The surface is uneven, warty, delicately hairy in young specimens, bare in older ones. Sometimes it is cracked. It is concentrically grooved. Initially it is grey-pink, then darker and darker – from purple-brown to black. The margin is lighter (pinkish) and sterile (without hymenophore), sharp in young specimens, blunt and wavy in older ones. Flesh: Firm, cork-like or woody; when torn it has a flocculose-fibrous structure. It is indistinctly striate. In the fresh state it is salmon-pink in colour, after drying dirty flesh-coloured. Hymenophore: Tubular, initially white-pink in colour, later dirty flesh-coloured. It darkens when pressed. The tubes are 5–7 mm long and form many indistinct layers. The pores of the tubes are angular and small; there are 3–4 (exceptionally up to 5) pores per 1 mm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs mainly in the Northern Hemisphere: in North America, Europe and Asia. Its occurrence has also been recorded on Grenada off the coast of South America and in Australia. In the scientific literature for Poland, 70 localities were reported up to 2020. It is much rarer than Fomitopsis pinicola, and is common only in the Białowieża Forest. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status E – an endangered species whose survival is unlikely if the threat factors continue to operate. In the 1980s.
Galerina marginata (Batsch) Kühner is a species of fungus belonging to the family Galerinaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 1.5–5 cm, initially hemispherical, later convex, finally flat. It usually has a blunt, broad umbo. It is strongly hygrophanous; when dry it is coloured from pale beige to yellow-ochre, in wet weather it becomes ochre-brown or red-brown. When drying it lightens from the top. In wet weather radial striations are visible, in dry weather the striations are invisible. Gills: Slightly ventricose, broadly adnate and notched with a tooth at the stem. Their colour is initially ochre-brown, later rusty-brown, the edges of the gills are lighter. Stem: Height 2–8 cm, thickness 0.1–0.6 cm. Cylindrical, hollow inside. It has a fugacious ring zone, above which it is ochre and mealy-dusted, below it is brownish and covered with longitudinal, silvery-white fibrils, and at the base it is darker (coloured from olive-brown to black). Flesh: Light ochre in the cap, umber-brown in the stem. The taste and smell are mealy with an admixture of radish. Spore print: Rusty-brown. Spores elliptical, with a rough or wrinkled surface, measuring 7–11 × 4–6 μm. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Galerina marginata is widely distributed across the whole Northern Hemisphere. In Central Europe it is common, in Poland as well. It grows on the wood of dead trees and on forest litter. Older mushroom atlases stated that it grows only on the wood of coniferous trees, but this is untrue. In the mountains it is indeed most often met under spruces, but in the lowlands it grows mainly on beech wood. It usually occurs in groups, smaller or larger. The fruiting bodies appear from August to the first frosts.
Ganoderma adspersum (Schulzer) Donk is a species of fungus belonging to the family Polyporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Perennial, hoof-shaped or semicircular, 10–30 cm in size, 4–10 cm thick. It is attached by its side. The cap on its upper surface is matt, red-brown, in older specimens brown-black. Its surface is strongly undulating and knobby, sometimes with distinct zones. The margin of the cap is rounded and pure white. The skin is hard and cannot be dented with a finger. Tubes: Small, round, white, turning brown when pressed. On older specimens they become brown. The length of the tubes is 10–15 mm. Flesh: Chocolate-brown or chestnut-brown. It is fibrous, cork-like and hard. Its thickness is several times greater than the length of the individual tubes and the annual growth zones are distinctly marked. Spore print: Red-brown. Microscopic features: Spores 6.5–8 μm. Similar species: Ganoderma pfeifferi Bres. The fruiting body is unzoned, copper-red or rusty-purple in colour, and the pores become yellowish with time. It grows on deciduous trees, mainly on beech. Ganoderma resinaceum Boud. The fruiting body is brick-red or almost black and sometimes shiny. It grows on deciduous trees, mainly on oak.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Ganoderma adspersum is recorded in North and South America, Europe and Asia. Most localities have been described in Europe. In the scientific literature for Poland numerous localities have been reported. It occurs in parks, in forests and by roads, mainly on deciduous trees. It is fairly rare. On coniferous trees it occurs rarely. It grows on living trees, but after their death it continues to grow for several years. In Poland it has been recorded on the following trees: Acer dasycarpum, horse chestnut, silver birch, plum, oak, small-leaved linden, elm.
Ganoderma applanatum (Pers.) Pat. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Polyporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Perennial, hoof-shaped or semicircular, 10–50 cm in size, 1–5 cm thick. It is attached by its side. The cap on its upper surface is coloured from red-brown to brown-grey. It is covered with a hard crust with a strongly zoned, undulating and knobby surface. It is often covered with a thick, rusty-brown layer of spores, which not only fall downward but, owing to air turbulence, also settle on the upper surface of the fruiting body. The margin of the cap is pure white, knobby and flattened. The surface is smooth, sometimes slightly shiny, but without a lacquered coating. Tubes: 5–10 mm long, round, white, turning brown when pressed. On a cross-section they form several layers, which are separated by a thin intermediate layer of brown colour. Urn-shaped galls of the fly Aganthomyia wankowiczi often occur on the pores. So far galls of this fly have not been observed on any other species of fungus. Galls may form on the hymenophore at the place where these insects feed. Flesh: Fairly soft, elastic, whitish in young fruiting bodies, later cinnamon-brown to dark brown. It darkens when pressed, and under the action of KOH it turns black.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A cosmopolitan species, occurring on all continents except Antarctica, also on many islands. In Poland it is common. Everywhere except in the higher mountain locations it is very common. It grows on living trees, on dead trunks and stumps. It can be found in the forest, but also in thickets, parks, by roads. The fruiting bodies grow throughout the year. It grows mainly on deciduous trees, rarely on coniferous ones.
Ganoderma carnosum Pat. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Polyporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Annual, of the bracket-fungus type, reaching a size of 3–18 × 5–22 × 14 cm. It consists of a stem and a cap. The cap is laterally attached, flat, semicircular or kidney-shaped. The upper surface is shiny, as if lacquered, even in young fruiting bodies, undulating, uneven, knobby in older ones, coloured from brown to black. The margin, which is the zone of active growth, is initially white to cream in colour, in older specimens it is brown. The stem is conical, often flattened, irregularly bent, 1–10 cm long and 0.7–4 cm thick. It is mostly lateral, rarely central, shiny like the cap, and coloured from brown to black. The context in the cap and stem is initially whitish to cream, then pale brown, soft and cork-like, up to 3.5 cm thick. After drying it is light. The hymenophore is tubular, whitish in young fruiting bodies, then cream, finally brownish. The tube layer is up to 2.5 cm thick and coloured from light brown to cocoa, separated from the stem by a groove. Pores number 3–4 per 1 mm. Microscopic features: The hyphal system in the context is trimitic. Generative hyphae hyaline, thin-walled, with clamp connections, 3–6 μm in diameter.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Ganoderma carnosum is recorded mainly in North America and Europe, and also at single localities in Morocco and Japan. Everywhere it is rare. In Europe it occurs in England; through Central Europe its range reaches the Carpathians in Ukraine, and it occurs scattered along the Mediterranean Sea and the North Sea. The localities furthest to the north are in southern Denmark and in Estonia. In the scientific literature for Poland many of its localities have been reported, but it is rare. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland.
Ganoderma lucidum (Curtis) P. Karst. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Polyporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 8–25 cm in diameter, flat, semicircular or kidney-shaped. Initially light, lemon-yellow, with age it fairly quickly changes colour to yellow-red, later darkens to purple, purple-brown, finally reddish-blackish. The surface is uneven, usually furrowed. The margin of the fruiting body is narrow, wavy, white or straw-yellow in colour. The most characteristic feature of this species is the glossy, as if lacquered, surface. Stem: Eccentric or lateral, of irregular, cylindrical shape and covered with bumps. It can be up to 15 cm long and up to 2 cm thick, has a colour similar to the cap and is also glossy. There are, however, forms without a stem, attached by the side, or with only a vestigial stem. Tubes: They usually form one layer, less often two or three. They are 2–20 (30) mm long. The pores are small, round, initially whitish, then cream, brown with age. There are 4–5 per 1 mm. They turn brown when touched. Flesh: Spongy, white, ochre just above the tubes, indistinctly striate, without any specific taste or smell. Microscopic features:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Apart from Antarctica it occurs on all continents, and also on many islands. In Europe it is fairly rare. In Poland about 150 localities were reported up to 2020. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status R – a potentially threatened species because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. It is also on lists of threatened species in the Czech Republic, Lithuania and Latvia. In Poland in 1995–2004 it was under partial protection, in 2004–2014 under strict protection, and since 2014 it is again under partial protection.
Ganoderma resinaceum Boud. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Polyporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Perennial, of the bracket-fungus type, large, reaching a diameter of up to 45 cm. It attaches to the substrate by its side, sometimes only a vestigial stem is present. The shape is semicircular or kidney-shaped. The surface is smooth, shiny or matt, weakly furrowed, yellowish in young fruiting bodies, covered with a thin resinous layer, in older ones darker and darker – brick-chestnut, dark red, and finally almost black. When dried it is often cracked. The margin is blunt, thick, coloured from whitish to cream. The hymenophore is tubular. The tubes are 5–20 mm long, usually forming only one layer, less often 2–5 layers. The pores are small, circular, numbering 2–2.5 per 1 mm. Microscopic features: Hyphal system trimitic. Generative hyphae hyaline, thin-walled, with clamp connections, 2–5 μm in diameter, difficult to observe in dried specimens. Skeletal hyphae abundant, thick-walled, unbranched or with a few branches, 3–5 μm in diameter at the base, sometimes with lateral outgrowths, usually separated from the main axis by simple septa. Binding hyphae long, hyaline or slightly yellowish, 3–5 μm in diameter at the base, with long, lateral light yellow branches.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Ganoderma resinaceum is recorded at numerous localities in North, Central and South America and in Southern and Central Europe and at a few isolated localities in southern Denmark. It is also recorded in Africa (Liberia) and Asia (Japan, the Philippines). In Poland the species is rare. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status R – a potentially threatened species because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. It occurs in parks, in forests and by roads, mainly on living deciduous trees, only sporadically on dead ones.
Geastrum coronatum Pers. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Geastraceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Spherical when young, sometimes somewhat flattened. 1–4 cm in diameter, entirely covered with a thin layer of mycelium. The outer covering splits to half the height of the fruiting body into 6–12 triangular non-hygroscopic lobes, which spread out in a star shape and hold a thick layer of mycelium with the substrate. Spread-out fruiting bodies reach 4–9 cm in diameter. The arms of fresh specimens are brown-grey or dark grey, lighter when dry, greyish or coffee-coloured. The inner covering is inversely pear-shaped, taller than wide, set on a distinct, short and thick neck. At the base of the inner covering there is a distinct apophysis. The apical opening is flat or somewhat raised, fringed, without a saucer, but with a lighter circular area. The interior of the fruiting body is black-brown. Microscopic features: Spore print black-brown. Spores brown, spherical, fairly coarsely warty-spiny, measuring 4–5.5 µm. Similar species: Geastrum coronatum can be confused with Geastrum pectinatum, whose spherical head is comb-like furrowed at the bottom.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In Poland it is fairly rare. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status V – a species vulnerable to extinction>. It is also on lists of threatened species in Austria, Denmark, Estonia, the Netherlands, Sweden and Lithuania. In Poland it was a strictly protected species; since 9 October 2014 it is no longer on the list of protected species. Proposed status: LC. It grows from August to November, old fruiting bodies can be observed almost all year round. It occurs in deciduous and coniferous forests, parks and gardens; rare, in some areas not encountered at all.
Geastrum fimbriatum Fr. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Geastraceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting bodies: Spherical, sometimes somewhat flattened, up to 2 cm in diameter. In mature ones the outer covering tears into 7–8 (up to 10) arms arranged in a star shape, which spread out and bend downward. The arms are fleshy, initially white-ochre, then beige to light ochre. Developed fruiting bodies reach a diameter of 2 to 8 cm. The inner covering of the fruiting body is of the same colour as the arms, 1.5–2 cm in diameter, sessile, without a neck. The opening at the top (peristome) is flat or slightly raised, fringed, without a saucer. The interior of the fruiting body is dark, grey-brown. Spores: Roundish, slightly warty. Similar species: Geastrum fimbriatum may be confused with Geastrum rufescens, which differs in its reddish flesh and larger fruiting bodies.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In the Polish mycological literature very many of its localities across the whole country have been reported. It is the most frequently encountered of all earthstars. It was, however, included in the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland of 2006 with the status R (potentially threatened species). In 2015 the species was given the status LC (least concern). It is on lists of threatened species in Norway. In Poland it was under strict protection from 9 October 2014 and is no longer on the list of protected species. Habitat: deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests.
Geastrum rufescens Pers. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Geastraceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Spherical, somewhat flattened, conically raised at the top, 2–5 cm in diameter. Entirely surrounded by a thin layer of ochre-brown to red-brown mycelium, which also grows through soil particles. The outer covering (ectoperidium) splits from the top to the middle of the fruiting body into 5–6 (up to ten) triangular, unequal arms, which spread out and then curve under the fruiting body. In the dried state they can bend back and cover the endoperidium again. Developed fruiting bodies reach a diameter of 3–8 cm. The arms are initially flesh-pink, later red-brown, after drying covered with small cracks. The inner covering (endoperidium) is up to 3 cm in diameter, roundish, somewhat raised at the top, light ochre to brownish, sessile, although in dry fruiting bodies a small neck may be outlined. The apical opening (peristome) has an uneven, fringed margin, is flat, without a saucer. The columella is fairly persistent, reaching at least to the middle of the endoperidium. The gleba is brown. Microscopic features: Spores spherical, up to 4.5 μm in diameter, light brown, rough, covered with low warts (up to 14 warts around the circumference). The hyphae of the capillitium are up to 9 μm thick. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs on all continents except Antarctica and Australia (but it is present in New Zealand). In Poland it is rare and is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status E – a species critically threatened with extinction. It is also on lists of threatened species in Norway, the Netherlands and Lithuania. In Poland it was a strictly protected species; since 9 October 2014 it is no longer on the list of protected species. Proposed status: LC. It grows in deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests, in thickets. It appears singly or in small groups.
Geastrum striatum DC. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Geastraceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting bodies: Closed when young, roundish, somewhat raised at the top, 1.5–4 cm in diameter. The surface is covered with remains of the mycelial substrate. The outer covering splits halfway into 6–10 triangular arms, which spread out and then curl under, as a result of which the fruiting body takes on a star-like shape. With the arms bent back it reaches a diameter of 4–6.5 (9) cm. The inner covering is strongly flattened, light, covered with a spongy bloom in young fruiting bodies. At the base there is a distinct apophysis with a sharp edge directed downward. The neck is distinct, 0.4–0.6 cm high. The apical opening (peristome) is up to 0.5 cm high, initially covered with a mealy bloom, later comb-like, with 16–20 notches, surrounded by a small ridge or without a ridge. Microscopic structure: The columella is well developed, reaching even to the top of the fruiting body. Spores spherical, measuring 4.3–6 μm. On the surface they are covered with warts (about 13 in number). The hyphae of the capillitium are up to 6.5 μm thick.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: W. Wojewoda in 2003 cites 10 localities for G. striatum. For the synonym G. schmidelii, 46 localities were reported up to 2020. Both under the name G. striatum and under G. schmidelii it is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status E – an endangered species. It is also on lists of threatened species in Denmark, Austria, Finland, Norway, the Netherlands and Lithuania. In Poland G. striatum was a strictly protected species; since 9 October 2014 it is no longer on the list of protected species.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: Geastrum striatum may be confused with Geastrum pectinatum, from which it differs in the apophysis. In Geastrum striatum the apophysis has a sharp edge directed downward. It forms a kind of collar at the base of the endoperidium.
Gloeophyllum sepiarium (Wulfen) P. Karst. is a species of fungus in the family Gloeophyllaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Up to 3 cm thick and up to 10 cm across. Usually grows attached by its side and is semicircular, circular, spread out, or sometimes bracket-like. The surface is reddish-brown to tobacco-brown, and the outer, fresh growth zone is orange-yellow. It is wavy-furrowed and zoned, bristly-haired when young and bare in older specimens. Hymenophore: Variable; usually gilled, sometimes gill-like with pores, or poroid. The gills are often joined by cross-connecting anastomoses. Colour from yellowish through orange and rusty to rusty-brown. Flesh: Thin, dark brown, leathery and flexible. Taste mild or slightly bitter. Spore print: White. Microscopic features: Spores cylindrical and flattened on one side, smooth and colourless. Size: 9–12 × 3–4.5 μm. Hyphal system trimitic; skeletal hyphae thick-walled, golden-brown; binding hyphae sparse, thick-walled, light golden-brown, twisted, with clamp connections. Generative hyphae thin- to thick-walled with clamp connections.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North America, Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia. In Central Europe it is a very common fungus, and so it is in Poland. The fruiting body is annual or perennial. It grows on dead wood of conifers, especially spruce; on trunks and stumps. It very often attacks wooden structures such as fences, bridges, pergolas, telegraph poles, house frames, railway sleepers and the like.
Gomphidius glutinosus (Schaeff.) Fr. is a species of fungus in the family Gomphidiaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 4–15 cm in diameter; in young specimens blunt-conical, later hemispherical, arched, and finally flat and concave in the centre or even funnel-shaped. The margin is always rolled under. The surface is smooth and covered with slime (it dries out during drought). Young fruiting bodies are violet-grey or grey-brown, older ones chocolate-brown, and finally ochre. Slimy remnants of the veil often hang from the cap margin. Gills: Distant, of varying length, running down the stem. Whitish in young specimens, darker in older ones. Stem: 2–5 cm tall, up to 3 cm thick, cylindrical, solid, slippery. It has a disappearing ring. The surface is whitish, yellow in places toward the base. Remnants of the slimy veil under the cap. Flesh: Brownish under the cap, lemon-yellow in places in the lower part, whitish elsewhere. Mild taste and faint smell. Spore print: Black. Microscopic features: Spores elongated, smooth, measuring 18–22 × 5–8 μm. Similar species: Gomphidius maculatus, which occurs under larches. It differs slightly in cap colour (flesh-ochre to brownish flesh-coloured) and is covered with dark brown spots; also Chroogomphus helveticus.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs across the whole Northern Hemisphere in the temperate climate zone. In Poland it is a rare species. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland, with status R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus. It grows in coniferous or mixed forests, almost exclusively under spruce, very rarely under other tree species (hornbeam, linden). Most often found on acidic, not very moist soils, especially where bilberries are present. Fruiting bodies appear from July to November.
Gomphidius roseus (Fr.) Fr. is a species of fungus in the family Gomphidiaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 3–6 cm in diameter; hemispherical in young specimens, later cushion-shaped, and flat with a depression in the centre in older ones. The cap margin stays rolled under for a long time. It is dry in dry weather and slippery in wet weather. Pink through grey-pink to bright red. Gills: In young specimens they are covered by a slimy veil. They are distant and thick with straight edges, running down the stem. At first white, later turning grey from the spores. Stem: 2–5 cm tall, up to 3 cm thick. Cylindrical and solid, with a fairly quickly disappearing and indistinct ring. Above the ring it is white, in the lower part yellow, and it is slippery all over. Flesh: Whitish in the cap, yellowish in the stem. Taste and smell indistinct. Spore print: Dark brown or black. Microscopic features: Spores 15–20 × 4–5.5 µm, olive-brown, spindle-shaped, smooth, containing several oil droplets. Similar species: A distinctive species, easy to tell apart from others.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North America, Europe and Asia. In Europe it is widespread. In Asia it has been reported only from Korea and Japan. In Poland it is a rare species. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland, with status R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. It is also on red lists of threatened species in Belgium, the Czech Republic, Germany, the Netherlands and Slovakia. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus. In Poland it occurs mainly in the mountains, much more rarely in the lowlands.
Grifola frondosa (Dicks.) Gray is a species of fungus in the order Polyporales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting bodies: Annual, large to very large, 20 to 60 cm across, branched like a bush, made up of many spatula-shaped caps growing from a common base. Individual caps are tongue-shaped or semicircular, flat, 4–10 cm across, thin, brittle, hazel or yellow-olive in colour. Cap margins uneven, cut and radially wrinkled. Tubes: 2–3 mm long, whitish, running down the stem. Pores small, about 0.5 mm across. Flesh: Thin, up to 0.5 cm thick, white, fleshy. Smell pleasant, mushroomy; taste mild. Spores: Colourless, broadly oval, slightly flattened on one side. Similar species: Polyporus umbellatus, whose fruiting bodies are attached centrally on stalks and are paler, whitish to light ochre. Meripilus giganteus, whose fruiting bodies are much larger and wider, made up of larger caps. It also appears on many tree species, whereas Grifola frondosa grows almost exclusively on oaks.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In Poland Grifola frondosa is rare. By 2020 about 130 of its localities had been reported. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland, with status V – vulnerable to extinction. It is also on lists of threatened species in Austria, Belgium, the Czech Republic, Germany, Denmark, Estonia, Lithuania, Norway, the Netherlands, Sweden and Finland. In 1983–2014 it was under strict protection, and from 2014 under partial protection. Harvesting of fruiting bodies for commercial purposes is permitted after obtaining the appropriate permits. A tree-dwelling fungus, a parasite.
Guepinia helvelloides (DC.) Fr. is a species of fungus in the order Auriculariales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: 5–12 cm tall, 3–7 cm wide, spatula-shaped, tongue-shaped or funnel-shaped, often formed like a cone, narrowed at the base, often with a slit. It is translucent. The surface is bare; in young fruiting bodies orange to salmon-red, in older ones coral-red to red-brown. The hymenium is on the inner side. At first it is smooth, later ribbed-wrinkled or veined and often whitish from the spores. Stem: Short, cylindrical or narrowing toward the base, hollow, torn at the top. Whitish. Flesh: 2–5 mm thick, at first springy and cartilaginous, then gelatinous; in older fruiting bodies it dissolves. At first orange, with time it fades and becomes yellowish. Tasteless, with a pleasant smell. Microscopic features: Spore print white. Spores elliptical, smooth, non-amyloid, measuring 9–12 × 4–8 μm. Basidia ovoid, measuring 14–21 × 9–13 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North and Central America and Europe. In southern Germany and the Alpine countries it is fairly common; outside these regions in Europe it is rather rare. In Poland it is rare. In the Tatra Mountains localities have been recorded, among others, in the Kościeliska, Strążyska and Mała Łąka valleys. By 2020, 81 localities had been reported. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland, with status R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. In 1995–2004 it was under partial protection, in 2004–2014 under strict protection, and from 2014 again under partial protection.
Gymnopilus junonius (Fr.) P.D. Orton is a species of fungus in the family Galerinaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 6–15 cm in diameter. In young specimens hemispherical and suede-like, then convex and finally spread out. Yellow-ochre, yellow-rusty, reddish or brown-orange; the surface is dry, covered with embedded brown scales. Gills: Moderately close, slightly decurrent with a small tooth or adnate. At first cream, then light yellow-brown, finally rusty-brown. Stem: 8–20 cm tall, 1–3 cm thick, cylindrical or spindle-shaped, thickened at the base and often rooting. It has a fairly persistent ring. Above the ring it is smooth, only dusted; below the ring it is covered with small brown fibrils and fine tufts. Light yellow, darkening toward the base to red-brown. Flesh: Firm, yellow. It has a pleasant mushroomy smell, but the taste is bitter. Microscopic features: Spore print rusty-brown. Spores rusty-orange, ellipsoid, rough, measuring 7–15 × 4.6–6 μm. Basidia 2- or 4-spored. Pleurocystidia absent. Cheilocystidia spindle-shaped, bulging, measuring 18–24 × 4–7 μm. Similar species: A species that is hard to confuse.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Widespread in Europe; it also occurs in North America (USA and Canada), Japan, Australia and New Zealand. In Central Europe it occurs sporadically, and in Poland it is rare. Fruiting bodies grow in forests, sometimes also in parks and along roads, on trunks and rotting wood, especially of birch, pine and oak. They appear from July to October.
Gymnopilus penetrans (Fr.) Murrill is a species of fungus in the family Galerinaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2–9 cm in diameter. In young specimens hemispherical with veil remnants on the margin, later arched, and finally flattened. The cap margin is not rolled under. Often has a blunt umbo. The surface in young specimens is finely felty, later almost bare, with small spots in places. Orange-rusty, usually lighter near the margin (golden-yellow) and darker in the centre (brown-red). It is hygrophanous and slippery in wet weather. Gills: Notched with a small tooth at the stem, broad. Yellow in young specimens, later darker; yellow-rusty or orange-brown. Despite the Polish species name, spots are not always present on the gills, especially in young specimens. Stem: 3–8 cm tall, up to 1.1 cm thick. Cylindrical, usually curved, at first solid, later tubular. Yellow just under the cap, otherwise brownish or brown-red. In young specimens there is a fibrous ring zone, which later disappears. White mycelium at the base. Flesh: Pale to red-yellowish in colour, brown at the base of the stem. Taste more or less bitter, smell indistinct. Spore print: Rusty-brown.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs on all continents except Antarctica. In Central Europe it is a common species, and so it is in Poland. A saprotroph. Fruiting bodies grow in small clusters or in groups on fallen trunks and branches lying on the ground, on wood waste, bark and sawdust, both in forests and at timber yards. It grows mainly on the wood of conifers, only rarely on deciduous trees. It prefers acidic soils. Fruiting bodies grow from August to November.
Gymnopus androsaceus (L.) Della Maggiora & Trassinelli is a species of fungus in the family Omphalotaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 3–12 mm in diameter. Semicircular with a flat or slightly depressed top. The surface is smooth, flesh-coloured or reddish-brown. The cap is often wrinkled and faded, with a striate margin. It shows a feature characteristic of marasmioid fungi: in dry weather the cap and stem dry out and shrink so much that they are almost invisible. After rain it regains firmness and continues to grow. Gills: Distant, of varying length, attached to the stem. Whitish or brownish. Stem: Thread-like, sometimes widened at the top, 2–6 cm tall and 1 mm thick. The surface is smooth, shiny, blackish-brown, almost black at the top. It is elastic and hard to break. Usually numerous hair-like outgrowths resembling the stem, but without a cap, also arise from the substrate. Flesh: Very thin, whitish in the cap. No smell, mild taste. Similar species: There are many similar species of small fungi. Some of them: Gymnopus perforans, which is very similar and, moreover, also grows on conifer needles, often together with Gymnopus androsaceus.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs mainly in the Northern Hemisphere: in North and Central America, Europe, Asia, and Morocco in North Africa. In the Southern Hemisphere it has been reported only from Australia and from Tierra del Fuego at the southern tip of South America. In Poland it is common throughout the country. A saprotrophic fungus. It grows mostly in coniferous forests, on fallen twigs and needles of conifers. It produces fruiting bodies from July to November, usually in groups. After rain its fruiting bodies often appear en masse on the needle litter.
Gymnopus dryophilus (Bull.) Murrill is a species of fungus in the family Omphalotaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 1.5–6 cm in diameter, smooth and bare. Light ochre, reddish-yellow, yellow-brownish to red-brown. It is hygrophanous; pale brown after rain, pale cream during drought and darker in the central part. Bell-shaped when young, later flat. The margin is mostly not grooved, only wavy in older specimens. Gills: Very crowded, thin and brittle, at first white, later ochre-cream. Stem: 3–6 cm tall, 2–4 mm thick, cylindrical, tubular-hollow, brittle. The surface is smooth and bare, ochre-brown (coloured similarly to the cap). The base is entwined with mycelial threads. When picking, delicate white to yellowish mycelial cords are often pulled out attached. Flesh: Thin, whitish and watery. Taste insignificant, smell indistinct. Spore print white. Microscopic features: Spores 5–6.5 × 2.5–3.5 µm, ellipsoid, smooth, colourless, non-amyloid. Pleurocystidia absent; cheilocystidia thickened, club-shaped, cylindrical or irregular, often branched. They measure 15–20 × 2–6 µm. Hyphae of the cap cuticle branched and tangled. They are 2–13 µm thick. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Widespread across the whole Northern Hemisphere. In Central Europe it is common. In Poland it is very common. A terrestrial saprotrophic fungus. Fruiting bodies appear from May to December in coniferous and deciduous forests, in forest meadows, parks, orchards and gardens. The Latin species name (dryophilus) comes from Greek and means oak-loving, but in fact this species grows not only under oaks but also under many other tree species.
Gymnopus fusipes (Bull.) Gray is a species of fungus in the family Omphalotaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 4–10 cm in diameter, at first bell-shaped, later low-arched, finally flat with a low umbo. The margin is irregular. The surface is smooth, bare, pale reddish, red-brown or pale brown, sometimes with dark brown spots. It is not hygrophanous; when moist, striation is visible only right at the margin. Gills: Very distant, wavy, at first white-cream, often with rusty spots, then flesh-red, dusted with white spores when mature. Stem: 6–15 cm tall, 1–2 cm thick, spindle-shaped, thickened in the middle, bent, narrowing toward the base, at first solid, later cottony inside. The surface is longitudinally fibrous, pale brown to red-brown, darker toward the base – brown-black. The stems are anchored deep in the substrate by a rooting stem base growing from an irregularly shaped black sclerotium. Flesh: Springy, whitish to cream, very hard in the stem, without distinct taste or smell. Microscopic features: Spores ellipsoid, sometimes almond-shaped, measuring 5.5–6.5 × 3–4 µm, Q = 1.3–1.9. Both the spores and all the hyphae are non-amyloid.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Gymnopus fusipes is very widespread in Europe. Its localities have also been reported in North America, Asia and New Zealand. W. Wojewoda cited numerous localities in his 2003 checklist of the large-fruited Basidiomycetes of Poland. More recent localities are given by the online fungi atlas, where it is placed on the list of rare species worth protecting. In Poland it is widespread but not very frequent. It occurs in deciduous and mixed forests and in thickets.
Gyromitra esculenta (Pers.) Fr. is a species of fungus in the family Discinaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting bodies: Resemble basidiomycetes in habit. They consist of a head and a stem and are hollow inside. Head: 5–12 cm tall, 5–15 cm wide. Irregularly spherical, strongly folded like a brain. Inside, the head is hollow and chambered, cream-coloured. The surface ranges from yellow-brown through brown to chestnut-brown and even black-brown. The hymenial layer is on the outer surface of the head. Stem: Short, irregular, dirty white, slightly thickened in the lower part. Over the whole surface it has irregular depressions. In young specimens it is solid, in older ones hollow inside. At first whitish, with time it takes on a violet-red tinge. Flesh: Cartilaginous, brittle, with an indistinct smell. Whitish and very fragile. Microscopic features: Spore print whitish. Spores spindle-shaped to ellipsoid, colourless, smooth, measuring 19–28 × 10–13 μm. Inside they usually contain numerous small guttules. Asci 8-spored. Reddish or red-orange paraphyses 4–10 μm wide, usually tangled together. Similar species: Gyromitra gigas is very similar.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In Europe it occurs only in some regions and is absent altogether in others. In Poland it occurs throughout the country except the higher parts of the mountains and is fairly frequent. A terrestrial saprotrophic fungus. Fruiting bodies appear from March to May, in pine forests, often on clearcuts and sandy soils. It is frequently found in places where the ground has been disturbed, such as pits, stream banks, ploughed forest soil, and places in the forest where the litter was disturbed during felling and timber hauling, and so on.
Gyroporus castaneus (Bull.) Quél. is a species of fungus in the family Gyroporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Rusty or chestnut-brown, convex when young, flat or cushion-shaped in the mature fruiting body. The cap skin is at first suede-like, later bald, and cracks into patches during drought. Tubes: White when young, then yellowish; they do not turn blue when cut. Pores small, round, white, then yellow. Stem: Irregularly cylindrical, variously bent. The surface is bare, dry, red-brown. Inside at first solid, then spongy, finally completely hollow or with empty chambers. Flesh: White, not changing colour when cut, hard and firm when young, brittle in older specimens. Taste insignificant, smell indistinct. Spore print: Pale yellow. Spores 7–10 × 4–6 µm, ovoid, smooth, almost colourless.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Rare in Poland. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland, with status R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. It is also on red lists of threatened species in Austria, the Czech Republic, Germany, Denmark, Norway, the Netherlands, Sweden and Finland. It occurs in deciduous forests, mainly under oaks, on sandy ground, and avoids calcareous soils. It produces fruiting bodies from July to October.
Gyroporus cyanescens (Bull.) Quél. is a species of fungus in the family Gyroporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 3.5–12 cm in diameter. Young fruiting bodies arched, later cushion-shaped, finally flat. The surface resembles suede, as it is covered with a thick fibrous layer of felt. Cream, straw-yellow or sulphur-yellow with a yellow-green tinge. Older fruiting bodies fade and become whitish. Dark blue spots appear where it is bruised. Tubes: White or cream, first attached to the stem, then free. They turn blue when cut. Pores small, angular-rounded, at first white, cream with age, turning blue when touched. Stem: 5–10 cm tall, 1–3 cm thick. Irregularly cylindrical, thinner at the top. At first spongy inside, later hollow, divided into chambers. The surface is bare in the upper part, otherwise felty, coloured the same as the cap. It turns intensely blue where bruised. Flesh: White or yellowish, turns blue quickly and intensely when cut. Taste insignificant, smell indistinct. Spore print: Pale yellow. Spores 8–15 × 4–6 µm, ovoid, smooth, pale yellowish.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North America, Europe, Asia and Australia. In Poland it is a rare species. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland, with status R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. It is also on lists of threatened species in Austria, Germany and the Netherlands. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus. It fruits from July to November in deciduous and mixed forests, on sandy ground, especially in the mountains and foothills. Most often it grows under pines, birches, oaks and beeches.
Helvella acetabulum (L.) Quél. is a species of fungus in the family Helvellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Apothecium type, consisting of a cup and a stem. The cup is 2–12 cm across, becoming flatter with age. The upper (hymenial) surface is yellow-brown to brown, bare and smooth; the lower surface is brown to yellow-brown, sometimes lighter near the stem and softly blurred near the edge, with forked whitish to brownish ribs that extend from the stem, sometimes almost to the edge of the cup. The stem is 2–9 cm tall and up to 5 cm thick, wider near the cup, deeply ribbed with sharp (sometimes blunt) forking ribs that also extend onto the lower surface of the cup. The surface is whitish to brownish and finely hairy. The flesh has no distinct smell or taste. Microscopic features: Asci 8-spored. Spores 16–20 × 11–14 µm, ellipsoid, smooth, with one central guttule. Paraphyses cylindrical with club-shaped or merely rounded tips 4–6 μm wide, hyaline to brownish. Similar species: The ribs on the lower surface of the fruiting body are of key importance for identification. In Helvella acetabulum they extend not only onto the stem but also onto the cup, sometimes almost to its edge.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Helvella acetabulum occurs in North America, Europe and Asia. In Europe it is widespread and many of its localities have been reported, from the Mediterranean to Iceland and the Svalbard archipelago in the Arctic Ocean. M.A. Chmiel cited numerous localities of this species in Poland in 2006. More recent localities are given by the online fungi atlas, in which it is on the list of threatened species worth protecting. A terrestrial fungus, probably mycorrhizal, growing singly or in groups under deciduous or coniferous trees, often near stumps or rotting wood.
Helvella crispa (Scop.) Fr. is a species of fungus in the family Helvellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: 2–10 (exceptionally up to 25) cm tall, with a distinct head and stem. The head measures 2–5 × 2–5 cm, is irregular in shape, lobed, irregularly folded, sometimes saddle-shaped and concave. The stem is 3–10 cm tall, 2–5 cm thick, distinctly furrowed, widened at the base. The flesh is thin and brittle. Both the head and the stem range in colour from whitish through cream-yellowish to dirty ochre. Spore print: White. Ascospores elliptical, smooth, colourless, measuring 19 × 11.5 μm (15–21 × 10–12 μm). Similar species: Its appearance is so characteristic that it is hard to confuse with other species. Helvella elastica is somewhat similar, but it has a smooth stem without pits and ribs, is smaller and has a saddle-shaped head.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Helvella crispa occurs in Europe and North America, from late summer to late autumn. In Poland it is moderately common. A terrestrial saprotrophic fungus. It grows in moist deciduous forests, especially readily on calcareous soils. It also grows outside forests: in parks and gardens, at the edges of roads.
Helvella lacunosa Afzel. is a species of fungus in the family Helvellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2–7 cm in diameter, 2–5 cm tall. Consists of 2–3 bent lobes of irregular shape, whose lower edge is attached to the stem. The outer surface is smooth, bare, ash-grey, grey, blue-grey or grey-black, often with brownish shades. The inner surface is also smooth, from grey to soot-grey. Often the outer surface is almost black. Stem: 3–10 cm tall, 1–3 cm in diameter. Hollow inside and narrowly club-shaped, cylindrical with longitudinal ribs, often also with deep pits. The surface is smooth, from grey through grey-brown to blackish. Flesh: Thin, brittle, whitish or greyish. Taste and smell indistinct. Microscopic features: Spores elliptical, smooth, with one large oily droplet, hyaline, measuring 14.5–22 × 10–14 μm. Paraphyses hyaline, brown in colour, with granular contents, 2.5–10 μm. Similar species: Helvella atra is smaller and has a grey stem and a smoky-brown cap; Helvella ephippium is smaller and greyish or brown.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In the Northern Hemisphere Helvella lacunosa is widespread; in the Southern Hemisphere it has been recorded only in New Guinea. In North America it is widespread in California, along the west coast and in the mountains. Many of its localities have been reported in Poland, but on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland it has the status of a rare species – potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas.
Helvella macropus (Pers.) P. Karst. is a species of fungus in the family Helvellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: At first almost spherical, later more and more spread out, forming a round cup 2–4 cm across. The spores are produced on the upper, concave surface of this cup. It is smooth, ash-grey, grey-brown or grey-black. The lower surface is grey-white and felty-hairy (as is the stem). Stem: 1–7 cm tall, when mature usually longer than the width of the cap, 1–5 mm thick; more or less cylindrical, sometimes with cracks near the base. The surface is brownish (similar in colour to the underside of the cap), whitish at the base, finely hairy but almost bare in older specimens. Flesh: Thin, whitish, with indistinct smell and taste. Microscopic features: Spores 18–25 × 10–12.5 µm, spindle-shaped or almost spindle-shaped (but occasionally ellipsoid, especially while still in the ascus), smooth or rough, usually with one large central guttule and a second, smaller one at each end, but when hydrated during microscopic observation usually with one large guttule and various smaller droplets. Paraphyses hyaline to ochre with club-shaped or hemispherical tips 5–10 µm wide.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Helvella macropus occurs in North America, Europe and Asia. In Europe it is widespread, occurring throughout from the Mediterranean to the northern tip of the Scandinavian Peninsula. In Poland it is fairly frequent. It grows singly or in groups on the ground or in moss under hardwood deciduous trees (especially oaks) or conifers, and also on rotting wood. Fruiting bodies appear from summer to late autumn.
Hemileccinum impolitum (Fr.) Šutara is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 5–20 cm in diameter, at first hemispherical, later arched, cushion-shaped and sometimes almost flat. Cream-grey with a slight olive tinge when young, then cream-olive up to beige-brown in older fruiting bodies. The layer under the skin is brownish. The cap skin is at first felty, covered with fine threads, somewhat frosted. Older fruiting bodies become bald and smooth in places. Damaged or rubbed skin turns brown and even takes on a reddish-brown shade. It sometimes cracks during drought or heat. Hymenophore: Tube pores small, first lemon-yellow, golden-yellow with age, with a greenish or olive tinge in old specimens. They do not change colour when pressed and turn slightly brown when dry. Tubes 15–30 mm long, the same colour as the pores. They do not change colour when cut. Stem: 50–180 mm long and 25–80 mm thick, at first light yellow, yellowish-grey with age. In the upper part under the tubes it often has a reddish or brown-reddish ring-like band, and sometimes the base is also flushed pinkish or reddish or covered with reddish dots.

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: A rare fungus. It produces fruiting bodies from May to mid-October. It grows in deciduous forests (oaks, hornbeams), parks, gardens, along paths and by ponds, especially under oaks, rarely under lindens or other deciduous trees, in lowlands and foothills, on calcareous ground. It prefers warm, sunny sites.
Pholiota populnea (Pers.) Kuyper & Tjall.-Beuk is a species of fungus in the family Strophariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 6–20 cm in diameter. In young specimens hemispherical, later remaining convex for a long time and only sometimes becoming flat in older specimens. Colour from cream-ochre through cream-brown to reddish-brown. The surface is densely covered with a woolly veil, which with time becomes scaly. In older specimens the scales remain only at the cap margin. Gills: Grey-beige in youth, later dark grey-brown. Stem: 3–8 cm tall, 1–3 cm thick. The cap is usually attached centrally, but sometimes laterally. It has a woolly ring and is usually thickened at the base. Its colour is slightly lighter than the cap, ochre-brown only at the base. Above the ring it is whitish and smooth, below it is covered with woolly scales. Flesh: Pale ochre-brown and bitterish. Spore print: Dirty brown. Spores measuring 6–10 μm. Similar species: Hemipholiota heteroclita (Fr.) Bon, but it has a chemical, gas-like smell and grows mainly on living birches and alders, rarely on poplar. Pholiota squarrosa, but it does not grow high on trunks of living trees, rather at the base of the trunk, and is smaller.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in the western part of the USA and in Europe. In Central Europe it is fairly rare, and so it is in Poland. A tree-dwelling fungus. It grows on dead wood of poplar or on living poplars, mainly in riparian forests. It has also been recorded on white willow and black locust. It produces fruiting bodies from August to October. They are fairly durable and can sometimes survive until spring of the following year.
Hericium cirrhatum (Pers.) Nikol. is a species of fungus in the family Hericiaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Up to 30 cm across, made up of many shell-shaped, irregular and folded lobes joined at the base on a common, thick stem. The individual caps are arranged in tufts, sometimes overlapping like roof tiles. Young fruiting bodies are whitish-cream, later yellowish, finally yellowish-brownish or ochre. Cap: Individual lobes shell-shaped, fan-shaped, 30–80 mm wide. At first convex, then flat to slightly concave, wavy with age. Their upper surface is covered with incompletely developed, sterile, non-protruding spines or is warty. The margin is sharp, often wavy or rolled under. Hymenophore: Spiny, the spines densely set, vertical, whitish, 5–15 mm long, located on the underside of the lobes. Flesh: The colour of the cap or slightly lighter, soft, thick and fleshy and brittle when young, later somewhat bast-like, and hardening with age. Smell pleasant, sweetish-fruity. Taste mild. Spore print: White. Microscopic features: Spores 3.5–4.5 × 3–4 μm, roundish or ellipsoid, smooth, amyloid. Basidia elongated, four-spored, club-shaped. Cystidia elongated, worm-shaped, with granular contents.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Localities of this species have been reported in North America, Europe, Australia, Asia and the Japanese islands. In Europe it is widespread; it occurs from the Mediterranean to the northern tip of the Scandinavian Peninsula. It is a rare fungus. It was included in the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland with status "V" – vulnerable. It is on red lists in many European countries, including Bulgaria, Germany, Great Britain, Denmark and the Netherlands". A tree-dwelling fungus.
Hericium coralloides (Scop.) Pers. is a species of fungus in the family Hericiaceae, the type species of the genus Hericium.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Irregularly oval, large, 10–40 cm across. It has a short stem branching into twigs that reach 3 cm thick in older specimens. These twigs end in tufts of soft, thin spines 1–2 cm long. In young specimens the fruiting body is pure white, in older ones it becomes creamy or cream-coloured. Flesh: White, brittle and not changing colour when cut. It has a faint smell and taste. Spore print: White, amyloid. Spores roundish-elliptical, hyaline, 3–5 × 3–4 μm. Their surface is covered with fine warts. Similar species: Hericium alpestre. It occurs only on fir and has no spines along the twigs; they are clustered in tufts at the ends of the twigs. They are hanging, longer than in Hericium coralloides and have sharp tips. Hericium erinaceus also has a fruiting body covered with hanging spines, but they are not branched.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Localities of Hericium coralloides have been reported on all continents except Antarctica, and in New Zealand and Madagascar. In Poland it occurs throughout the country, but mainly in the south and north, within the range of beech forests. By 2020 about 300 of its localities had been reported. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland, with status V – a species vulnerable to extinction. It is also on lists of threatened species in Belgium, the Czech Republic, Germany, Denmark, England, Lithuania, Norway, the Netherlands, Sweden and Finland.
Hericium erinaceus (Bull.) Pers. is a species of fungus in the family Hericiaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Spherical or cushion-shaped, sometimes thatch-like, 8–20 cm in size, but growing up to even 30 cm. White in youth, then white-cream, yellow-blue, finally ochre-brownish. It is attached to the tree by its side or by a bulbous part, which becomes woody in older specimens. It is densely covered with spines 2–6 cm long and 1.5–2 mm thick (at the base). The spines are whitish-yellow when young, later creamy, and with age range from yellow-orange to greyish-brownish. Flesh: Fleshy, flexible, springy and slightly fibrous. It is white, compact and perforated. Taste sweetish, smell mushroomy. Spore print: White, amyloid. Spores very finely dotted, measuring 5–6 × 4–5 µm. Similar species: Hericium coralloides and Hericium alpestre also occur in Poland, but they differ quite considerably in the shape of the fruiting body and in the spines.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North America, Europe and Asia. In Poland it is rare. By 2021, 3 historical and 55 contemporary localities had been reported, among others on a common beech – natural monument no. 1066 in the Tricity Landscape Park in Gdańsk. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland, with status E – endangered. It is also on lists of threatened species in Austria, Belgium, the Czech Republic, Switzerland, Germany, Denmark, England, the Netherlands, Sweden and Slovakia. A tree-dwelling fungus, a saprotroph developing on dead wood, or a weak parasite colonising living, older or weakened trees.
Heterobasidion annosum (Fr.) Bref. is a species of fungus in the family Bondarzewiaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Perennial, durable, bracket-shaped, shelf-like, spread out and reflexed or irregular, often wavy and bent. It is attached to the substrate by its side or base. Fruiting bodies grow singly or several together, and may then fuse at their bases. 5–10 cm across, red-brown to dark red-brown, also black-brown in the central part. The growth margin is white. The surface is matt, forming a thin crust, often unevenly knobbly. Tubes: White-cream, in older specimens also arranged in layers. Pores fairly small, 0.2–0.4 mm, roundish and decurrent. Flesh: 0.5–3 cm thick, the colour of light wood, bast-like and corky. Smell sweetish. Spore print: White. Microscopic features: Spores non-amyloid, roundish-elliptical, finely dotted, measuring 5–6 × 4–4.5 μm. Similar species: Two other species of Heterobasidion occur in Poland: Heterobasidion abietinum, developing mainly on fir, rarely on spruce, and Heterobasidion parviporum, developing mainly on spruce, rarely on fir.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North and Central America, Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia. It occurs in coniferous and mixed forests, both on dead wood and on living trees. It grows mainly on conifers, but also on some deciduous trees (birch, beech and oak). Fruiting bodies grow low – in the ground-level part of trunks, on root collars of trees, on stumps or on roots protruding above the ground. The presence of fruiting bodies indicates that the tree is already very advanced in decay.
Hortiboletus bubalinus (Oolbekk. & Duin) L. Albert & Dima is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Up to 5 cm in diameter, at first hemispherical, then convex, finally flat. The surface is dry, velvety, later smooth or finely cracked. Ochre, yellowish-brown with or without an apricot tinge, light brown, reddish-brown, yellow-brown to honey-brown, and usually lighter at the margin. Tubes: Light yellow to yellow with an olive-green tinge. They turn blue when injured. The pores are the same colour and turn blue when injured. Stem: Cylindrical, spindle-shaped or club-shaped. The surface is yellowish and usually almost completely covered with very fine red granules, which change colour with age. It turns blue when damaged. Flesh: In the cap whitish with a pinkish tinge under the skin. In the stem yellowish and orange-brown at the base, sometimes with a few orange-red dots. In the cap it turns blue when damaged. Taste and smell are indeterminate. Microscopic features: Spores measuring 11–15 × 4.5–5 μm, smooth.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been reported in some European countries, in one region of eastern Canada and in New Zealand. In Poland its locality was first reported in 2017 in the Białowieża Forest. In 2020 it was also found in Greater Poland. In both cases it was described under the scientific name Xerocomus bubalinus, without giving a Polish name. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus living in symbiosis with lindens and poplars. In England one occurrence under hornbeams has been reported. It probably also lives with other deciduous tree species. It occurs in forests, parks and gardens.
Hortiboletus rubellus (Krombh.) Simonini, Vizzini & Gelardi is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 3–10 cm in diameter, hemispherical in young specimens, later spread out, finally flat. The surface is dry, suede-like, and may be cracked in dry weather. Colour at first intense carmine-red, later red, finally matt pink. The skin cannot be separated from the flesh. Tubes: 6–15 mm long, greenish-yellow, notched or slightly decurrent at the stem. Pores at first lemon-yellow to light yellow, later olive. They turn blue when pressed. Stem: 3–12 cm tall, 0.4–2.5 cm thick, cylindrical, often curved. The surface is light yellow, often flushed with red or with red spots. Flesh: Yellowish, reddish only under the cap skin. Turns blue when cut. Without distinct taste or smell. Microscopic features: Spore print olive-brown. Spores measuring 10–13 × 4–5 μm with a smooth surface. In KOH they turn golden. Cystidia more or less numerous, measuring 60 × 12.5 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in Europe and North America, where it was probably introduced with tree seedlings from Europe. It is rare everywhere. In Poland it is not very frequent. It occurs from July to September in deciduous forests under oaks, lindens and birches.
Humaria hemisphaerica (F.H. Wigg.) Fuckel is a species of fungus in the order Pezizales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Apothecium type without a stem, at first cup-shaped, becoming wider and wider during development and reaching up to 3 cm across. The upper surface is white to bluish-white and fairly smooth; the lower surface is brown and densely hairy, with hairs protruding above the rim of the cup. Flesh brownish, brittle, without smell. Microscopic features: Asci 8-spored with non-amyloid tips. Paraphyses thread-like with club-shaped tips, septate, hyaline in KOH. Spores 20–24 × 10–12 µm, smooth in KOH, warty or rough in Melzer's reagent, elliptical, often with slightly flattened ends, at first with two guttules, which break up into small droplets when mature. Hairs with pointed tips, smooth, brown in KOH, often septate, 7.5–12.5 µm wide, thick-walled. Similar species: There are many species of fungi with cup-shaped fruiting bodies on the ground, but Humaria hemisphaerica is easy to distinguish. Other species of these fungi are either brightly coloured, or have smaller fruiting bodies, or occur only on burnt ground. Species of the genus Jafnea are similar, but do not occur in Poland.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Humaria hemisphaerica is widespread in North America, Central America, Europe and Asia; isolated localities have also been reported in South America. In Europe it occurs from the Mediterranean to Iceland and the northern tip of the Scandinavian Peninsula. In Poland M.A. Chmiel cited numerous localities of this species in 2006, and many more localities were reported in later years. A terrestrial, mycorrhizal fungus living in symbiosis with trees, but sometimes also a saprotrophic fungus developing on heavily rotted wood.
Hydnum repandum L. is a species of fungus in the family Hydnaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 4–10 (15) cm across, usually concave in the centre, whitish to pale orange. The surface is dry, bare and smooth, sometimes delicately mossy. Shape variable, margin curved under and irregular. A characteristic feature is its brittleness. Fruiting bodies are often fused together in groups of several. During drought the colour fades and becomes distinctly lighter. Hymenophore: Spines up to 6 mm long, crowded and sometimes slightly running down the stem. Whitish to pale orange. Brittle in the same way as the cap. On young fruiting bodies they are short and pale yellow, only later becoming longer and taking on the same colour as the cap. Stem: Up to 7 cm tall, 1.5–4 cm thick, usually eccentric, hard, solid, often irregularly bent. Colour from white through cream to rusty-brownish. Spore print: White to pale cream, non-amyloid. Spores colourless and smooth, almost spherical, measuring 6.5–9 × 5.5–7 μm. Similar species: Hydnum rufescens, which has a more intense colour, the boundary between the spines of its hymenophore and the stem is very clearly marked, and the spines do not run down the stem; also bielaczek owczy, especially young specimens.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Widespread in North America and Europe. In Poland it is also common. A mycorrhizal fungus. It grows from July to October (November) in coniferous, deciduous and mixed forests. It likes clay soils with a high calcium content. It most often forms mycorrhiza with spruce and beech. Fruiting bodies often grow in large groups.
Hygrocybe acutoconica (Clem.) Singer is a species of fungus in the family Hygrophoraceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 1.5 to 5 cm across; sharply conical when young, later broadly conical, the margin may be lobed-wavy near the edge, flatly spread out and radially cracked in older fruiting bodies, always with a distinct umbo, sticky in wet conditions, radially fibrous during drought, yellow-orange, orange or red-orange, margin not striate. Gills: Free to very weakly attached at the stem, up to 8 mm wide, light yellow in young fruiting bodies, then salmon-orange with a yellow edge, fading to lemon-yellow in old specimens.
