Stem: 2 to 7 cm tall, 3 to 8 mm in diameter, cylindrical with a rounded base, hollow, sometimes longitudinally fibrous, reddish, coloured the same as the cap, white at the base. Flesh: The colour of the cap, light yellow in the stem. Taste and smell indistinct. Microscopic features: Spore print: White. Microscopic features: Spores elliptical, non-amyloid, smooth, measuring 9–12 × 5–7 μm. Basidia mostly 4-spored, up to about 55 μm long. Cystidia absent. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Hygrocybe acutoconica is widespread in Europe. It also occurs in some regions of North America and in Japan and on the Korean Peninsula. In Poland it is rare. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland, with status R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. It is also on lists of threatened species in Germany, Norway and the Netherlands. In Poland it occurs in foothill and mountain regions. It grows on the ground, in moist pastures and meadows.
Hygrocybe conica (Schaeff.) P. Kumm. is a species of fungus in the family Hygrophoraceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 1–3 (6) cm across; sharply conical when young, later bell-shaped convex, finally spread out, radially cracked, with a sharply pointed umbo, sticky in wet conditions, silky shiny during drought, saturated yellow, red-yellow, scarlet-red, turning black when pressed and with age. Gills: At first almost free, later free, broad, bulging, thick, pale yellow to lemon-yellow. Stem: 6 to 8 cm tall, 0.5 to 1 cm in diameter, cylindrical, hollow, fibrously cracked lengthwise, yellow, orange-yellow, often with a greenish tinge, turning black when pressed and with age. Flesh: Brittle, yellow to orange-yellow, turning black. Smell fruity, taste astringent. Spore print: White. Spores (on 4-spored basidia) 7–9 × 4.5–6 µm or (on 2-spored basidia) 8–12 (14) × 6–7.5 µm. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs on all continents except Antarctica and Africa. In Poland it is common. A terrestrial fungus. It appears from June to October. Frequent in moist meadows and pastures.
Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca (Wulfen) Maire is a species of fungus in the family Hygrophoropsidaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2 to 7 cm across; in young specimens thin-fleshed with a rolled-under margin and fawn in colour, later funnel-shaped and sunken in the centre, with wavy or bent margins. Colour from yellow through orange-yellow and orange to red-orange. The skin is smooth, slightly matt, dry, felty in some places. Gills: Thin, crowded, forking, running down the stem, sometimes wavy. Orange-yellow or orange in colour. Stem: 3–5 cm tall, 3–10 mm thick, cylindrical below, widening conically above and passing smoothly into the cap. Solid in young specimens, hollow in older ones. The colour is like that of the gills, only blackish at the base; the skin is felty. Flesh: White or cream, juicy and soft. Taste and smell mild, bitter-sour. Spore print: Pale yellow or cream. Spores elliptical, with a smooth surface, measuring 6–7 × 4 μm. Similar species: Cantharellus friesii.

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: Grows in coniferous and mixed forests, singly or in groups, sometimes in large numbers. It grows on humus formed from needles, leaves and various wood waste, but sometimes also on the ground. Fruiting bodies appear from September and occur until November. It grows under firs, beeches and pines.
Hygrophorus eburneus (Bull.) Fr. is a species of fungus in the family Hygrophoraceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 3 to 7 cm across; hemispherical when young, later convex to spread out, the margin rolled under for a long time. The surface is smooth, strongly slimy in wet conditions, silky shiny during drought. Colour white, later ivory, then cream. Gills: Thick, fairly distant, running down the stem, 3 to 5 mm wide. Always pure white. Stem: 4 to 11 cm tall, 5 to 12 mm in diameter, cylindrical, narrowing toward the base, firmly rooted in the ground, solid. Under the cap it is dry and covered with fine scales and tufts. Its surface is slimy, white or ivory-coloured. Flesh: Soft, springy and juicy in the cap, fibrous in the stem. It is white and has a faint taste and smell. It does not change colour when damaged. Spore print: White. Spores ellipsoid, with a smooth surface. Size 6–7 × 5 μm. Similar species: There are several species of white waxcaps. Telling them apart is difficult even for mycologists. Microscopic examination is sometimes necessary.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North America, Europe and Asia. In Europe it is widespread, occurring from the Mediterranean to the northern regions of the Scandinavian Peninsula. In Poland it is a fairly frequent species. A terrestrial fungus. It grows singly or in small groups, in deciduous and mixed forests, in parks and old avenues. It grows mainly under beeches, less often under oaks. It does not like acidic soils. It also grows outside forests – in pastures and meadows, especially on soils rich in calcium.
Hygrophorus hypothejus (Fr.) Fr. is a species of fruiting-body-forming fungus in the family Hygrophoraceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 1–6 (up to 10) cm across, olive-brown, olive-brownish, slightly darker in the centre, in mature fruiting bodies fading yellowish in places, covered with a slimy skin. The shape of the cap is hemispherical or bell-shaped in young fruiting bodies, then convex or spread out, mostly with an umbo in the centre. In older specimens the slime on the skin dries up or is washed off by rain. Sometimes (rarely) a variety with an orange-yellow cap can be found. Hymenophore: Gilled; the gills are at first cream-coloured, then yellow, broad and widely spaced, soft and slightly running down the stem. Stem: Cylindrical, sometimes narrowed at the base, 5–7 cm long, 0.3–0.7 cm in diameter, yellowish, in young fruiting bodies covered with a thick layer of slime below the ring zone. Cracking slime may form a banded pattern. Flesh: Yellowish, soft, rather bast-like in the stem, with no or only a slight fruity smell. Spores: Elliptical, measuring 7–9 × 4–5.5 μm, smooth, hyaline. Spore print is white, non-amyloid. Similar species: The fruiting season of Hygrophorus hypothejus limits the possibility of confusing its fruiting bodies with other species.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been confirmed in Austria, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, France, Spain, Japan, South Korea, North Korea, Germany, Norway, Poland, Slovenia, the United States, Sweden and the United Kingdom. In Poland it is a rare species. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland, with status I – a species of indeterminate threat. A terrestrial fungus. In Europe it appears only after the first frosts (late autumn and early winter). Sometimes its fruiting bodies can be found even under snow. It occurs both in the lowlands and in the mountains.
Hymenochaete rubiginosa (Fr.) Lev. is a species of fungus in the family Hymenochaetaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Very thin, attached to the wood only by its central part, slightly bell-shaped, standing away from the substrate by up to 2 cm, densely overlapping like roof tiles; dark, red-brown with a narrow black band. Spore-bearing layer: Red-brown; smooth, with sharp bristles on the surface visible only at high magnification, usually covering a large area of the wood and fusing with the small caps; some specimens have no cap margins. Flesh: Dark brown, bast-like. Microscopic features: A layer of densely packed hairs covering the fruiting body (tomentum) up to 250 μm thick, darker than the hyphal layer. Cortex 30–55 μm thick, rusty-brown, made up of glued-together hyphae, beneath it a hyphal layer 100–600 μm thick; hyphae compact, arranged lengthwise. Bristle layer 70–500 μm thick, made up of overlapping rows of hairs. Hyphal system dimitic. Generative hyphae 2–3.5 μm in diameter, almost hyaline, thin-walled; skeletal hyphae 3–5 μm in diameter, thick-walled, brown.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs on all continents except Antarctica, also on many islands. In Poland it is common. A tree-dwelling saprotroph.
Hypholoma capnoides (Fr.) P. Kumm. is a species of fungus in the family Strophariaceae. In earlier classifications it was placed in the genus Psilocybe as Psilocybe capnoides.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 3–7 cm in diameter, hemispherical when young, then flat-convex, fairly often with a small inconspicuous umbo, finally flat. The cap margins are mustard-yellow to ochre-yellow, the centre darker – rusty-yellow. The cap margin is smooth and in young specimens is joined to the stem by a cobweb-like veil. Gills: Fairly crowded and broadly attached, whitish when young, later grey-violet, dark violet-brown in older specimens. Stem: 4–8 cm tall, 3–5 mm thick, cylindrical. Colour from light cream-yellow to yellow-brown, but without green tinges. Darker at the base (rusty-yellow to rusty-brown). In young specimens it is covered with faintly visible white fibrils. Flesh: Pale brown, somewhat darker in the stem than in the cap. Taste mild, smell mushroomy. Spore print: Rusty-brown. Spores smooth, ellipsoid, measuring 8–9 × 4–5 μm. Similar species: Galerina marginata. It has smaller fruiting bodies, brittle and rusty-brown. Hypholoma fasciculare.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In Central Europe it is a common species, and in Poland it is also frequent. A saprotroph. It usually grows in clusters, gregariously. It is most abundant in late autumn, but fruiting bodies appear throughout the year, also in winter when there is no snow. It is rarest in the months of May to August. It usually grows in clusters on rotting coniferous wood, especially on spruce.
Hypholoma fasciculare (Huds.) P. Kumm. is a species of fungus in the family Strophariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter up to 7 cm, semicircular in young specimens, then convex to flat, with a slight bulge in older ones. The cap surface is dry and smooth. Colour yellow or sulphur-yellow, the centre of the cap orange to rusty-brown. Gills: Crowded, rounded at the stem. Colour from sulphur-yellowish in young specimens, through dirty greenish, to violet-black in older ones. Covered by a thin veil in very young fruiting bodies. Stem: Up to 0.7 cm thick, up to 10 cm tall. Irregularly cylindrical, bent, hollow inside. Yellowish with a slight greenish tinge, covered (especially at the bottom) with brownish fibrils. It does not change colour when damaged. Stems in a cluster of fruiting bodies are fused at the base. Flesh: Thin and flexible, yellowish or sulphur-yellow, brown at the base of the stem. Taste very bitter. It does not change colour when damaged. Spore print: Grey-violet, sometimes almost black. Spores ellipsoid, smooth, measuring 6–8 × 4 μm. Similar species: Hypholoma capnoides. Hypholoma lateritium.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Except for Africa and Antarctica it occurs on all continents, also on many islands. In Europe it is widespread. In Poland it is very common. Fruiting bodies grow from April to December in clusters of even several dozen fruiting bodies on stumps of dead deciduous and coniferous trees. Among fungi growing in clusters on stumps it is one of the most common, and sometimes it even grows on construction timber. It occurs from spring to late autumn.
Hypholoma lateritium (Schaeff.) P. Kumm is a species of fungus in the family Strophariaceae. In earlier classifications it was placed in the genus Psilocybe as Psilocybe lateritia.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 3–9 cm in diameter, hemispherical when young, then arched, finally flat. It is fleshy, smooth and bare. Sticky in wet weather. The centre of the cap is brick-red and the margins are yellow-orange. Near the margins there are fibrous-scaly, whitish-yellowish veil remnants. Gills: Crowded, at first yellow, then olive-brown, chocolate or olive-black. Stem: 2–4 cm tall, 1.5–3 mm thick, cylindrical, with a ring that disappears early. It is fibrous, pale yellow at the top and brownish at the bottom. Flesh: Yellowish, slightly bitter, without smell. Microscopic features: Spore print violet-brown. Spores smooth, ellipsoid, thin-walled, measuring 6–7 × 3–4 μm. They turn yellowish with KOH. Spindle-shaped, sharply pointed pleurocystidia measuring 40 × 10 μm are numerous. Cheilocystidia, spindle-bulging or cylindrical, hyaline and thin-walled with semicircular tips, measure 35 × 8 μm. Similar species: Hypholoma capnoides. Hypholoma fasciculare does not have a brick-coloured cap, has dirty greenish gills, is smaller and more bitter.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been described in Europe, the eastern regions of North America and in Japan. In Central Europe it is common, and in Poland very common. It usually grows in clusters on rotting stumps or trunks of deciduous trees, less often coniferous. Sometimes it also occurs on the litter of deciduous trees.
Hypsizygus ulmarius (Bull.) Redhead is a species of fungus in the family Lyophyllaceae.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In the scientific literature, numerous localities were reported up to 2003. Other and more recent localities are given by the online fungi atlas. A tree-dwelling parasite and saprotroph. It occurs on deciduous trees in forests, parks, botanical gardens and along roads. Most often found on European white elm (Ulmus laevis) and field elm (Ulmus minor), but also recorded on sycamore maple (Acer pseudoplatanus), horse chestnut (Aesculum hippocastanum), aspen (Populus tremula), birch, beech, oak and linden. Fruiting bodies from July to November.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 6–15 (exceptionally up to 30) cm in diameter, convex with a broad margin. The surface is dry, smooth, whitish to cream. Gills: Attached or slightly decurrent, broad, crowded, white. Stem: 6–13 cm tall, 2–3 cm thick, cylindrical, smooth or finely fibrous. The surface is white. No ring. Flesh: Smell sour, insignificant or sometimes slightly mealy. Taste mild. Microscopic features: Spore print cream. Spores 3.5–6.5 × 3–5 µm, non-amyloid.
Imleria badia (Fr.) Vizzini is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Reaches up to 15 cm in diameter. Bare and smooth, in young specimens semicircular with rolled-under margins, dark brown with a reddish tinge or chestnut-brown. In older specimens the cap is spread out, fairly flat, sometimes with margins turned upward. Tubes: Slightly notched around the stem. Colour from pale ochre to olive-yellow. When damaged they turn blue-green. Pores are at first white, later yellow to yellow-greenish. Stem: Up to 4 cm thick, up to 10 cm tall. Light brown, with longitudinal, darker streaks. In young specimens the stem is usually swollen, later cylindrical. It turns dark blue where damaged. Flesh: Firm, woody in older stems. White, slightly yellow in older specimens. Turns slightly blue when cut. Taste and smell pleasant. Spore print: Olive-brown. Spores ellipsoid, smooth, measuring 4–5 × 12–17 μm. Similar species: Young specimens of Imleria badia can be confused with Tylopilus felleus. Doubts can be settled by a taste test (Tylopilus felleus is bitter).

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North America, Europe, Australia and Japan. In Europe it is common. It grows in coniferous and mixed forests on the ground, sometimes right next to stumps, often in moss. Most often found under Scots pine and Norway spruce. It forms fruiting bodies from summer to late autumn.
Infundibulicybe geotropa (Bull.) Harmaja is a species of fungus in the order Agaricales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 10–25 cm in diameter, brown-ochre; in young fruiting bodies at first white, smooth and bare. First convex with rolled-under margins and an umbo in the centre. In older fruiting bodies the cap is funnel-shaped. Gills: First white, then ochre-cream, crowded, thin, slightly or distinctly decurrent. Stem: 5–15 cm tall, 1–4 cm thick. Cylindrical, solid, smooth, somewhat fibrous, overgrown at the base with white felty mycelium. It is the same colour as the cap. Young fruiting bodies often have a long stem and a very small cap. This happens because at first the stem grows much faster than the cap. Flesh: White, compact, not changing colour when cut. Taste insignificant, smell indistinct. Spore print: White. Spores almost spherical, smooth, colourless, 6–8 × 5–6 µm. Similar species:
Infundibulicybe gibba (Pers.) Harmaja is a species of fungus in the order Agaricales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 5–15 cm in diameter, in young fruiting bodies arched with a rolled-under margin and an umbo, but it quickly becomes concave and funnel-shaped with a straightened margin. The margin is sometimes wavy and speckled. The cap is thin-fleshed, with a smooth surface in pale ochre, ochre-cream or reddish-brown, the colour fading in older fruiting bodies. Gills: Fairly crowded and running far down the stem, at first white, later yellowish. Stem: 4–10 cm tall, up to 1 cm thick, cylindrical, slightly widening toward the base, soft and flexible, cottony inside in young fruiting bodies, hollow in older ones. The surface is bare, whitish or pale yellow, overgrown with white felt at the base. A characteristic feature is that the colour of the stem is lighter than that of the cap. Flesh: Cream-white, with a slight almond smell, or without smell. Microscopic features: Spores broadly ellipsoid, non-amyloid, pointed at one end, smooth. Size 5–9 × 3.5–6 μm. Cystidia absent. Hyphae in the cuticle tangled, 2–7 μm wide, encrusted with pigment. Clamp connections present.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Infundibulicybe gibba is widespread in North America, Europe and Asia. In the Southern Hemisphere it is known only from Australia. In Poland it is very common. It occurs in both deciduous and coniferous forests on fallen leaves and needles, also on rotting bark, but avoids acidic and poor soils. It grows under various tree species, in particular fir, grey alder, hornbeam, beech, spruce, pine and black locust. Fruiting bodies appear from June to November.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: Infundibulicybe costata, Paralepista flaccida, which usually has brownish spots on the cap and has no umbo.
Inonotus hispidus (Bull.) P. Karst. is a species of fungus in the order Hymenochaetales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting bodies: Annual, attached to the substrate by their side, occurring singly or overlapping like roof tiles in small groups. A single one is usually up to 10 cm wide, rarely up to 35 cm, and up to 10 cm thick. Its upper (hymenial) surface in young fruiting bodies is smooth, even and matt, from yellow-red to apricot, then becomes red-brown, somewhat wrinkled, covered with warts and hairs. These are bristly-felty, slimy in wet weather and sticking together in tufts. In old specimens the upper surface becomes bare, rough, cracked, without zoning. The margin in young fruiting bodies is sharp, protruding and sulphur-yellow, in older ones yellow-brown, blunt, thin, wavy. The flesh is at first soft, spongy and juicy, from yellowish to ochre, with time rusty-brown, hard, dry and zoned, brittle in dried specimens, radially fibrous. It is up to 8 cm thick. It quickly turns brown when damaged. Hymenophore tubular, sulphur-yellow in young fruiting bodies, ochre with age, finally grey-ochre. It has pits 2–4 mm in diameter exuding a watery, bitter substance. It has a pleasant smell and a slightly sour taste. Microscopic features:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Widespread in North America, Europe and Asia; its occurrence has also been reported in the Republic of South Africa and on the east coast of Australia. In Poland W. Wojewoda cited numerous localities of it in 2003, but some are already historical. More recent localities are given by the online fungi atlas. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland, with status R – a species potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. It is also on lists of threatened species in Denmark, Finland, Norway and the Netherlands.
Inonotus obliquus (Ach. ex Pers.) Pilát is a species of fungus in the family Hymenochaetaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: It produces two kinds of fruiting bodies: an asexual and a sexual form. The asexual fruiting body (anamorph) takes the form of a perennial, knobbly, warty, cracked outgrowth attached by its side to the tree. It is very strongly fused with it. The outgrowth has irregular shapes and can reach up to 50 cm across. The trunk of the tree near the outgrowth is often thickened. The outer layer of the fruiting body is dried out, hard, flaking, charred and slag-like. The surface is matt, black-brown or black-navy, with a reddish-brown tinge in fresh cracks. In these cracks chlamydospores are produced asexually, by which the fungus spreads until the host dies. They also serve as resting spores. After the tree dies, the fungus produces the second form of fruiting body, the sexual fruiting body (teleomorph), which produces sexual spores – basidiospores. This fruiting body is, however, difficult to observe, as it develops under the bark of the tree or between layers of wood. It is annual, flat, spread out (resupinate). It grows near the outgrowth, is 5–10 mm thick, up to several dozen centimetres wide and covers the trunk over a length of up to several metres.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Recorded across the whole Northern Hemisphere. Many of its localities in Poland have been reported in the scientific literature, but it is rare. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland, with status R – a species potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. In Poland it is under partial species protection. It occurs in various types of forests, less often in parks. It develops on trunks of deciduous trees, mainly on silver birch and aspen, but it has also been recorded on maples, alders, hornbeams, beeches, rowans and elms.
Ischnoderma benzoinum (Wahlenb.) P. Karst. is a species of fungus in the family Ischnodermataceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: An annual bracket fungus attached to the substrate by its side. A single fruiting body is fan-shaped or semicircular, up to 20 cm long, up to 14 cm wide and up to 2 cm thick. The upper surface of young fruiting bodies is felty, of older ones bare, with a slight sheen. It is concentrically zoned. Young fruiting bodies are red-brown or brown, older ones become violet-black from the resin covering them. The margin is thin and always lighter in colour, often wavy and bent downward. Hymenophore: Develops only in the final phase of development of the fruiting body. Tubes are about 10 mm long. Pores are round or polygonal and very small; 4–6 fit in 1 mm. At first whitish, then darker and darker, brown in older fruiting bodies. They darken when pressed. Flesh: About 1 cm thick. In young fruiting bodies it is white and fleshy, in mature ones it becomes ochre and hard. Microscopic features: Spore print white. Spores cylindrical, smooth, non-amyloid, measuring 5–6 × 2–2.5 μm. Cystidia absent. Basidia 4-spored, measuring 10–15 × 3–4 μm. Similar species: Ischnoderma resinosum. It occurs on the wood of deciduous trees.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs sporadically in the Northern Hemisphere. It is fairly rare. In Poland it is a rare species. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland, with status V – a species vulnerable to extinction. It is also on lists of threatened species in Germany. According to observations from 2005–2014, however, in Poland this species is not very rare. It develops on trunks and stumps of dead coniferous trees.
Ischnoderma resinosum (Schrad.) P. Karst. is a species of fungus in the family Ischnodermataceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: An annual bracket fungus attached to the substrate by its side. A single fruiting body is bracket-shaped or semicircular, 6–15 (30) cm wide and 1–2 (3) cm thick. The margin is thick, rounded and lighter in colour. The upper surface of young fruiting bodies is felty, of older ones bare, with a slight sheen. Colour from rusty-red through red-brown to black-brown. Older fruiting bodies are darker. The hymenophore often exudes dark drops. Under the skin there is a thin resinous layer of rusty colour. Hymenophore: Develops only in the final phase of development of the fruiting body. Tubes are 10–15 mm long, their pores are small (0.15–0.25 mm in diameter), white to ochre. They turn red-brown when pressed. Flesh: Juicy, fleshy-fibrous, several times thicker than the tube layer. When dried it becomes corky and brittle. Microscopic features: Hyphal system dimitic. Generative hyphae with clamp connections. In the cap cuticle brown and with very thick walls, with a few scattered clamp connections, moderately branched, 4–10 μm wide. Generative hyphae in the context mostly colourless and widened in the middle to 12 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North America and Europe. In North America it is widespread and fairly frequent. In Europe it is widespread, occurring from Spain to Russia, but more often in the southern part. In Northern Europe it is rare; in Sweden it is known from only one locality, and similarly in Denmark. In Poland it is a rare species. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland, with status V – a species vulnerable to extinction. It is also on lists of threatened species in Austria, Germany, Denmark, Sweden and Slovakia.
Kuehneromyces mutabilis (Schaeff.) Singer & A.H. Sm. is a species of fungus in the family Kuehneromycetaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2–7 cm in diameter. After rain cinnamon-brownish and slimy; during drought it dries from the centre toward the margins, so that the centre is pale ochre and the margin brownish, striate. Semicircular when young, completely flat with age, smooth, bare, with a blunt umbo in the middle. Gills: Covered by a veil when young, crowded. At first whitish, then yellow-brown, finally rusty-brown. They are closely set and attached to the stem, sometimes slightly running down it. Stem: 5–7 cm long, 5–8 mm thick, cylindrical, bent. It has a colour similar to the cap. It is bast-like and hollow inside. In the upper part it has a leathery ring with numerous protruding scales. Below the ring the stem has dark brown tufts; above the ring the stem is smooth or delicately striate. Flesh: Thin, whitish, soft and watery in the cap, hard and rusty-brown in the stem. Taste insignificant, smell pleasant, reminiscent of freshly cut wood. Spore print: Rusty-brown. Spores 6–7 × 4–4.5 µm, ovoid, smooth, pale brown. Similar species: These two species can be told apart only by the appearance of the stem (in Galerina it is covered with white tufts of the veil, which form a zigzag pattern).

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs across the whole Northern Hemisphere. In Poland it is common. It grows gregariously in deciduous and mixed forests, parks and gardens on stumps and dead trunks (close to the ground) and branches of deciduous trees. Fruiting bodies appear from April to November. It is associated with these tree and shrub species: grey alder, black alder, silver birch, hornbeam, hazel, beech, willow, oak and small-leaved lime. Very rarely found on the wood of fir, pine and spruce.
Laccaria amethystina (Huds.) Cooke is a species of fungus in the family Hydnangiaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2–6 cm in diameter, in young specimens hemispherical or bell-shaped with a rolled-under margin and a depression in the centre, in older ones becoming arched, finally flat and funnel-shaped with wavy margins. It is hygrophanous. The skin is smooth, in adult specimens delicately lobed with slightly grooved margins. In wet weather it is violet or brown-violet, in dry weather, or in older specimens, whitish-violet. Gills: Thick, distant, often wavy. They are broadly attached to the stem or only slightly decurrent. In young specimens violet, later dusted whitish with spores. Even when the fruiting bodies are faded, their gills remain violet. Stem: 3–12 cm tall and 3–10 mm thick, hollow inside, fibrous, slightly thickened at the base. The colour is the same as that of the cap. Flesh: Watery, slightly violet in wet weather, pink-brownish in dry weather, with indistinct smell and taste. Spore print: White. Spores warty, measuring 7–10 μm. Similar species: The difference: a less slender fruiting body and a characteristic smell of radish or turnip.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A widespread species. Occurs in Asia, Europe, North and Central America and New Zealand. In Central Europe it is a common species. In Poland it is also common. It grows not only in forests but also in gardens, parks and other habitats on rotten wood or on the ground, under both deciduous and coniferous trees, but most often under trees of the order Fagales. Scientific research has shown that Laccaria amethystina is a nitrogen-loving fungus – it grows most numerously and abundantly in soil with a high content of ammonia and nitrogen compounds.
Laccaria laccata (Scop.) Cooke is a species of fungus in the family Hydnangiaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 1–5 cm in diameter, convex with a rolled-under margin when young, later flat, finally concave and wavy. Colour orange, rusty-brown, flesh-pink or pink, sometimes, but rarely, orange-ochre or olive-ochre. It is hygrophanous; when moist it is translucently grooved, when dry the grooving is not visible. Gills: Widely spaced, broadly attached, salmon or brown-reddish. Sometimes running down the stem. Stem: 2–8 cm tall, cylindrical, slender, often twisted, slightly fibrous lengthwise, overgrown at the base with white mycelium. The colour is the same as that of the cap. Flesh: Pale reddish in the cap, stronger and pinker in the stem. Taste and smell indistinct. Spore print: White. Spores round to broadly elliptical, 7–10 µm, with spines up to 2 µm long. Basidia 4-spored. Similar species: Laccaria proxima. It has a larger fruiting body with usually pink gills; Laccaria bicolor, which has violet mycelium at the base of the stem.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Widespread in North America, Asia and Europe; it also occurs in North Africa and Australia. In Poland it is widespread and very common. A mycorrhizal fungus. It grows in various types of forests, also on their edges and in parks. It forms mycorrhiza with trees, among others of the pine, beech and birch families, and often occurs en masse in forest nurseries. Sometimes it also grows outside forests, in grasses, even in treeless places. It produces fruiting bodies from June to November.
Laccaria proxima (Boud.) Pat. is a species of fungus in the family Hydnangiaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2–8 cm in diameter, hemispherical when young, then convex, finally spread out, flat with a slightly concave centre, sometimes wavy. In wet weather it is striate; in dry weather the striation is absent, and the grooving of the margins is also invisible. The surface of young fruiting bodies is delicately felty, later rough, covered with small, protruding scales. Colour from yellowish-reddish through orange-red and flesh-brown to brown-red. In dry weather it fades and becomes pale ochre. Fairly often the cap cracks radially along the gills. Gills: 3–10 mm wide and attached to the stem. Pink or flesh-reddish. Besides the main gills there are intermediate gills (lamellulae). Stem: 6–12 cm tall, 5–8 mm thick, cylindrical, often curved, thickened at the base, at first solid, later hollow. The surface is strongly fibrillose, sometimes cracked, red-brown or dark brown. The base is darker than the rest of the stem and covered with white mycelial hyphae. Flesh: Whitish with a flesh-brownish tinge, hard in the cap, cartilaginous in the stem. Taste mild, indistinct, smell faint, indeterminate.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North and Central America, Europe, Asia, Australia and Morocco in North Africa. In Europe it is widespread. It grows on the ground in forests and at their edges, exclusively under pines. It prefers moist places, among Sphagnum mosses. It is also found on organic waste. It produces fruiting bodies from June to November.
Lacrymaria lacrymabunda (Bull.) Pat is a species of fungus in the family Psathyrellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 3–8 cm in diameter, bell-shaped in young specimens, then broadly spread out, completely flat with age but not depressed. Colour from cream-ochre through orange-brown to rusty-brown. Its surface is covered with fibrils and scales, and in older specimens with tufts. In young specimens, veil remnants hang from the cap margin. Gills: In young specimens grey-yellow, then brown-black. They are often violet-grey. A characteristic feature of this species is that the gills exude droplets of liquid, on which black-brown spores collect. Stem: 5–12 cm tall, 5–8 mm thick. It is cylindrical, hollow, longitudinally fibrous and covered with tufts. Colour from ochre to brown, with a weakly marked fibrous ring zone. Above this zone it is bare. Flesh: Pale grey-brown, without distinct smell. Microscopic features: Spore print brown-black. Spores ellipsoid, measuring 8–12 × 5–8 μm. Thickened pleurocystidia measuring 48–62 × 9–14 μm and sac-shaped are present, often clustered in threes or fours. Cheilocystidia are numerous.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The most numerous localities of this species have been described in North America and Europe, but it also occurs in Africa, Japan and New Zealand. In Central Europe it is frequent. In Poland it is frequent. It grows on roadsides, in parks, gardens, on field boundaries and forest roads, mainly on fertile soils. It produces fruiting bodies from early summer to late autumn.
Lactarius blennius (Fr.) Fr. is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 5–20 cm in diameter, early funnel-shaped, with a margin rolled under and generally bent, older also lobed or coarsely scalloped. The margin stays rolled under for a long time and usually does not fully flatten out. It is uniformly olive-grey to grey-green and only occasionally distinctly, concentrically banded; when young – strongly slimy – when older usually dry and shiny. Gills: Fairly crowded, sometimes forked, narrow and narrowing both at the margin and at the stem. Intermediate gills are present. At first the gills are white, later become straw-coloured, finally light ochre. In wet weather they weep. When pressed they turn olive-brown. In older specimens the gill edge becomes spotted olive-rusty. Stem: 3–8 cm tall, 1–2.5 cm thick, cylindrical or narrowing toward the base, at first solid, later cottony or hollow. In dry weather the surface is shiny, in wet weather sticky. It is lighter than the cap. In older specimens the stem is covered along its whole length with shallow pits. Flesh: Thick and hard. It is white, with only a faint olive tinge under the cap skin. In older specimens it turns brown. Taste acrid, no distinct smell. Latex:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Localities of this species have been reported in Europe, North America, Asia and New Zealand. In Poland it is common. It is one of the most frequently occurring milkcaps. It is recorded throughout the country, both in the lowlands and in the mountains. In the Tatra Mountains it has been found at an altitude of 1400 m above sea level. It occurs in various types of forests, both deciduous and coniferous. It prefers areas with high humidity, overgrown with mosses. It is associated with birches, beeches and lindens. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus.
Lactarius camphoratus (Bull.) Fr. is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: It produces terrestrial fruiting bodies consisting of a cap and a stem, whose flesh is built of spherical cells that cause their specific brittleness and irregular fracture. Cap: 2–5 cm in diameter, dark orange-brown or red-brown. In the centre of the cap there is always a fairly distinct umbo, with a depression around it. In young specimens the cap is arched, later spread out. The margins are scalloped and delicately wrinkled. Covered with a dry, bare and matt skin without concentric zones. Hymenophore: Gilled; the gills are crowded, only slightly running down the stem, at first light flesh-reddish, after ripening red-brownish, with a white bloom of spores during spore deposit. Brown spots form when pressed. Stem: 3–8 cm tall, up to 1 cm thick, cylindrical, sometimes flattened. Dark red-brown, blackening at the base during ripening, hollow inside. Flesh: With a mild, sometimes bitterish taste and a smell reminiscent of camphor or true bugs (Hemiptera), and after ripening or during drying of lovage (Levisticum sp.) or chicory (Cichorium sp.). Latex: Fairly abundant, thin, watery white. It has a mild taste, but leaves a bitterish aftertaste.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North, Central and South America, in Europe and in Asia. In Polish mycological literature it has been described from very many localities. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus occurring in deciduous and coniferous forests, mostly in the presence of spruces (Picea sp.), pines (Pinus sp.) or beeches (Fagus sp.). In Europe it produces fruiting bodies from July to November. It is sometimes attacked by the parasitic fungus Hypomyces lateritius, causing mouldiness and underdevelopment of its gills and hardening of the flesh.
Lactarius deliciosus (L.) Pers. is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 4–12 cm in diameter, flesh-reddish or in various shades of orange, sometimes with an admixture of green. The surface is concentrically zoned, sometimes pitted-spotted. In young fruiting bodies the cap is convex, maturing concave with a shallow depression in the centre, funnel-shaped in old specimens, with the margins rolled under for a long time. Covered with a skin that is slimy at high air humidity. Hymenophore: Gilled; the gills are orange-yellowish, similar to the cap, of various lengths (mixed), straight-attached or slightly decurrent on the stem, thin and brittle. When damaged they turn slightly greenish. Stem: 3–7 cm long and 1–2.5 cm in diameter, the colour of the cap or lighter, with darker pit-like spots (otherwise smooth), saturated with latex. Cylindrical, at first solid, then hollow, narrowed at the base. Flesh: Built of spherical cells, which cause its specific brittleness and irregular fracture. Pale orange, compact, brittle in mature fruiting bodies, saturated with bright orange latex. Turns green when damaged. It has a slightly bitterish, astringent taste and a sweetish, fruity smell. Latex:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Widespread across the whole Northern Hemisphere in areas with a temperate climate. It also occurs in Australia. In Poland it is common. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus. It grows on the ground in coniferous forests and young stands, on sandy soils. It forms ectomycorrhiza with pines (Pinus sp.). In Poland it appears from August to November.
Lactarius deterrimus Gröger is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 4–10 cm in diameter, arched in young specimens, then flat with a concave centre, funnel-shaped in old specimens. The margin stays rolled under for a long time. Colour reddish-orange. In wet weather the skin is slippery, in dry weather glossy frosted. On the cap there are concentric, darker bands, sometimes faintly visible. After frosts the cap turns green. Gills: Red-orange, brittle, fairly crowded and slightly decurrent on the stem. When damaged they turn green. Stem: 3–7 cm tall, 1–2.5 cm thick, cylindrical, hard. At first solid, but quickly becomes hollow. Colour red-orange, green-spotted. No pits on the stem. Flesh: It is cream, but the latex stains it orange. Under the cap skin it can be strongly grey-blue. It has a pleasant, fruity smell and an acrid taste, although older specimens are mild in taste. Latex: Flows fairly abundantly. It is orange and does not change colour in air for a long time, becoming wine-red only after about 15 minutes. Microscopic features: Spore print light ochre. Spores oval, measuring 8–10 × 7–8 μm. On the surface they have low warts joined by an irregular network. Basidia measure 36–45 × 8–9 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In Central Europe it is common. In Poland it is also fairly frequent. It occurs in coniferous and mixed forests. It grows exclusively under spruces, hence it is much more frequent in the mountains and foothills, where spruce forests occur. It occurs on various soils. In North America it also occurs under such trees as pine, hemlock and fir.
Lactarius helvus (Fr.) Fr. is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 5 to 15 cm in diameter, at first flat-convex, later flat with a broad depression, sometimes with a low umbo. The margin is rolled under, flattens slowly and not completely, usually staying slightly curved under. The surface is smooth, dry and matt. In dry weather it sometimes becomes granular, and in older specimens even cracks into patches. The skin cannot be peeled off. It is uniformly coloured, without banding; in dry weather ochre-pink or fawn-pink, even with a violet tinge, in wet weather with a rusty or orange tinge. Gills: Crowded, with intermediate gills, sometimes forked at the stem and forming anastomoses. Both at the margin and at the stem they are sharp. At first white-yellowish, later ochre-yellow with a lemon or grey tinge. Stem: 4–13 cm tall, 0.5–4 cm thick, cylindrical. At first solid, later hollow. The surface is smooth, sometimes woolly, and granular-shaggy in the top part. It is slightly lighter than the cap: red-ochre or yellow-reddish. Flesh: Fairly thick, slightly brittle, ochre-rusty, sometimes with a narrow, watery band above the gills.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North America, Europe, Asia, Australia and New Zealand. In Europe it is widespread. In Poland it is common. In the Tatra Mountains it occurs up to an altitude of 1200 m. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus. It grows from June to October in deciduous and coniferous forests, on acidic soils, in peat bogs, among Sphagnum mosses; frequent.
Lactarius pubescens Fr. is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 5–12 cm in diameter. Convex when young with a dent in the centre and strongly rolled-under, shaggy-woolly margins. The skin is slightly sticky when moist, drying quickly. Colour whitish, light pink, yellowish or cream with spots, but without concentric zones. Gills: Narrow and very crowded, slightly decurrent. Colour whitish, then cream with a salmon tinge. Stem: 2–5 cm tall, 1–2 cm thick, cylindrical, hollow, narrowed near the ground and hollow inside. Whitish, with a flesh-pink sheen. Flesh: Built of spherical cells, which cause its specific brittleness (as in all Russulaceae) and irregular fracture. It is white, brittle, not changing colour when cut. Only as the fungus dries does it change colour to yellow. Under the action of FeSO4 it turns grey-yellow. Latex: White, not changing colour after flowing out. In older fruiting bodies it flows weakly. Strongly burning in taste. Spore print: Pale cream. Spores ovoid, colourless (hyaline), measuring 6.5–8.5 × 5.5–6.5 μm, with a finely warty-reticulate surface, without a germ pore, amyloid.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in Europe, Asia, North America and Australia. In Poland it is not rare, and numerous localities have been reported in mycological literature. It occurs, however, less often than mleczaj wełnianka. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus. It grows in deciduous forests, in parks, in grass, in the presence of birches, in moist places in forests, in peat bogs, without particular soil requirements. It produces fruiting bodies (in Europe) from August to November.
Lactarius quietus (Fr.) Fr. is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 3–8 cm in diameter, convex in young fruiting bodies, then flat, slightly depressed or funnel-shaped after maturing, always without an umbo. The margin is at first rolled under, then wavy. The surface is dry, matt, from red-brown through cinnamon-brown to flesh-brown, sometimes with delicate concentric bands. It fades in dry weather. Hymenophore: Gilled; the gills are fairly crowded, decurrent. At first whitish, later grey-yellow, finally cinnamon-brown. On their edges there are brown spots, and in mature fruiting bodies they are dusted with spores. Stem: 3–10 cm tall, 0.6–1.7 cm thick, cylindrical. The surface is smooth, of a similar colour to the cap, red at the base. When pressed it turns brown-red. Flesh: Built of spherical cells causing its specific brittleness and irregular fracture. Taste mild, smell sometimes slightly bitter, reminiscent of cod-liver oil or true bugs (Hemiptera). Latex: Young fruiting bodies exude latex abundantly, older ones weakly. It is white with a cream tinge, mild in taste, but after a longer tasting it leaves a bitterish taste. Microscopic features: Spore print light yellow.

sections.head: Distribution and range
sections.text: Distributed worldwide; except Antarctica it occurs on all continents and on many islands. In Europe in the north its range extends as far as the Svalbard archipelago. In Poland it is common. It grows on the ground in deciduous and mixed forests, especially in the presence of oaks. In Europe it produces fruiting bodies from June to October. Scientific research has shown that it forms mycorrhiza exclusively with oak.
Lactarius rufus (Scop.) Fr. is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 3–8 cm in diameter, broadly conical with a rolled-under margin when young, later flat-arched (usually with an umbo in the centre), finally slightly funnel-shaped. Colour evenly red-brown, skin smooth and without banding. Gills: About 5 mm wide, crowded and slightly decurrent on the stem. Yellowish in young specimens, then light cream, flesh-ochre in older ones. They often have red spots. In older specimens they are dusted with white spores. Stem: 3–12 cm tall, 8–18 mm wide. It is cylindrical and brittle, spongy in young specimens, then hollow. Colour at first whitish, then light red-brown. Flesh: Fairly thin, reddish-brown in colour. When drying it gives off a strong spicy smell. Latex: Flows fairly abundantly. It is thin, watery white, mild in taste, but leaves a bitter aftertaste. Spore print: Whitish. Microscopic features: Spores 8–10 × 6–7.5 μm, oval, with a surface covered with small warts and thin connections forming an incomplete network. Basidia 36–40 × 7–10 μm. Cystidia 50–60 × 7–10 μm, narrowly spindle-shaped, numerous on the gill edge, sparse on the sides. Similar species: There are many species of milkcaps with a brown cap.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs across the whole Northern Hemisphere in areas with a temperate climate; in the Southern Hemisphere its localities have been reported in Africa and New Zealand. In Central Europe it is common, rare only in areas with calcareous ground. In Poland it is very common. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus. It occurs in coniferous forests, and also at the edges of swamps and peat bogs. It grows on acidic soils, almost exclusively under spruces and pines, very rarely under birches.
Lactarius salmonicolor R. Heim & Leclair is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 5–15 cm in diameter, convex in young specimens, then flat with a concave centre. The surface is orange-yellow, peach-yellow or orange, concentrically zoned with rusty-orange bands. In wet weather wine-brown spots may appear. There is no green colour, only in older fruiting bodies a greenish tinge may appear. The margin is rolled under and slightly frosted, but in older fruiting bodies it becomes smooth. Gills: Slightly decurrent, moderately crowded, sometimes forking at the stem. In young fruiting bodies they are light ochre with an orange tinge. When damaged they do not turn green, at most they become redder. Stem: 3–6 cm tall, 1–2.5 cm thick, cylindrical, brittle. At first solid, but quickly becomes hollow. Colour as in the cap, the surface delicately frosted. Flesh: Cream; when damaged, orange, slightly bitter latex appears immediately. After about 10 minutes it changes colour to minium (red-lead), after 1–2 hours to orange-brown or wine-red. It gives off a faint, fruity smell. Spore print: Pale ochre. Microscopic features:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North America, Europe and Asia. In Central Europe it is common in some regions (e.g. in the Alps), rare in others. It occurs in coniferous and mixed forests. It grows exclusively under firs. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus. In Poland it occurs mainly in the mountains; in the Pieniny, the Gorce, on Babia Góra and in the Roztocze. It is on lists of threatened species in Austria and Germany.
Lactarius subdulcis (Pers.) Gray is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 3–7 cm in diameter, at first convex with a conical umbo and a curved-under margin, later gradually flattening, finally flat with a straight margin, sometimes shortly scalloped and slimy. The surface is smooth, matt, uniformly coloured, without banding, at first red-brown, chestnut, later lightening, more fawn. Gills: Crowded, with lamellulae, at first whitish, then light ochre with a coffee tinge, changing colour to grey-rusty when damaged. Stem: 5–7 cm tall and 0.3–1 cm in diameter, cylindrical, sometimes channelled in older specimens. The surface is at first pale yellowish, but quickly takes on the colour of the cap, with mycelium at the base. Flesh: Whitish-flesh-coloured with a rusty tinge, darker in the stem. Taste mild, smell similar to that of true bugs. The latex is exuded abundantly at first, is watery white or white, not changing colour, at first mild in taste, but after a longer time somewhat bitter and acrid. Spore print: Cream. Microscopic features: Basidia 36–45 × 9–811 µm. Cheilocystidia numerous, pleurocystidia sparser, spindle-shaped, 55–65 × 6–8 µm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Its localities are known in North and Central America, in Europe, Asia, Australia and New Zealand. In Europe it occurs throughout, from the Mediterranean to the northern tip of the Scandinavian Peninsula; it is absent from Iceland. In Poland W. Wojewoda listed it in 2003 as a common species, and its localities are also given by authors of later mycological literature. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus. It occurs in forests, especially beech forests, in the company of beech, fir, hazel and pedunculate oak. Fruiting bodies appear from summer to autumn.
Lactarius theiogalus (Bull.) Gray is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2–5 cm in diameter, at first flat, but quickly spread out and depressed, usually with an umbo. The margin is thin, staying rolled under for a long time. The surface is matt when dry, shiny when moist, sometimes rough. Colour orange-rusty with a reddish tinge, sometimes cinnamon-brown. Gills: Broadly attached, cream in young specimens, later clay-pink. Stem: 2–8 cm tall, 3–10 mm thick, cylindrical or club-shaped, at first solid, later hollow. Colour at first rusty-brown, later ochre, cinnamon, finally dark brick-red. Lighter in the upper part. Flesh: Built of spherical cells, which cause its specific brittleness (as in all Russulaceae) and irregular fracture. It usually has a mild taste, but sometimes slightly acrid or bitter. Latex: In young fruiting bodies it flows abundantly, in older ones hardly at all. It is watery white and on the flesh turns sulphur-coloured. At first it has a mild taste, but leaves a bitter aftertaste on the tongue. Microscopic features: Spore print whitish-cream. Spores oval, covered with large, single warts, sometimes joined by short connections.

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: Occurs in North America, Europe and Japan. In Poland it is frequent, and mycological literature lists numerous localities of it across the whole country. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus. It grows in coniferous and deciduous forests, mainly under birches, pines and spruces, especially in moist places overgrown with Sphagnum moss. In Poland it produces fruiting bodies from June to October.
Lactarius torminosus (Schaeff.) Gray is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 4–10 (up to 15) cm in diameter, with a central depression, covered with a felty skin that becomes slightly sticky at high air humidity. The cap margin is mostly rolled under, covered with woolly tufts hanging from it. Cap colour flesh-pink, brown-red, fading to orange-ochre in older specimens. Hymenophore: Gilled; the gills are light cream or white, with smooth edges, crowded (with lamellulae), slightly decurrent on the stem. Stem: Cylindrical, 4–8 cm long and about 1.2 cm in diameter, light pink, ochre-pink or white, solid in young fruiting bodies, then hollow inside. Flesh: Built of spherical cells, which cause its specific brittleness and irregular fracture. White, hard, with a fruity or turpentine-like smell and an acrid, burning taste. Under the action of FeSO4 it becomes greyish-yellow. Latex: At first it flows abundantly. It is white and does not change colour in air. It burns strongly on the tongue and in the throat. Spore print: Cream. Microscopic features: Spores broadly ellipsoid, measuring 7–9 (10) × 6–7 μm. On the surface they have low but distinct warts joined by an incomplete network.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Widespread across the whole Northern Hemisphere in the temperate climate zone. It also occurs in Australia. In Poland it is common. It grows in forests and parks in the presence of birches, with which it forms mycorrhiza. It can be found on sandy or clayey, acidic soils, usually in the company of mosses. In Poland it produces fruiting bodies from July to November.
Lactarius necator (Bull.) Pers. is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 5–15 cm in diameter, low-arched in young specimens, spread out and depressed in the centre in older ones. It is firm, the margins stay rolled for a long time, no umbo. The surface is slippery, without zoning, or with faintly visible zoning. Colour from dirty olive-green to black-brown. Gills: Narrow and crowded, of various lengths, slightly decurrent on the stem. First whitish, then cream-yellow, with brown spots in old age. Darkening when damaged. They exude abundantly white latex with a very burning taste, which does not change colour in air. Stem: 3–7 cm tall, up to 2.5 cm thick, cylindrical, at first solid, later hollow. The surface is shiny when dry, slippery in wet weather, sometimes rough or pitted. Colour from pale olive through greenish to dirty olive. Flesh: Thick and firm, white, only faintly olive under the cap skin. In older specimens the flesh turns brownish. It has an acrid taste and a faint smell. Latex: Exuded abundantly. It is white or watery white, does not change colour in air. In taste it is very burning. Microscopic features: Spore print light cream.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North America and Europe. In Asia its occurrence has been reported only in Japan. In Poland it is a common species. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus. It grows in deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests, under birches or spruces, on acidic soils, from July to November.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 5–15 cm in diameter, convex with slightly rolled-under margins when young, later almost flat with a dent in the centre, finally shallowly concave. The margins are at first rolled under, later curved under, finally straightened. No umbo. The surface is smooth, without banding, rusty-orange, yellow-rusty or orange-brown. Gills: Fairly crowded, adnate-decurrent. At first white, later light yellowish and light ochre. When damaged they turn rusty-brown. Stem: 6–12 cm tall, 1–3.5 cm thick, cylindrical, solid, smooth, bare. It is much lighter than the cap, usually orange-yellowish. Flesh: Firm, whitish in young specimens, light yellow to light ochre in older ones. It has a fairly strong smell reminiscent of herring. Latex: Very abundant, white, not changing colour in air. It is mild in taste, but leaves a bitter aftertaste. Microscopic features: Spore print light cream. Spores almost spherical, slightly spiny and reticulate. Size: 8–10 × 8–9.5 µm. Spindle-shaped cheilocystidia and pleurocystidia measuring 60–100 × 8–12 µm are numerous.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North America, Europe, China, Korea, Japan, Morocco in North Africa and in Australia. In Poland it is common. It grows on the ground, in both deciduous and coniferous forests, especially under beeches, oaks, hornbeams, aspens, spruces and pines. It produces fruiting bodies from June to October.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: There are many similar species of orange milkcaps that are hard to tell apart externally, e.g. Lactarius subdulcis, Lactarius aurantiacus. It is also easy to recognise thanks to the uniformly rusty-orange coloured cap.
Laetiporus sulphureus (Bull.) Murrill is a species of fungus in the order Polyporales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Usually without a stem, thick-fleshed, attached by its side to the tree, 10–40 cm across. Fruiting bodies often occur overlapping like roof tiles one above another. Young specimens often have a tuberous shape, later becoming fan-shaped, hemispherical or irregularly deformed. The upper surface is hilly, uneven, radially wrinkled. Colour sulphur-yellow to orange (often with a pink tinge), fading with age. The margin is irregular, wavy, rolled under. Fruiting bodies with a sharp margin are also encountered. The margin is often lemon-coloured. Hymenophore: Tubular, not separating from the flesh. Tubes short (up to 1.5–5 mm long), sulphur-yellow. Tube pores very small (3–5 fit in one mm), at first sulphur-yellow, then ochre-yellow. Flesh: White to cream-yellow, soft and juicy in young specimens, brittle in older ones. Taste pleasant, slightly sour, smell mushroomy. Spore print: Light yellow, quickly lightening to white. Spores colourless, smooth, ovoid to oval or teardrop-shaped. They have a sharply pointed base and droplets in the centre. Size: 5–6.5 × 3.5–4.5 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A cosmopolitan species, occurring on all continents except Antarctica. Most numerously recorded in the Northern Hemisphere, especially in North America and Europe. In Poland it is a common species. Fruiting bodies are annual, appearing from April to October, but mainly in spring. It usually occurs in parks, on roadside trees, in orchards and gardens. It is rarer in forests. It occurs mainly on deciduous trees, on coniferous trees very rarely. It most often attacks oaks, birches, willows and fruit trees.
Leccinum aurantiacum (Bull.) Gray is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 3–15 cm in diameter. Spherical when young, then hemispherical, finally becoming low-arched. Colour orange-red, red-orange, dark or brick-red. The cap margin is thin, and the skin on the edge of older specimens usually hangs beyond the tubes as a thin membrane. Tubes: Greyish with an olive tinge. Pores round, small, at first white, then greyish-ochre, finally olive. Stem: 5–18 cm tall, cylindrical, solid, wider at the base. It is whitish and covered with whitish scales when young, later orange-red. Under the cap the scales stay white for a long time. Flesh: Thick, firm, juicy, white, darkening when cut. Taste insignificant, mild, smell indistinct. In older specimens the flesh in the stem becomes bast-like, while in the cap it is softer and watery. Spore print: Brown or olive-brown. Spores 13–17 × 4–5 µm, smooth, yellow-brownish. Similar species: Leccinum versipelle is very similar. It is paler and grows under birches. It is easiest to tell apart by the black scales on the stem.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The most numerous localities of this fungus are known in North America and Europe, but it also occurs in Central America and Japan. In Central Europe it is widespread but occurs unevenly; in some regions it is fairly frequent, in others rare. In Poland it is fairly frequent, but it is on red lists of threatened species in Germany and the Netherlands. It occurs in forests and thickets, exclusively under aspen. It produces fruiting bodies from June to October.
Leccinum cyaneobasileucum Lannoy & Estadès is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 4–8 cm in diameter, round, usually regular, sometimes only slightly deformed with a wavy margin. At first convex, in the mature state arched, but never becomes completely flat. The surface is very delicately woolly, in various shades of brown, but whitish albino forms are also encountered. Tubes: Broadly attached to the stem, 1 to 1.5 cm long and 0.5 mm in diameter, round, from dirty white to grey-brown. Pores of the same colour. When crushed they do not turn blue, but slowly turn brown. Stem: 1–2.5 cm thick, 7–14 cm tall. The shape is at first barrel-like, then slightly club-shaped, narrowing toward the top. Flesh: The flesh of the stem base is white, always blue when damaged (although often only in a very limited area). It is also blue in places gnawed by snails or insects. At the top it is white, sometimes turning pinkish when damaged. Microscopic features: Spores spindle-shaped, 13–19 × 4–6.5 µm, mainly 4-spored, but usually with a few 2-spored basidia. Of great importance for identifying this species is microscopic analysis of the cuticle hyphae and caulocystidia. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been reported in many European countries and at several localities on the east coast of the USA. Since Leccinum scabrum, the base species for this taxon, is widespread in the world, it should be assumed that Leccinum cyaneobasileucum is also widespread, but these species are often not distinguished. In the scientific literature its occurrence in Poland was described in 2019 in the Gryżyński Landscape Park. Current localities are also given by the online fungi atlas. A terrestrial ectomycorrhizal fungus living in symbiosis exclusively with birches.
Leccinum duriusculum (Schulzer ex Kalchbr.) Singer is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter up to 15 cm, hemispherical in young specimens, then cushion-like flattened. It is fleshy, dry, matt and felty in dry weather, and the cap surface is sticky in wet weather. When young the surface is smooth, with time it becomes wrinkled. Colour from red-grey to dark brown, with yellow spots near the margin. The surface is scaly and fibrously felty. Tubes: Up to 30 millimetres long, deeply notched at the stem. Colour from white in young to grey in older specimens. Pores roundish, grey-olive in older individuals. When pressed the pores turn brown. Stem: Up to 3 cm thick, up to 15 cm tall, cylindrical. It is white or cream and covered with numerous small scales and grains, which are pale brown in young specimens and blackish in older ones, especially in the lower part of the stem. Flesh: White in the cap, salmon when cut, grey-violet in the upper part of the stem, turning blue at the base. Taste and smell pleasant. Spore print: Spores smooth, spindle-shaped, measuring 13–17 × 5–7 μm. Similar species: Leccinum scabrum has a smooth cap skin and its flesh does not change colour. It grows under birches.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Its occurrence has been described only in Europe. Here it is widespread, in the north reaching the northern tip of the Scandinavian Peninsula. In Poland it is rare, but not especially threatened. It is, however, on red lists of threatened species in Austria, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Slovakia and the Czech Republic. In autumn it is found under aspens and white poplars. Fruiting bodies appear from August to October.
Leccinum holopus (Rostk.) Watling is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: The cap is white or whitish, 5–15 cm in diameter. Tubes: The tubes are whitish, turning brown when pressed. Stem: Whitish with white or grey scales. Flesh: The flesh is white, usually turning pinkish, sometimes bluish at the base. Similar species: Leccinum rotundifoliae is similar; it has a similar colour, but prefers dry areas and does not turn blue at the base of the stem. Albino forms of other bolete species growing under birch may also be similar.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North America and Europe. Władysław Wojewoda gives no localities in Poland, but it is found by mushroom pickers. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus. It grows from July to October under birches in wetlands and peat bogs.
Leccinum scabrum (Bull.) Gray is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter up to 20 cm, semicircular to cushion-shaped in young specimens, smooth in older ones. In wet weather the cap surface is slippery, slightly slimy. Colour from light brown to dark brown. Stem: Up to 3.5 cm thick, up to 17 cm tall. Solid, cylindrical, slender, narrowing toward the cap. White, covered with numerous dark brown to black tufts. Tubes: Up to 25 mm long, deeply notched at the stem. Colour from whitish in young to grey-brown in older specimens. Pores almost round and small. Damaged tubes do not change colour. Flesh: White to white-cream, may be white-greenish at the base. Fibrous, firm in young specimens, soft to watery in old ones. It does not change colour when damaged. Taste and smell pleasant, faint. Spore print: Brown to olive-brown. Spores smooth, spindle-shaped, measuring 14–20 × 4.5–6.5 μm. Similar species: Leccinellum pseudoscabrum is also similar, but it grows only under hornbeams and its flesh, when damaged, stains a colour from dirty pink to blackish.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs across the whole Northern Hemisphere. In the Scandinavian Peninsula it reaches 66° latitude. In the Southern Hemisphere its occurrence has been reported only in Australia and New Zealand. In Central Europe it is common. In Poland too it is common from summer to autumn. A terrestrial fungus growing in deciduous and mixed forests, often also outside forests. It grows exclusively under birches, since it forms mycorrhiza with them.
Leccinum versipelle (Fr. & Hök) Snell is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Brick-orange or orange-yellow. It is 5–15 cm in diameter, cushion-like convex, usually shaggy and rough; on its margin membranous remnants of hanging skin are visible. Tubes: The tubes are whitish with a shade of grey. Stem: It is 6–15 cm long and 1–3 cm thick. The surface is white or light grey, covered with small black scales, which turn brown in older specimens. Flesh: When cut, the flesh turns pink-grey-violet, and in the lower part of the stem green-bluish. This colour change may also occur in Leccinum aurantiacum. Spore print: Brownish. Spores smooth, elliptical-spindle-shaped, measuring 13–16 × 4–5 μm. Similar species: Leccinum aurantiacum is very similar. It is easiest to tell apart by the scales on the stem; Leccinum aurantiacum has scales that are at first whitish, later red-brown, but never black. It also has a more intense, bright red cap and grows only under aspen. Also similar are: Leccinum vulpinum and Leccinum piceinum.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Its occurrence has been described in North America, Europe and Asia. In Europe it is widespread. In the north it reaches the northern coasts of the Scandinavian Peninsula; it also occurs in Iceland. In Poland it is common. It is on the red list of threatened species in Germany and the Netherlands. It occurs under birches, in places numerously, from June to October. It grows exclusively under birch or in the close vicinity of this tree.
Lentinellus cochleatus (Pers.) P. Karst. is a species of fungus in the family Auriscalpiaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2–7 cm in diameter, colour at first flesh-brown, later brown-reddish, and in older specimens yellow-brown or ochre. When young it is funnel-shaped or horn-shaped, later becomes shell-shaped, spatula-shaped or gill-like. It is bare, thin, springy and delicately wrinkled. It often has irregularly bent margins. Stem: 2–8 cm tall, 5–10 mm thick, flesh-reddish in colour and red-brown at the bottom. It is usually eccentric, i.e. not attached exactly in the centre of the cap, but somewhat to the side. It is solid, ribbed-wrinkled, bare and springy. The stems of neighbouring fruiting bodies are often fused. Gills: At first whitish, later brownish, running deeply down the stem to its base. They have a serrated or scalloped edge. Flesh: White to flesh-brown. It is tough, springy and has an anise smell and a mild taste. Spore print: White. Spores: 4–6 × 4 μm, nearly spherical, delicately dotted. Similar species: These also occur in Poland: Lentinellus flabelliformis, Lentinellus ursinus and Lentinellus vulpinus.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been described in Europe, North and Central America, Australia and Japan. In Central Europe it is common everywhere. In Poland it is also frequent. A saprotrophic fungus. It grows in deciduous and mixed forests, on old tree trunks, on tree roots and on branches of deciduous trees lying on the ground, rarely on conifers. It always occurs gregariously. Sometimes it seemingly grows on the ground, but in fact its mycelium develops on twigs or tree roots buried in the soil. It occurs more often on alkaline soils.
Lentinus brumalis (Pers.) Zmitr. is a species of fungus in the family Polyporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2–8 cm in diameter, round and flatly spread out, slightly funnel-shaped in older specimens. The surface is bare, delicately felty, or scaly, the cap margin sometimes hairy. Colour from dark brown to almost black. Tubes: Decurrent, up to 1 mm long. Pores white or cream, angular, 2–3 mm in diagonal. Stem: 3–6 cm tall, about 0.5 cm thick. It is central or almost central. The surface is bare, colour from light brown to grey-brown. Flesh: White, flexible, thin, with a faint sour smell. Spore print: White. Spores cylindrical, smooth, measuring 5–7 × 1.5–2.5 μm. Similar species: Lentinus substrictus, but its fruiting bodies appear only from spring to summer. It has small pores, a zigzag stem and a shaggy or hairy cap; Lentinus arcularius also has large pores, but a lighter cap and distinctly visible bristles on the margin.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A species widespread in the world. In Poland it is common. Fruiting bodies appear only in late autumn and winter (hence the species name). It grows on dead branches and trunks of deciduous trees. Fruiting bodies also grow during a mild winter; when the winter is severe they appear again in spring. Occurrence has been recorded on the following trees: grey alder, silver birch, downy birch, hornbeam, beech, oak.
Lentinus tigrinus (Bull.) Fr. is a species of fungus in the family Polyporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2–9 cm in diameter, arched when young, then depressed, finally funnel-shaped. The surface when dry is uniformly grey-brown, olive-brown or blackish. In older specimens the skin cracks, producing concentrically arranged patches contrasting with a white or cream-ochre background. Gills: Broad, crowded, running deeply down the stem. They have delicately serrated edges. At first whitish, then cream, finally yellowish. Stem: 3–7 cm tall, 4–8 mm thick, cylindrical. It is central or eccentric, scaly, whitish in the upper part, yellowish in the middle, grey-brown at the base. Sometimes it has a membranous ring in the upper part, but as a rule it quickly disappears. Flesh: White or yellowish, springy, and in mature fruiting bodies springy-leathery. Taste indistinct, smell intense.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Widespread in North America, Europe and Asia. In the Southern Hemisphere it has been recorded only in Uruguay and on the island of Western Caroline in Oceania. In Central Europe it is common in the lowlands, but rare elsewhere. In the scientific literature many of its localities in Poland have been reported, yet it is rare. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland, with status R – a species potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. A saprotroph occurring on dead wood in forests, parks and along roads.
Lepiota clypeolaria (Bull.) P. Kumm. is a species of fungus in the family Agaricaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 4–7 cm in diameter. Young – egg-shaped, later bell-shaped, finally flat, with a blunt smooth rusty-brown umbo in the centre. The surface is whitish, white-cream or yellowish with ochre-yellow to brownish shaggy scales arranged concentrically. Veil remnants hang from the cap margin. Gills: Free at the stem, crowded, white or light yellowish. Stem: 4 to 10 cm tall, 0.5 to 1 cm in diameter. Cylindrical, thickened at the bottom, can be snapped off, tubular. It has a ring, but it quickly disappears. Above the ring the surface is smooth, below it on a white background it is covered with woolly, yellowish or brownish scales. Older specimens lose the scales. Flesh: White to light ochre. Smell unpleasant, taste mild. Spore print: White. Spores spindle-shaped or almond-shaped, smooth, measuring 11–18.5 × 4–6.5 μm. Cheilocystidia inconspicuous, pleurocystidia absent. Similar species: A characteristic feature that makes it possible to tell this species from several similar Lepiota species is the strongly woolly covering of the stem.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Widespread in North America and Europe. Outside these continents the occurrence of this species is poorly studied; it is also known to occur in Japan and Korea. In Central Europe it is fairly common. It grows on the ground in coniferous and deciduous forests and in parks. It produces fruiting bodies from July to October. It prefers sunlit places.
Lepiota cristata (Bolton) P. Kumm. is a species of fungus in the family Agaricaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 3–4 cm in diameter. It emerges from the soil at first as a closed cone and gradually unfolds into a spread-out cap with a distinct, umbo-like centre. The umbo has an intense brown-red or dark ochre colour. The surface of the rest of the cap is whitish, covered with light ochre scales. In places rich in nitrogen compounds (e.g. on compost heaps) it can produce very large fruiting bodies with a cap diameter of up to 8 cm. Gills: Whitish, not attached to the stem, crowded and slightly bulging. Stem: Slender, cylindrical, club-like thickened at the base. It does not exceed 7 cm in height and about 0.5 cm in thickness. The surface is cream-white, covered with a few tufts coloured like the cap. In younger specimens there is a thin, membranous, funnel-like raised ring under the cap, which disappears with age. The stem is at first solid, in older specimens hollow. Flesh: White, flesh-pink only in the cortex of the stem. It gives off a strong, unpleasant smell similar to that of puffballs. Spore print: White. Spores wedge-shaped or spherical, smooth, measuring 5–8 × 3–5 μm, strongly or weakly dextrinoid.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Except for Antarctica it occurs on all continents, and also on many islands. In Central Europe it is a common species, probably the most frequently encountered Lepiota. It grows in groups along grassy forest roads, in gardens, thickets, pastures and forests of all types. It also occurs in timber yards and on compost heaps, especially often in places enriched in nitrogen compounds. It often occurs in the company of small balsam, nettle and elder. It produces fruiting bodies from May to October.
Leucocoprinus birnbaumii (Corda) Singer is a species of fungus in the family Agaricaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Conical, with age bell-shaped to spread out; 1 to 8 cm in diameter, shiny, sulphur-yellow. The surface is covered with fibrous scales, bare and striate at the margins. The margin is wavy-grooved. Gills: Broad, light yellow to sulphur-yellow. Stem: The colour of the cap, fragile, with a thin ring. Cylindrical, widening toward the base; up to 10 cm long. Flesh: Thin, sulphur-yellow, with a faint, somewhat unpleasant smell. Spores: The spore print is white; the spores are ellipsoid, measuring 8–12 × 5–9 μm. Non-amyloid, smooth. Similar species: In flower pots and greenhouses other, similar species of exotic fungi may grow, such as the white Leucocoprinus cretatus, which differs in colour.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A tropical fungus; in Poland it most often grows all year round in greenhouses and in pots with ornamental plants. A saprotroph, it decomposes peat and other dead organic matter contained in the soil.
Lycoperdon echinatum Pers. is a species of fungus in the family Lycoperdaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting bodies: Inverted pear-shaped or spherical, 2–6 cm across. Their lower part is shortly narrowed and connected to the substrate by whitish mycelial hyphae. The outer covering (exoperidium) is at first light brown, dark brown, finally umber. It has dense, sharp, wedge-shaped and angular spines up to 5 mm long. These spines do not touch at their tips. After they fall off, a net-like pattern in the form of polygonal areolae remains. The spines at the base of the fruiting body are much shorter. The endoperidium is soft, papery, at first white, then light cream, light brown, finally ochre-brown. The mature fruiting body bursts with a circular opening at the top. The subgleba is small, fairly compact, with small chambers. At first it is white, then grey-violet. During maturation of the fruiting body it gradually passes into the columella.
