The interior of the fruiting body is filled with gleba. At first it is white, then grey-violet, finally chocolate-brown. Microscopic features: Spores spherical, up to 6 μm in diameter, not hyaline. They are coarsely warty and have shortly broken-off sterigmata; remnants of sterigmata remain in the hymenium next to the spores. The capillitium is elastic, fairly thick.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North and Central America, Europe and Asia. In Poland it is rarer than other puffballs, although numerous localities have been reported in the scientific literature. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland, with status R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. It is also on lists of threatened species in Estonia, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Germany. It grows from July to October, usually in deciduous forests, under beeches on calcareous soils, on the ground, rarely moving onto rotting wood.
Lycoperdon excipuliforme (Scop.) Pers. is a species of fungus in the family Lycoperdaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Height mostly 8–12 cm, sometimes up to 15 cm, but exceptional specimens up to 26 cm tall have occurred. Width up to 5.5, sometimes up to 9.5 cm. Club-shaped or mace-shaped, sometimes inverted pear-shaped. The base is sometimes folded or pitted. The outer covering (exoperidium) is white, matt and smooth in young specimens, then rough, finely granular and scabby. In mature fruiting bodies it becomes light brown or hazel. The top part of the fruiting body is covered with delicate spines clustered in a conical manner. The spines fall off easily, leaving behind only a faintly visible pattern. The inner covering (endoperidium) is thin, smooth, in colour from ochre through grey-brown to rusty-brown. During maturation of the fruiting body, both coverings, together with the flocculent gleba inside, break up into fragments, which remain on the substrate nearby for quite a long time. After they fall off, a fairly durable, column-like or goblet-like brown subgleba remains. Microscopic features: Spores brown, spherical, 4–5.5 µm in diameter, with a warty surface and one droplet inside. Short (up to 3 µm) sterigmata are sometimes preserved on them.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of Lycoperdon excipuliforme has been described in North, Central and South America and in Europe. In Poland it is common. A terrestrial saprotrophic fungus. It appears from July to November in deciduous and coniferous forests, in clearings, meadows, less often in city parks and on railway tracks. Remnants of old fruiting bodies sometimes persist until the summer of the next year.
Fuscospina nigrescens (Pers.) R.L. Zhao & J.Xin Li, in Li, Cao, Phurbu, He, Zhu, Parra & Zhao is a species of fungus in the family Lycoperdaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Up to 4 cm in diameter, 3–6 cm tall, spherical or pear-shaped. At the base there is a tuft of hyphae. The surface is matt, papery, cream to grey-brown. It is covered with numerous large spines, which are dark from the very beginning; light brown in young fruiting bodies, brown in older ones. The spines are 2–3 mm tall and grow on cones with blackish tips. After the spines fall off, a net-like structure remains on the endoperidium (similar to Lycoperdon perlatum). The gleba is at first yellow-olive, then becomes brown. The subgleba is at first light brown, then grey-brown with an olive or violet tinge. It forms relatively large chambers with a well-developed columella. It has an unpleasant, metallic smell. Microscopic features: Spores spherical, light brown, with an almost smooth or slightly warty surface. They measure 3.4–4.8 μm. Broken sterigmata are present between the spores. The capillitium is dichotomously branched, 0.7–0.9 μm thick, medium thick-walled, rarely septate, with pits.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North America, in Europe and in Japan. In the Polish Tatra Mountains it reaches as far as the dwarf-pine zone. It appears in various forests and thickets, less often in meadows. It grows on the ground, often among fallen tree needles. It produces fruiting bodies from August to November. In Poland it is fairly rare.
Lycoperdon perlatum Pers. is a species of fungus in the family Lycoperdaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: 3–7 cm tall, 2–4 cm in diameter, club-shaped or pear-shaped, with a rounded top or one ending in an umbo. It is covered with warty spines. At first the whole fruiting body is white, when mature it becomes ochre or brown and bald. The spines break off easily when touched, leaving round scars. In the mature fruiting body its whole interior turns into an enormous number of spores; the fruiting body bursts at the top and the spores are released through the resulting opening (under the influence of wind or when touched by animals or people). Even raindrops 1 mm in diameter are enough to eject the spores. The lower part of the fruiting body is the subgleba. At first it is white, during maturation it darkens and becomes light brown, at the same time gradually turning into gleba and columella. The gleba occupying the upper part of the fruiting body is at first white, later gradually yellow, olive and grey-brown. Microscopic features: The spore mass is olive in colour. A single spore is spherical, transparent, colourless or light yellow, weakly warty and measures 3–4.5 μm. The capillitium is elastic, yellow-brown.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A cosmopolitan species, occurring almost across the whole globe; its occurrence has been recorded even in the subarctic regions of Greenland and the subalpine regions of Iceland. In Poland it is a very common species. A terrestrial saprotrophic fungus growing in forests and thickets. It sometimes also grows on rotten trunks. It occurs from summer to autumn, singly or gregariously.
Lyophyllum decastes (Fr.) Singer is a species of fungus in the family Lyophyllaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting bodies rarely grow singly, usually they grow in bundles, and their stems are fused at the base. Sometimes they grow in rows or form so-called fairy rings. Cap: 5–10 cm in diameter. Young - hemispherically convex with slightly rolled-under margins, mature - flat with sharp margins and somewhat wavy. Colour grey, grey-brown to olive-brown-blackish, silky shiny and radially delicately fibrous. Gills: First white, then greyish-cream, moderately crowded, notched with a small tooth at the stem. They are of unequal length and slightly decurrent. Stem: 7–13 cm long, 1–2 cm thick. Irregularly cylindrical, solid and usually curved. Sometimes eccentric. The surface is whitish, silky shiny (with time it becomes brown toward the bottom), bare or delicately fibrous. Flesh: White, not changing colour when cut, firm, flexible. Taste insignificant, smell indistinct. Spore print: White. Spores 5–7 µm in diameter, spherical, smooth, colourless. Similar species: Lyophyllum fumosum. It has a darker cap, a mealy smell and is more fleshy.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been reported in North America, Europe and Japan. In Poland it is not very frequent. It grows from September to early December in large clumps in meadows, gardens, deciduous forests and on rubble.
Macrocystidia cucumis (Pers.) Joss. is a species of fungus in the order Agaricales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2–5 cm in diameter, at first bell-shaped, later convex to flat. The surface is smooth and velvety, colour from red-brown to dark chestnut. The margins are lighter – yellow-brown or flesh-pink, but their lighter colour quickly disappears and in older specimens the cap margins are coloured the same as the cap. Gills: Fairly crowded, bulging, sinuately notched at the stem, at first whitish, later ochre, ochre-pink, salmon. Stem: 4–8 cm tall, 0.5 cm thick, cylindrical, hard, cartilaginous. The surface is white-mossy, in colour from dark red-brown to black-brown, lighter only right under the cap. Flesh: Dark brown, with a characteristic smell similar to cucumbers or herring. Taste mild. Some even consider that it smells of cod-liver oil. It is so intense that after taking the mushroom in the hand it lingers on the fingers for a long time. Microscopic features: Spore print ochre. Spores smooth, elliptical, non-amyloid, measuring 7–19 × 3–4.5 μm. They have a variable colour: whitish, pinkish, dirty yellowish, pale pink-brown. Cystidia lance-shaped, up to 20 μm wide and up to 90 μm long. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Macrocystidia cucumis occurs in North America and in Europe. In Poland it is fairly frequent. It grows singly or in small clusters in forests (especially under pines and firs), gardens, parks, fields, along roads. It develops on wood debris among grasses and on needles. It has also been observed on potato plantations. It produces fruiting bodies from June to November.
Macrolepiota excoriata (Schaeff.) Wasser is a species of fungus in the family Agaricaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Height from 5 to 15 cm. The colour of the fungus is white to cream. Cap convex, vaulted with a convex centre, up to 10 cm in diameter. The surface has a brownish centre, covered with scales ranging from ochre-yellow to pale brown. Gills white to cream in colour, stem smooth, cylindrical, with a bulbous base and a ring. Spores smooth, hyaline, ellipsoid. Spore print white, cream or yellowish. The ring is whitish to white. Flesh white, fibrous and does not change colour. Macrolepiota excoriata is similar to Macrolepiota procera, but Macrolepiota procera is larger.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Macrolepiota excoriata occurs in North America and Europe and can be found in fields, lawns and on roadsides. In Poland W. Wojewoda cited many localities in 2003. In foreign studies it is listed as a threatened species. A threat to this species is the overgrowing of ungrazed and unmown meadows. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus. It occurs in clearings, pastures, parks, gardens and various grassy areas, along roads and at the edges of pine forests. Fruiting bodies usually from July to October.
Macrolepiota mastoidea (Fr.) Singer is a species of fungus in the family Agaricaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 5 to 12 cm in diameter, young – egg-shaped, later convex to spread out, light brown, light flesh-ochre; the skin is at first star-like cracked, in mature fruiting bodies it remains so only in the centre, where it is also darker, elsewhere delicately dense, radially and granularly scaly, with a paler background showing through between the scales. Gills: Free at the stem, white. Stem: 10 to 15 cm tall, 0.8 to 1.5 cm in diameter, cylindrical, with a bulbous base (up to 2.5 cm), can be snapped off, smooth or slightly streaked, bast-like, tubular, the colour of light, brownish wood. It has a distinct double ring that can be slid. Flesh: Whitish, taste slightly nutty. Spore print: White. Spores measuring 13–16 (–18) × 7–9.5 (–11) µm. Similar species: Macrolepiota procera has larger fruiting bodies and a cap covered with thick, overlapping scales. Macrolepiota excoriata has a lighter stem and scales on the cap.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs only in Europe. In Poland it occurs throughout the country, is fairly rare, but is not on the list of threatened species. It produces fruiting bodies from August to November in open deciduous and coniferous forests, at their edge, along forest roads. In places it is fairly common.
Macrolepiota procera (Scop.) Singer is a species of fungus in the family Agaricaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Umbrella-shaped, 10–30 cm in diameter with an umbo in the centre, with cracked, flaking skin. Egg-shaped and closed when young, then conical, low-arched, finally flat and spread out. In young ones the whole cap is brown, in older ones whitish with large brown scales. The cap margin is ragged, usually white. Gills: Crowded, broad, not reaching the stem. In older specimens they have an ochre bloom. Stem: 15–40 cm long and up to 2 cm thick, cylindrical, ending at the bottom in a bulb up to 4 cm in diameter. It is easy to snap off. At first it is solid and spongy, in older fruiting bodies hollow inside. It has a movable ring. Above the ring the stem skin is whitish-brown and smooth, below there are darker transverse bands. Flesh: Soft in the cap, bast-like in the stem. It is white, does not change colour when damaged. Taste mild, pleasant. It gives off a delicate mushroomy-fruity smell. Spore print: White. Spores ellipsoid, smooth, measuring 15–20 × 10–13 μm. Similar species: The most similar is the so-called Chlorophyllum rhacodes.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North America, Europe, Korea, Japan and New Zealand. In Poland it is fairly common throughout the country. A terrestrial fungus, a saprotroph. It grows at the edges of deciduous and coniferous forests, in forest clearings and clearcuts, in meadows, parks, on roadsides, in cemeteries. It avoids acidic and wet habitats, growing most often on clayey soils rich in calcium. It produces fruiting bodies from summer to late autumn.
Typhula fistulosa (Holmsk.) Olariaga is a species of fungus in the family Typhulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Thin and slender, up to 300 mm tall, but usually not exceeding 20 cm in height. Diameter 5–10 mm. Rod-shaped, narrowly club-shaped, sometimes cylindrical, slender, elongated, at first pale yellow, with age darkens and becomes yellow-brown, brownish, red-brown to brown. Single, unbranched, the tip not forked, rounded or pointed. Hollow inside, walls thin. The hymenial layer is on the outside of the fruiting body, occupying the surface of about 2/3 of its height in the upper part. It looks as if lightly dusted. Stem: There is no stem as such, but the lower part of the fruiting body, about 1/3 of its height at the base, is sterile – it lacks hymenium and so does not produce spores. Its colour is slightly darker than the rest of the fruiting body, and the surface is visibly smoother. Flesh: In young fruiting bodies it is hard and stiff, with age it becomes softer. Taste and smell imperceptible. Spore print: White. Spores smooth, ovoid, hyaline. Measuring 12–18 × 5–7 µm. Similar species: Typhula fistulosa is a fungus of characteristic appearance and large size.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North America and Europe. In Poland it is a rare species. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland, with status R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. Fruiting bodies appear in late autumn on old oak and beech leaves; usually singly, less often in small groups.
Typhula juncea (Alb. & Schwein.) P. Karst. is a species of fungus in the family Typhulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Very thin and slender; usually single, sometimes forked at the top; smooth and hollow inside; ochre-yellow to flesh-brown, slightly fibrous-felty at the base. It is up to 5 cm tall, but only 1–2 mm thick. Similar species: Typhula fistulosa occurs in late autumn on fallen leaves, but is much larger (up to 20–30 cm tall and about 5–10 mm thick). It usually grows singly and is relatively rare.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs on all continents except Antarctica. In Poland it is a rare species. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland, with status R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. It grows in forests, on fallen leaves of deciduous trees and shrubs, especially silver birch, poplar and oaks. It produces fruiting bodies from October to November.
Marasmius oreades (Bolton) Fr. is a species of fungus in the family Marasmiaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 1–4 (up to 6) cm in diameter, leather-yellow or ochre-brownish (paler, whitish when dry), hygrophanous, with a margin striate from the gills showing through, smooth and bare. Conical when young, later convex, flat in the mature fruiting body, often with a blunt umbo in the centre. Gills: Very distant, whitish, ochre after rain, cream during drought, slightly darker when moistened. Stem: 6–7 cm tall, about 0.5 cm thick. Cylindrical, solid, flexible, not brittle, pale ochre, whitish-yellowish. Flesh: Pale yellow. Thin, white, not changing colour when cut. It has a pleasant mushroomy smell and a delicate taste. Spore print: White. Spores 7–10 × 4–6 µm, ovoid, smooth, colourless. Similar species: Some funnel caps (Clitocybe). They differ in attached and strongly decurrent gills. They also have a less flexible stem, more crowded gills, a frosted cap and a different smell. Gymnopus peronata.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in the temperate zone across the whole Northern Hemisphere, and also in Australia. In Central Europe Marasmius oreades is very common, and so it is in Poland. It grows in meadows, pastures, along field paths, at the edge of forests. It produces fruiting bodies from May to November. Its fruiting bodies often form fairy rings. Sometimes they reach a diameter of 20 cm. Its mycelium releases ammonia, which colours the grass around it blue-green and causes it to die.
Marasmius rotula (Scop.) Fr. is a species of fungus in the family Marasmiaceae. The type species of the genus Marasmius.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 6–15 mm in diameter, hemispherical and deeply scalloped, as a result of which it resembles a baking mould. The surface is bare, whitish, with an ochre-brown depression in the centre. Gills: Whitish, with a regular trama, very widely spaced. At the stem they fuse, forming a collar around it. Stem: Shiny, thread-like, red-brown (lighter near the cap, blackish at the base). Flesh: Very thin, without smell and taste. Similar species: There are many similar, small species of Marasmius living on leaves and wood debris. Marasmius rotula can be recognised fairly easily by the characteristic collar ("collarium") formed by its gills around the stem. Similar are: Marasmius epiphyllus. It grows on leaves and has a milky-white, more spread-out cap. Older caps are wrinkled. It is easy to tell apart by the gills, which are very narrow, almost vein-like; Marasmius tremulae. Very small, grows on aspen leaves. It has different microscopic features (among others two-spored basidia and cylindrical spores); Marasmius bulliardii.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Widespread in Europe and North America. Its localities are also known in South America, Central America and Korea. In Central Europe very common. In Poland also very common. A saprotroph. It occurs on leaves and twigs of deciduous trees, sometimes also on partly buried plant remains. It produces fruiting bodies from May to October, in clumps or gregariously.
Megacollybia platyphylla (Pers.) Kotl. & Pouzar is a species of fungus in the order Agaricales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 5–15 cm in diameter, hemispherical in young specimens, later flat-convex, finally flat and radially cracked. It often has a small, blunt umbo. The surface has distinct, grown-in fibrils, colour brown-grey, olive, grey-brown, smoky-brown. Gills: Very broad, distant and sinuately notched. They are white to dirty white, sometimes veined in the lower part. They have serrated or scalloped edges and are rounded at the stem. Springtails often live between the gills. Stem: 6–15 cm tall, 1–2 cm thick. It is longitudinally fibrous, at first whitish, then grey-brown, lighter than the cap. At the base of the stem there are large rhizomorphs, which can reach a length of even several metres. They penetrate wood and soil, and fruiting bodies often appear only at some distance from the organic matter on which the fungus feeds. Flesh: White and fairly bast-like. Thin, so that the cap seen against the sun is translucent. Taste mild, smell indistinct. Spore print: White. Spores nearly spherical, smooth, measuring 7–8 × 6–7 μm. Similar species: Pluteus cervinus.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Megacollybia platyphylla is widespread in Europe and Central America. Beyond these two continents constituting the main area of its occurrence, its localities have also been described in Central America and Japan. In Central Europe it is a fairly common species, and so it is in Poland. A saprotroph. It occurs in various types of forests, more often deciduous. Fruiting bodies appear from May to October on heavily rotten wood (most often deciduous). It grows on rotting wood of deciduous and coniferous trees, most often on beech wood.
Meripilus giganteus (Pers.) P. Karst. is a species of fungus in the family Meripilaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting bodies: This is one of the largest tree-dwelling fungi, whose single rosettes reach a weight of up to over a dozen kilograms, and clusters of fruiting bodies at one trunk up to several dozen kilograms. Fruiting bodies are annual, large, reaching a diameter of 30 to 80 cm, with many overlapping, fan-shaped or semicircular caps growing from a common base, sometimes on short stems. The surface of the caps is at first yellow-brown, later brownish, chestnut, distinctly concentrically banded, covered with small scales. The margin of the caps is lighter, cream, rounded, wavy with age. Tubes: Short, whitish, turning brown when damaged and then blackening. Pores very small, circular, about 0.3 mm in diameter. Flesh: White, bast-like, fibrous, blackening on the cut surface, with a strongly mushroomy smell and a sourish taste. Spores: Smooth, colourless, ovoid to circular. Similar species: Grifola frondosa, which occurs almost exclusively on oaks and has much smaller and narrower caps.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Recorded in North America, Europe, Asia, North Africa and New Zealand. In Poland numerous localities have been described in the scientific literature. Until October 2014 it was on the list of protected fungi. A tree-dwelling fungus. It grows at the base of various species of deciduous trees, exceptionally also coniferous trees. Usually near dead trunks, less often as a parasite of living trees. It readily grows in anthropogenic habitats: parks, roadside trees. In natural forest complexes it is found exceptionally rarely.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Head: Mostly 3–10 cm tall and 3–7 cm in diameter, beige or ochre (sometimes grey or almost black), of oval or conical habit (hollow inside), attached to the stem, with irregular alveoli (pits) on the surface, between which the ribs are arranged in a way that shows no particular direction. Stem: 2–6 cm long and 2–4 cm in diameter. Cream, yellow or whitish, hollow inside, with a rough or granular surface. In mature fruiting bodies the base of the stem is widened and folded. Flesh: Whitish, brittle, of waxy consistency, mild taste and spicy smell. Spores: Elliptical, smooth, measuring 16–23 × 11–14 μm, with a surface often covered with droplets. The spore print is yellow-ochre. Similar species: Gyromitra esculenta and Gyromitra gigas – have a head that is not so elongated but wide and folded like a brain; Morchella crassipes – is larger and has a thick stem, which in addition is granular and warty at the top.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The most localities have been reported in Europe, where it occurs throughout. In Poland it is rare. On the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland it has status R – rare species. It occurs throughout the country; by 2020 about 260 of its localities had been reported. They need to be checked for the correctness of the species identification, however, because taxonomy of these fungi has changed a lot recently. A terrestrial fungus. It develops in deciduous and mixed forests, also in meadows and riparian forests, often under ash trees, sometimes on green-overgrown dumps, on fertilised soils.
Morchella importuna M.Kuo, O'Donnell & T.J.Volk is a species of fungus in the family Morchellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Head: Conical in shape, sometimes egg-shaped, differing greatly in size among specimens. Height 3–15 cm, diameter 2–9 cm. The surface is ribbed; between tall and thin vertical ribs there are alveoli forming vertical rows of 12–20 separated by low ridges. The ribs are pale to dark grey, with age become dark grey-brown to almost black; the alveoli are grey to dark grey when immature, grey-brown, greyish-olive or brownish-yellow when mature. Stem: 3–10 cm tall and 2–6 wide, hollow inside, very brittle. The surface is smooth, bare, scalloped in mature specimens, at first whitish, then yellowish or ochre. It is often slightly thicker near the base. Its whitish to pale brownish surface is smooth or finely mealy with whitish granules. Flesh: The flesh is whitish to watery brown, 1–3 mm thick in the hollow cap; in the stem this tissue is sometimes arranged in chambers or layers. The sterile inner surface of the cap is whitish and hairy (covered with a short, soft "pile"). Microscopic features:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Morchella importuna is a saprotroph whose fruiting bodies grow in wood and bark chips, gardens, fire sites, flower pots and places of anthropogenic disturbance in cities. Kuo suggests that this species has a tendency toward mycorrhiza when it grows among trees. This morel is known primarily from northern California and the Pacific Northwest; it has also been recorded in British Columbia (Canada), California, Washington, Nevada and Oregon, and there were isolated cases in the Midwest and eastern North America. The fungus fruits in spring, from March to May.
Morchella semilibera DC. is a species of fungus in the family Morchellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Head: Bell-shaped to bell-conical in shape, differing greatly in size among specimens. Height 2–8 cm, diameter 1.4 cm. It is attached to the stem by its upper part; the lower 1/3 to 1/2 is free. The surface is ribbed; between tall and thin vertical ribs there are alveoli forming vertical rows separated by low ridges. The alveoli range from yellow-brown through light brown to olive-brown, the ribs and ridges from dark brown to black-brown. Stem: Tall in relation to the head (5–12 cm) and thick (1–3 cm), hollow inside, very brittle. The surface is smooth, bare, scalloped in mature specimens, at first whitish, then yellowish or ochre. Flesh: 2–3 mm thick, waxy, brittle, white. Smell pleasant, spicy, fairly strong. Microscopic features: Spore print olive-yellow to pale ochre. Spores ellipsoid, hyaline, smooth, without guttules, 20–30 × 12–18 µm. Similar species: Morchella elata is distinguished by a dusted stem. Verpa bohemica has the head attached only at the top.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of Morchella semilibera is known in Europe and North America. In Poland it occurs throughout the country, but is rare. About 100 of its localities have been reported. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland, with status R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. Since 2014 in Poland it has been under partial protection of fungi (specimens growing outside gardens, horticultural crops, forest nurseries and outside green areas are protected). In 1983–2014 it was under strict protection.
Multiclavula mucida (Pers.) R.H. Petersen is a species of lichen. It is a representative of a small group of lichens in which the mycobiont is a fungus classified in the phylum Basidiomycota.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Forms slender, club-shaped fruiting bodies measuring 5–17 × 1–2 (3) mm. They are mostly single, rarely branched. They are white to cream, older fruiting bodies sometimes have a pinkish tinge. At the top they are mostly darker. The fruiting body grows from a delicate primary thallus forming a thin film on the surface of the trunk, composed of white fungal hyphae and green algae of the genus Coccomyxa. Spores: Thin-walled, cylindrical to slightly kidney-shaped, measuring 5.0–6.8 × 2.2–2.9 µm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of Multiclavula mucida is known on all continents except Africa and Antarctica. In Poland four localities had been reported by 2003, some of them old. In 2016 two new localities were reported in the Bieszczady National Park. Current localities are also given by the online fungi atlas. Multiclavula mucida occurs on rotting, moist wood. It is regarded as an indicator species of natural forests.
Mutinus caninus (Huds.) Fr. is a species of fungus in the family Phallaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Young fruiting bodies (the so-called egg): ovoid, up to about 4 cm tall and 2.5 cm wide, whitish. The mature fruiting body reaches a height of 16 cm and a thickness of 1 cm. The cap is cone-shaped, covered with a sticky dark olive spore mass. After the spores are dispersed, the upper part of the cap and the upper part of the stem are apricot or yellow-orange. The smell of young fruiting bodies is pleasant, resembling tobacco or fruit; older specimens have a smell similar to that of Phallus impudicus, but much weaker. Spores: Ellipsoid, smooth, coloured, measuring 4–5 µm in length and 1.5–2 µm in width. Similar species: Mutinus ravenelii.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Widespread. Recorded on all continents except Africa and Antarctica. In Poland it is rare. On the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland it has status V – vulnerable to extinction. In Poland it was a strictly protected species. Since 9 October 2014 it has been removed from the list of protected fungus species. It grows most often in moist, shady deciduous forests, on fertile soils. It usually occurs in groups. Fruiting bodies appear in summer and autumn.
Mutinus ravenelii (Berk. & M.A. Curtis) E. Fisch. is a species of fungus in the family Phallaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: At first it has the form of an egg measuring 2–1.5 cm, covered with a white and smooth peridium. The developing fruiting body pierces the upper part of the peridium and grows upward, forming a cylindrical receptaculum. Sometimes part of the ruptured peridium remains at the tip of the receptaculum, forming a kind of small cap. The receptaculum is 6–7 cm tall, exceptionally up to 10 cm, and 1 cm thick. It is cylindrical in shape, with a slightly narrowed base and a pointed tip. Inside, the receptaculum is hollow, and sometimes there is a small opening at the top. The lower, sterile part of the receptaculum is whitish with a raspberry tinge, sometimes completely white. The upper, fertile part is strongly raspberry-coloured and covered with an olive-green, slimy spore mass, which produces a strong and very unpleasant smell similar to that of faeces or rotting meat. With this smell it attracts carrion-feeding insects, which land on the fruiting body, and spores stick to their legs, being carried by the insects often over considerable distances. It has also been observed that the fruiting bodies of this fungus are readily eaten by dogs, without harm to their health. Spores: Smooth and ellipsoid, measuring 4–6 × 1–3 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A synanthropic species originating from North America. It is expanding its range. In Europe it was first found in Germany in 1943. At present it is widespread in Europe, and has also appeared in New Zealand. It is also found in Poland. In Poland Mutinus ravenelii was first observed in Kraków in 1965. It occurred there in moist places, on humus soil. In natural habitats it was first observed in 1987 in the Kampinos National Park.
Mycena crocata (Schrad.) P. Kumm. is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 5–25 (–38) mm in diameter, conical, bell-shaped or parabolic with a small umbo, shallowly grooved, slightly translucent-striate. The surface is dusted, in the centre ranging from dark red through orange-brown to grey-brown, lighter near the margin – whitish or greyish, with yellow-red to orange-red spots. Gills: 15–20 reach the stem, narrow, with yellow-red to orange-red spots. Stem: 50–95 mm tall, 1–2 mm thick, cylindrical, hollow inside, straight or slightly bent, firm. The surface is delicately or strongly hairy, more or less shiny, at the base ranging from bright orange to reddish, rooting. When cut it exudes saffron-red latex. The base is densely covered with long, thick fibres whitish to orange-yellow. Flesh: Without distinct smell. Microscopic features: Basidia 25–37 × 8–10 µm, club-shaped, 4-spored with sterigmata 5–7 µm long. Spores 8.2–11.5 × 5–7 µm, pipette-shaped, smooth, amyloid.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of Mycena crocata has been described in North America, Europe, Japan and Korea. Władysław Wojewoda cited numerous localities in his 2003 checklist of the large-fruited fungi of Poland. Numerous and more recent localities are given by the online fungi atlas. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland, with status R – a species potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. A saprotrophic fungus.
Mycena epipterygia (Scop.) Gray is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 1–3 cm in diameter, at first bell-shaped, later bell-arched and usually with a flat umbo. The bands of the gills show through. The margin is serrated. The surface is smooth, radially grooved, sticky and slippery. It has a very varied colour; yellow-greenish, yellow-brown, greenish, ochre or grey-yellowish. The top of the cap is darker than the margins. Hygrophanous – whitish when dry. In mature fruiting bodies it is sometimes covered with brown spots. When pressed it discolours brown-red. The skin is rubbery, easily peeled off the whole cap. Mycena epipterygia is characterised by a great variety of colour forms. In Poland, besides the typical form, two varieties have been described: green-stemmed (var. epipterygioides) and tree-dwelling (var. viscosa). Hymenophore: Gilled; the gills are whitish or greyish, sometimes with brownish spots, broadly attached or decurrent on the stem, with a regular trama. The gill edges are gelatinous and easily separating. Stem: 3–8 cm tall, 1–3 mm thick, cylindrical, hollow inside, smooth, slippery, yellowish or green-yellowish. Like the cap it is covered with a slippery skin that is easily separated.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Mycena epipterygia occurs on all continents except Antarctica. In Poland it is common. A saprotroph developing in coniferous and deciduous forests, on the ground or wood. Fruiting lasts from August to November. It often grows among mosses.
Mycena galericulata (Scop.) Gray is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2–6 cm in diameter, conical-bell-shaped in young specimens, flat with an umbo in older ones, indistinctly wrinkled, bare. Horn-brownish, grey-brown or flesh-brownish in colour, darker in the centre. Hymenophore: Gilled; the gills are distant, at first whitish, then always slightly pinkish or beige-pink, with a regular trama, sinuately attached to the stem and joined by veins. Stem: 3–7 cm tall, 2–4 mm thick, cylindrical and hollow inside, hard, smooth, shiny, with a rooting base. Colour whitish or greyish. Flesh: Bast-like in the stem, with a faint mealy smell released on rubbing. Taste cucumber-mealy. Spore print: White, amyloid. Spores ellipsoid, measuring 9–12 × 6.5–9 μm with a smooth surface, without a germ pore. Basidia two-spored. Similar species: Mycena polygramma – distinguished by a distinctly scalloped stem and in adult specimens the gills are not pinkish; Mycena inclinata is distinguished by a cucumber smell and also lacks pink gills.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Mycena galericulata is widespread across the whole Northern Hemisphere. In Europe it occurs both in the lowlands and in the mountains. In Poland it is very common. It grows in various types of forests. Fungi of this species develop on dead wood of coniferous and deciduous trees, also on forest litter. Fruiting lasts from May to November, and the fruiting bodies often grow in groups.
Mycena haematopus (Pers.) P. Kumm. is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 1–3 cm in diameter, hemispherical in young fruiting bodies, later bell-shaped, conical-bell-shaped with an umbo in older ones. The margin is slightly serrated and usually hung with colourless hyphae (as if with a hem). The surface is smooth, grooved to the middle of the cap, in colour from flesh-brown through reddish-brown to pink-brown. The centre is usually darker. Damaged places discolour blood-red. Gills: Decurrent with a small tooth on the stem or attached to it. Colour in young fruiting bodies from whitish to pink, in older ones darker. Edges smooth. Stem: 3–7 cm tall, up to 3.5 mm thick, cylindrical, hollow inside. The surface is of a similar colour to the cap, entirely covered with small flakes, so that it looks frosted. The base is usually felty. Flesh: Very thin; from a damaged one a blood-red liquid oozes. Taste mild, smell indistinct. Microscopic features: Spore print white. Spores broadly elliptical, smooth, measuring 8–11 × 5–7 µm, weakly amyloid. Cheilocystidia numerous, spindle-shaped, with elongated and slightly pointed tips. They measure 80 × 12 µm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North America and in Europe. In Poland a very common species. It develops on dead wood of deciduous trees: on trunks, stumps and fallen branches. It produces fruiting bodies from April to October. In Poland it has been recorded on the wood of sycamore maple, grey alder, silver birch, cherry, dogwood, hazel, hawthorn, beech, ash, plum, pedunculate oak, sessile oak, black locust, willow and linden. On coniferous trees it occurs rarely.
Mycena pseudocorticola Kühner is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2–12 mm in diameter, hemispherical, parabolic, broadly conical to convex, sometimes with a small papilla, often slightly flattened in the centre, grooved, translucent-striate. The surface is dusted, glistening, dark blue, bluish-grey or grey, turning brown with age. Gills: 8–14 reach the stem, fairly broad, convex, broadly attached and decurrent with a short tooth, grey to pale bluish-grey or grey-white, becoming pale sepia-brown with age. Edges lighter. Stem: 5–25 mm tall, 0.2–1 mm thick, straight or bent. The surface is flocculose-dusted, from grey to bluish-grey, more brownish with age. The base is densely covered with long, white fibrils. Flesh: Without smell. Microscopic features: Basidia 25–36 × 9–12 µm, club-shaped, 4-spored with clamp connections, or 2-spored without clamp connections, with swollen sterigmata up to 13 µm long. Spores on 4-spored basidia 8–10.5 × 7.5–10 µm, on 2-spored basidia 13 × 12 µm, spherical or almost spherical, smooth, amyloid.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of Mycena pseudocorticola is known in some European countries; its occurrence has also been reported in North America and Morocco. Władysław Wojewoda in his 2003 checklist of the large-fruited fungi of Poland cites 10 localities, noting that this species is rare. More recent localities are given by the online fungi atlas. It is classed there as a rare species worth protecting. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland.
Mycena pura (Pers.) P. Kumm. is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: The colours of this species are very variable. In young fruiting bodies there are lilac and violet shades, but during maturation they change considerably and the fruiting bodies take on whitish, yellowish, pink, brown and even red colouring. The colour of the fruiting bodies is not sufficient to identify this Mycena. Cap: 2–6 cm in diameter, shape at first convex to bell-shaped, then spread out. The surface is bare, at first lilac-violet, later whitish, yellowish, pink-brown or reddish. Gills: Moderately crowded, sinuately attached to the stem, colour from whitish to grey-white, often flushed pink or violet. Near the stem they are often joined by anastomoses. Stem: 4–10 cm tall, 0.4–0.6 cm thick, cylindrical, hollow, fragile. The surface is shiny, smooth or with fine hairs, whitish or the colour of the cap. Flesh: Watery, whitish or greyish. Smell and taste distinctly resembling radish. Microscopic features: Spore print: White. Microscopic features: Spores long-elliptical or almost cylindrical, weakly amyloid or non-amyloid, with a smooth surface. They measure 6–10 × 3–4 μm. Basidia with 4 sterigmata.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A widespread species; except Antarctica it occurs on all continents and on many islands. In Europe the northern limit of its range runs through Iceland and the northern regions of the Scandinavian Peninsula. In Central Europe it is one of the most frequently occurring fungi, and in Poland too it is very common. It produces fruiting bodies from spring to autumn. It occurs in deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests, in thickets, but also in open areas; in meadows, fallow land, grassy swards and so on.
Mycena renati Quel. is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 1–3 cm in diameter, bell-shaped in young fruiting bodies, later broadly bell-shaped, finally arched. Margins usually serrated. The surface is smooth. It is hygrophanous. In dry weather it is matt, radially fibrous, and pinkish with a darker apex. In wet weather it becomes grooved with gills showing through, and ranges from yellow-brown to red-brown. It usually has a smaller or larger umbo. Gills: Broad, decurrent with a small tooth, white or slightly pinkish, with smooth edges. Stem: 3–8 cm tall, 2–4 mm thick. It is cylindrical and hollow. The surface is smooth, bare, shiny, golden-yellow or orange-yellow. At the base there is felty mycelium. Flesh: Thin, watery, brittle, yellow in the stem, whitish in the cap. Taste mild, similar to radish; the smell of young fruiting bodies resembles chlorine, of older ones radish. Similar species: Mycena inclinata. It also grows on rotten wood, but has greyish gills and the stem is red-brownish in the lower part; Mycena alcalina. It is distinguished by a smell of ammonia.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs only in Europe. In Poland it occurs mainly in Carpathian beech forest, less often in spruce and pine forests. It usually grows in clumps. It grows in moist forests on dead and already heavily rotten wood of deciduous trees, especially beeches and oaks. It produces fruiting bodies from May to September.
Mycena rosea Gramberg is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2–5 cm in diameter, spherical when young, then flat, finally completely spread out. In the centre it has an umbo. It is markedly hygrophanous; when moist the cap is striate because the gills show through. Colour from pale pink to pink, while the umbo in dry weather, as a result of drying, is cream-yellow or yellow. Gills: Distant, bellied, and at the stem notched and narrow. Gill edges smooth. At first white, with time becoming pale pink. Stem: 4–7 cm tall, up to 0.7 cm thick, cylindrical, straight, with a slightly thickened base. Solid in young specimens, tubular in older ones. Colour whitish or white-pink, surface delicately fibrous. Flesh: Thin, white, with a faint taste and smell of radish. Spore print: White. Spores broadly elliptical, amyloid with a smooth surface. On one side they have a bent-back beak. Size: 6–9 × 2.5–4 μm. Similar species: It may be confused with Mycena pura. That Mycena has a more violet shade and occurs in coniferous forests.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs on all continents except Australia and Antarctica. In Europe it is common. A saprotroph. It grows on the ground in deciduous and mixed forests on forest litter, particularly often on calcareous soils. Fruiting bodies appear from May to October.
Mycena tintinnabulum (Paulet) Quél. is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 0.5–2 cm in diameter, bluntly bell-shaped in young ones, later conical, finally spread out. The centre of the cap is usually flat. The gills show through, as a result of which the cap is radially striate. It is hygrophanous; when moist it is sticky. The surface is bare, smooth, silky shiny, brown, sepia, grey-brown, or dark red-brown, sometimes dark chocolate-brown. Hymenophore: Gilled; the gills are attached and slightly decurrent with a small tooth, with wavy edges. Intermediate gills are present. At first the gills are light grey with a pinkish tinge, later flesh-pinkish. Stem: 1–7 cm tall, 1–3 mm thick, tubular, bent, hard and cartilaginous. The surface is smooth, slightly sticky when moist, shiny when dry. Pale grey, beige, often reddish at the base and passing into a pseudorhiza covered with protruding white hyphae. Flesh: Very thin, beige-grey, with an indistinct, bitter taste. It has a smell similar to potato peelings or chlorine. The smell quickly fades. Spore print: White. Spores ellipsoid or stone-shaped with an indistinct beak, with a smooth surface, amyloid and hyaline.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Mycena tintinnabulum occurs mainly in Europe; besides that, in the USA it is known from only a few localities. In Poland it is fairly rare. It grows in various types of forests, parks and avenues on dead wood; on stumps, fallen trunks and boughs of deciduous trees. It has been observed on the wood of grey alder, birches, beeches, oaks and willows. It occurs particularly often on the wood of alders and willows. It produces fruiting bodies from August to December. It is one of the few fungus species that appear very late in autumn and in winter during frost-free periods.
Mycena zephirus (Fr.) P. Kumm. is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2–5 cm in diameter, shape at first parabolic or conical, with a rounded umbo, gradually flattening. It is grooved to 2/3 of the diameter. The margin is uneven. The surface is smooth, matt in dry weather, ranging from dirty whitish through light cream and light pink to flesh-brown. The apex of the cap is distinctly darker. On the cap there are rusty-brown, radial spots. Gills: Broad and fairly distant, attached or weakly sinuately notched. They are white-grey, and in older specimens red-brown spots occur on them. Transverse anastomoses are frequent. Stem: 3–8 cm tall, up to 4 mm thick. It is cylindrical, hollow inside (tubular). The surface is fibrillose, grey-brown, covered with short white tufts only at the top. White hairs also occur at the base of the stem. Flesh: Thin, watery and brittle. Grey in colour, taste mild, smell similar to radish. Microscopic features: Basidia with four sterigmata, thickened, measuring 28–32 × 7–8.5 μm. Spores elongated, almost cylindrical, smooth, amyloid, measuring 8.5–12.2 × 4–5 (–6) μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs only in Europe. In Poland it is common. It most often grows in coniferous forests on rotting needles of trees, forest litter, among mosses. It is particularly frequent under spruces and pines. It also occurs in parks. It produces fruiting bodies from August to November.
Mycetinis alliaceus (Jacq.) Earle ex A.W. Wilson & Desjardin is a species of fungus in the family Omphalotaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 2–4 cm in diameter, shape at first bell-shaped, later convex, finally spread out. Colour fairly variable; from light ochre to dark brown. The surface is matt, dry, sometimes wrinkled, the margin smooth or grooved. Gills: Dirty whitish or greyish, with a regular trama. Stem: Thin and long. It is up to 10 cm tall and 1–2 mm thick. The surface is matt, black-brown or black and white-frosted (felty). The base is rooting. It is tough, fibrous, of cartilaginous consistency and so flexible that it cannot be snapped. Flesh: Thin, whitish. It has a mild taste and a strong smell of garlic. Spore print: White or cream. Spores broadly ellipsoid to almost spherical in shape, smooth, measuring 7–11 × 6–8 µm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in Europe. In Poland it is not very frequent. It is found in deciduous forests and in parks, always in the presence of beeches. It grows on the ground, on wood debris, especially wood located underground. It produces fruiting bodies from May to November.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: Mycetinis scorodonius. It also has a garlic smell, but is smaller and grows in coniferous forests. Its stem is not black but purple-brown.
Neolentinus lepideus (Fr.) Redhead & Ginns is a species of fungus in the order Gloeophyllales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 5–11 cm in diameter, conical when young, later flat with a blunt umbo or shallowly depressed in the centre. The surface is matt, dry, cream to light brown, covered with adhering, darker (brown) scales. These scales are larger in the centre, finer near the cap margin. Gills: Broad and broadly attached, running down the stem as far as the ring zone. They have wavy and serrated edges. Stem: 3–7 cm tall, up to 2 cm thick, cylindrical or conical in shape, solid and springy. The surface is whitish; above the ring zone in young specimens there is a felty sheath, below it the stem is covered with scales, and the base itself is brown to black-brown. Flesh: Soft in young specimens, springy, hard and woody in older ones. Whitish, smell sweetish-anise, taste indistinct. Spore print: White. Spores ellipsoid, smooth, measuring 10–15 × 4–5 μm.

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: Occurs across the whole Northern Hemisphere. A tree-dwelling fungus. It appears in coniferous and mixed forests, but also in cities, on railway sleepers and in coal mines. It develops on roots, beams and posts, mainly on pine and larch wood. It is also not rare on plantations of coniferous trees. It produces fruiting bodies from June to November.
Otidea onotica (Pers.) Fuckel is a species of fungus in the order Pezizales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Ear-shaped on one side, usually with a slit down to the base, bent, somewhat rooting and white-felty; the spore-bearing layer strongly orange to yellow; on the outside delicately mealy. Up to 4 cm wide. Flesh white, without smell, with a mild taste. Similar species: A whole series of species that are hard to tell apart are known. Otidea leporina differs only in its rusty-yellow colour – when young, and later cinnamon-brown. In beech forests the relatively rare Otidea conccinna occurs; it has densely growing, strongly lemon-yellow fruiting bodies, rolled up and slit on one side.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Otidea onotica is recorded in Europe and North America, and besides that its localities have been reported only in Bhutan. In Poland it is relatively rare. A saprotrophic fungus. It grows mostly in small groups in deciduous and coniferous forests.
Mucidula mucida (Schrad.) Pat. is a species of fungus in the family Physalacriaceae. Worldwide there are 15 species of monetka growing in the tropical and temperate zones.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 3–10 cm in diameter, hemispherical in young specimens, then flatter and flatter, finally spread out with a blunt umbo. The margin is sharp, wrinkled-striate. The surface is pure white or whitish, ivory-coloured, at the top sometimes ochre, sometimes translucent. In wet weather very sticky, slimy and gluey, in dry weather silky matt, smooth. Gills: White, broad, bulging, distant, straight-attached, sinuately notched to slightly decurrent. Stem: 4–10 cm tall, 0.5–1 cm thick, cylindrical, solid, hard, often bent. The surface is smooth, sticky and whitish, brownish only toward the bottom. It has a large drooping or protruding ring. Flesh: White, very thin and soft in the cap, fibrous and hard in the stem. Taste mild, no smell. It does not change colour when damaged. Spore print: White. Spores almost spherical, smooth, measuring 14–18 × 12–16 µm. Similar species: It is hard to confuse with other species of fungi, since none of the species growing on wood has such a pure white, porcelain-shiny and slippery cap.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been described only in Europe and East Asia: in Japan, Korea and Taiwan. In Poland it is not very frequent. It grows in forests and parks. Fruiting bodies grow in bundles from June to November, on logs and trunks of dead beeches, often at a great height.
Panellus mitis (Pers.) Singer is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 1–2 cm in diameter, shell-shaped, hemispherical or kidney-shaped. Colour whitish, in older specimens turning clay-brown or red-brown. The surface is delicate, felty on young fruiting bodies, smooth on older ones. It is rubbery, sticky and can be peeled off easily. Gills: Crowded and running down the stem. They are white, with coloured, band-like discolourations on the edges. Stem: 2–5 mm long, 3–5 mm thick. It grows laterally, is short, triangular in cross-section and solid. The surface is white, covered with small scales. Sometimes the stem is absent. Flesh: Thin, bast-like, white. Taste mild, no smell. Spore print: White. Spores sausage-shaped, amyloid, measuring 3.5–5 × 1–1.5 μm. Similar species: It may be confused with Crepidotus mollis, which differs among other things in having no stem, or with Pleurocybella porrigens, which also has no stem and is larger.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Occurs in North America and Europe. In Central Europe it is fairly common. It grows on the wood of coniferous trees; on dead trees, on dead branches hanging or lying on the ground, in brushwood piles. It is a late-autumn and winter fungus, its fruiting bodies appearing mainly from September to April, although sometimes they also appear in summer.
Panellus stipticus (Bull.) P. Karst. is a species of fungus in the family Mycenaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 1–4 cm in diameter, round or kidney-shaped, with a wavy and rolled-under margin. Ochre in colour. The cap skin is matt, at first smooth, in older specimens scaly with a mosaic pattern. Gills: Crowded and clearly delimited from the stem. Colour from pale beige to ochre-brown. Stem: 1–2 cm tall, 0.5 cm thick. It grows laterally, is short and very broad at the point of attachment to the cap. The surface is felty, ochre-brown in colour. Flesh: Thin, bast-like, ochre-coloured. Smell faint, taste bitter, strongly astringent. Spore print: Light ochre. Spores smooth, broadly ellipsoid, very small, measuring 2–3 × 1–1.5 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A cosmopolitan species. Except for Antarctica it occurs on all continents, and also on many islands. In Poland it is very common. It occurs on dead and rotting wood, mainly of deciduous trees, on the wood of coniferous trees very rarely. It grows particularly often on oaks. It usually occurs in clumps.
Panus conchatus (Bull.) Fr. is a species of fungus in the order Polyporales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: The vast majority of species in the order Polyporales have a tubular hymenophore. Panus conchatus belongs to a small group of species with a gilled hymenophore. However, phylogenetic studies have shown that despite this distinctness it is closely related to the family Polyporaceae. Cap: 4–12 cm wide, shell-shaped or tongue-shaped, funnel-like depressed in the centre. The surface is smooth or velvety, lilac in young specimens, from ochre to red-brown in older ones. Gills: Running deeply down the stem, crowded, from pale lilac to ochre in colour. Stem: 1–3 cm tall, 1–2 cm thick, eccentric. The surface is felty, colour from ochre-brown to lilac. Flesh: Whitish, bast-like and leathery. Spore print: White. Spores elliptical, non-amyloid, measuring 7–5 × 2.5–3 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Recorded in North, Central and South America, Europe and Asia. It is widespread, but rare everywhere. Its fruiting bodies grow from summer to autumn on dead wood of deciduous trees, mainly on trunks and stumps. It most often occurs in moist riparian forests. It usually occurs gregariously. It grows on various tree species, most often on birches, aspen and oaks. Fruiting bodies grow from July to November.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: Lentinus suavissimus is similar, but differs in its anise smell, is smaller and grows only on willows.
Parasola auricoma (Pat.) Redhead, Vilgalys & Hopple is a species of fungus in the family Psathyrellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: At maturity it reaches 1–6 cm in diameter. At first egg-shaped, then slightly conical or convex, finally almost flat. Over almost the whole surface it is deeply, radially grooved. The surface seen with the naked eye is smooth, under a hand lens finely hairy, orange-brown in young fruiting bodies, greyish in older ones. No veil remnants. Gills: Free or almost free, moderately crowded, at first whitish, then dark grey, finally black. Stem: 3–12 cm tall, up to 3 mm in diameter, cylindrical, brittle, hollow inside. The surface is smooth or delicately silky, in colour from whitish to slightly yellowish. No ring. Flesh: Thin, without smell and taste. Microscopic features: Spore print black. Spores ellipsoid, smooth, 10–16 × 6–9 µm; with a central germ pore, dark brown in KOH. Basidia 4-sterigmate. Cheilocystidia cylindrical, spindle-shaped or sac-shaped, about 90 × 25 µm. Pleurocystidia similar; up to about 130 × 35 µm. In the hymenium there are scattered or abundant thick-walled setae, up to about 400 × 10 µm, dark red in KOH. Clamp connections present. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of Parasola auricoma is known in Europe, both Americas, Asia and New Zealand. It is common, but is often confused with other species, especially Parasola plicatilis. W. Wojewoda in 2003 gives 7 localities in Poland. B. Gierczyk in 2011 gives 5 more. Numerous and more recent localities are given by the online fungi atlas. It is classed there as a threatened species worth protecting. A saprotroph. Found on the ground and on wood chips in meadows, lawns and roadsides.
Parasola plicatilis (Curtis) Redhead, Vilgalys & Hopple (Polish: parasolka fałdowana, czernidłak fałdowany) is a species of fungus in the family Psathyrellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Initially cylindrical, 5–10 mm in diameter, then successively ellipsoid or egg-shaped, hemispherically convex, horizontally flattened, and flat-convex with a slightly depressed centre. When mature it reaches a diameter of up to 3.5 cm. At first smooth, later deeply grooved from the margin almost to the centre. The gills show through, appearing in mature specimens as deep, radiating, parallel furrows. The surface is at first yellowish-honey to pale brown, later grey, with only the centre tinged cinnamon. The margin quickly becomes crenate. Stem: Height 3–7 cm, thickness 1–2 mm, cylindrical, delicate and hollow inside. The base is slightly thickened and somewhat woolly. The surface is smooth, sometimes slightly longitudinally silky. The colour is whitish at first, then pale ochre. No ring. Gills: Fairly distant, notched, thin, up to 2 mm wide, sometimes slightly bulging. In young fruiting bodies the edges are fringed. At first white, then grey from the spores, finally deliquescing. Flesh: Very thin and brittle, white. No distinct smell or taste. Microscopic features: Spore print black.

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: A widespread species. It occurs on all continents except South America and Antarctica. Władysław Wojewoda, in his 2003 list of the large fungi of Poland, does not give its localities, because this species is common throughout Poland. Saprotroph. It occurs in deciduous forests, parks, gardens, at forest edges and by roadsides. Fruiting bodies grow on the ground among grasses, from April to October. It prefers substrates rich in organic matter, especially nitrogen compounds. They usually appear after prolonged rain.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter up to 13 cm. In young specimens gently arched with a distinctly inrolled margin, later flat or somewhat concave, but still with an inrolled margin. The colour is yellow-brown, olive, ochre-brown or red-brown. Young specimens have a slightly felty cap, which later becomes bald. When damaged, the cap skin is spotted dark brown. In dry weather the cap is dry and shiny, in wet weather it becomes very slimy. Gills: Thin, crowded and clearly decurrent on the stem. Wavy in young mushrooms. They are yellowish or rusty and turn brown when damaged. Stem: Height 3–7 cm, thickness 1–2 cm. Cylindrical, thick, solid, bare and sometimes narrowed in the lower part. The colour is similar to that of the cap, usually slightly paler. It turns brown when damaged. Flesh: Yellow, yellowish-white or pale ochre, at first firm, later soft; after the mushroom is cut it changes colour to red-brown or rusty brown. The taste is slightly sour, the smell not very intense. Spore print: Ochre-brown. Spores ellipsoid, smooth, measuring 8–18 × 4.5–6 µm. Similar species: Similar to Paxillus filamentosus (Polish: krowiak olszowy).

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs throughout the Northern Hemisphere in areas with a temperate climate. In Europe it is common. It appears in autumn and summer in all types of forest. It grows under various tree species, e.g. birch, oak, alder, pine and spruce. It usually occurs in groups.
Peniophora quercina (Pers.) Cooke (Polish: powłocznica dębowa) is a species of fungus in the family Peniophoraceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting bodies: Annual, spread out or spread out with a reflexed edge. Single ones are circular in shape, but neighbouring fruiting bodies often merge to form a uniform crust. They are firmly attached to the substrate. In drought they shrink and crack. The thickness of the fruiting bodies is 0.2–2 mm and varies with the weather; they are thicker in wet weather and thinner in dry weather. In young specimens the whole surface of the fruiting body adheres to the substrate and its margin is delicately fringed, whitish and fibrous; in older fruiting bodies the margin lifts away from the substrate and curls back. The outer side of the fruiting body that lifts away from the substrate is rough, uneven and dark brown or black, on oaks growing in wet terrain violet-blue. Hymenophore: Covers the whole surface of the fruiting body. It is smooth, wrinkled, knobbly, matt, radially folded, and cracked in older fruiting bodies. The colour is grey-pink, light brown or grey-violet, turning brown in older specimens. Flesh: Very thin. Soft and waxy in young specimens, brittle and leathery in older ones. Spore print: Pink. Spores cylindrical, with a pointed base and bent into a sausage shape.

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: It is common in Europe and has also been recorded in Asia. It grows mainly on the bark of oaks (especially pedunculate oak), rarely on grey alder, lime and beech. It occurs in deciduous and mixed forests and in parks. It colonises mainly dead, fallen branches and dead trunks and stumps. It is common throughout Poland (except in the mountains, where it is rare).
Phaeolus schweinitzii (Fr.) Pat. (Polish: murszak rdzawy) is a species of fungus in the family Laetiporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: An annual bracket fungus consisting of a cap and a stem. It produces single fruiting bodies or groups in which the fruiting bodies often fuse at their bases. Cap: Circular, semicircular, kidney-shaped or irregular in shape, 8–30 cm wide, 1–4 cm thick. The margin is wavy or inrolled, cut in places and usually without hymenophore. The surface is uneven, wrinkled and knobbly, at first felty, hairy or shaggy, becoming bare with age. The margin is sulphur-yellow or yellow-ochre, the centre from orange to dark red, the base almost black. Stem: Short, lateral or central, funnel-shaped or flattened. It is covered with hymenophore. Dimensions: 3–8 × 2–5 cm. Flesh: 1–1.5 cm thick. In young fruiting bodies spongy and juicy, hardening with time. After drying it becomes fibrous and corky, brittle and light. The colour is orange to brown; it darkens when pressed or under the influence of KOH. It has a weak smell and a sourish taste. Hymenophore: Tubular, maze-like, yellow, rusty yellow, ochre or olive-green. The tubes are up to 1 cm long and form only one layer, which also runs down the stem.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is distributed mainly in the Northern Hemisphere, but also occurs in Australia, and has also been recorded in western Central Africa. It grows on the roots, trunks and stumps of various coniferous trees, usually at the base of still living trunks. In Poland it is common.
Phallus hadriani Vent. (Polish: sromotnik fiołkowy) is a species of fungus in the family Phallaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Young fruiting bodies: in the form of a spherical or egg-shaped egg. The mature fruiting body (receptacle) consists of a volva and a stem up to 20 cm long, usually 6–10 cm. The colour of the covering is violetish or pinkish. It has a weaker smell than Phallus impudicus. Flesh: The flesh of the stem is whitish, spongy, with numerous chambers, very brittle. Similar species: Phallus impudicus is very similar. It differs in its less violet colouring, smaller disc at the top of the cap, stronger smell and place of occurrence.

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: It grows on sandy, dry coastal dunes on the Baltic coast, sporadically inland. Fruiting bodies appear in summer and autumn. Very rare.
Phallus impudicus L. (Polish: sromotnik smrodliwy) is a species of fungus in the family Phallaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Young fruiting body: This is a fungus of unusual structure. The fruiting body of young specimens is spherical or egg-shaped, white or cream, sometimes with a yellow tinge. It measures 4–6 × 3–5 cm and is attached to the substrate by mycelium resembling fairly thick cords. It is partly hidden underground. This is the so-called egg, also commonly called the devil's egg. In cross-section the beginning of the fruiting body can already be seen inside the egg's covering. During development the egg bursts and the more typical mature fruiting body (the so-called receptacle) appears. Young fruiting bodies have a faint smell similar to that of radish. In appearance they resemble puffballs, but differ from them in the covering; it consists of two layers, between which there is a gelatinous mass. As the fungus matures the mass becomes more liquid and, after the covering tears, covers the head of the receptacle. Receptacle: It is 10–30 cm tall, cylindrical, narrow at the top, porous, fragile and hollow inside. It is white, with a volva at the base and a poorly differentiated head at the top. The head resembles morels in appearance. It is a dozen or so cm long, cone- or thimble-shaped, and covered with a green gelatinous mass in which the spores are found.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs throughout the Northern Hemisphere in the temperate climate zone, and also in South America and Asia (Japan, Ceylon, Java). In Poland it is common. A ground-dwelling fungus. It grows singly or in groups in parks, forests and thickets and is fairly common everywhere (except at higher mountain elevations).
Phellinus igniarius (L.) Quél (Polish: czyreń ogniowy) is a species of fungus in the family Hymenochaetaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: It attaches to the substrate by its side; no stem. Width 15–25 cm, thickness 8–15 cm, the shape at first bulbous, later flat or hoof-shaped. The surface is grey, darkening with time, sometimes cracked. It is smooth or finely suede-like, sometimes green from algae growing on it, and irregularly, concentrically zoned. The skin is hard, the cap margin broad and rounded. Hymenophore: Tubular. The tubes form many layers, each up to 5 mm thick. They are the same colour as the fruiting body, or paler. The pores of the tubes are very small, round. Flesh: Up to 2 cm thick. It is woody, zoned and dark rusty brown to chestnut brown. Spore print: White. Spores colourless, measuring 4–6.5 × 4–5.5 μm. Similar species: Fomes fomentarius (Polish: hubiak pospolity). It has softer and paler flesh and is not as firmly attached to the trunk. Phellinus hartigii (Polish: czyreń jodłowy), but it grows mainly on firs; Phellinus tremulae (Polish: czyreń osikowy), but it grows only on aspen

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America, Europe, Asia and the Canary Islands. In Poland it is very common, both in the lowlands and at lower mountain elevations. A tree-dwelling fungus. It occurs most often in riverside forests, along streams, but also in orchards, gardens and various types of forests and thickets. It grows mainly on willows, but also on other deciduous trees; on beech, hornbeam and others. It also attacks fruit trees.
Phellinus pomaceus (Pers.) Maire (Polish: czyreń śliwowy) is a species of fungus in the family Hymenochaetaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Perennial, of very varied shape. It may be spread out (resupinate), spread out and reflexed, cushion-shaped, knobbly, hoof-shaped, hemispherical, and also irregular in shape. The size is usually up to a few cm; often individual fruiting bodies fuse together or occur one above another like roof tiles, forming large clusters. The surface of young fruiting bodies is sandy-ochre, later through cinnamon-yellow and yellowish-brown it becomes chestnut, finally grey and almost black. It is at first slightly mossy, but quickly becomes smooth, later cracked. The margin of the fruiting body (the growth zone) is blunt, paler and lacks hymenophore. Hymenophore: Tubular, multilayered. Tubes 2–3 mm long, rusty brown, in older fruiting bodies sometimes overgrown with mycelium. Pores yellow-ochre, later rusty, finally brown. They are round or angular, sometimes elongated, 1–2 mm in diameter. Flesh: Yellow-brown or rusty brown, corky or woody. Spore print: White. Spores almost spherical, with slightly pointed ends, a smooth surface and measuring 5–7 × 4–5.5 µm. Setae very few, hard to notice.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in Europe and some regions of South America, Africa and Asia. In Poland it is common. A tree-dwelling fungus. It grows mainly on fruit trees, especially in neglected orchards, most often on plums, but sometimes also on apricots, cherries, apple trees and pear trees. It grows on trunks and branches (mainly on their lower side).
Phellodon tomentosus (L.) Banker (Polish: korkoząb kieliszkowaty) is a species of fungus in the family Thelephoraceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: A single one is circular with a depressed centre and 2–6 cm in diameter, but neighbouring caps often fuse into an irregular cap reaching a diameter of up to 20 cm. The surface is matt, felty, with fibres growing over it radially. It is concentrically zoned, darker in the middle, grey or reddish-brown, the margin whitish. Hymenophore: Spiny. The spines are up to 3 mm long and run slightly down the stem. They are white in young fruiting bodies, greyish in older ones. Stem: Height 1–3 cm, thickness up to 0.8 cm. Cylindrical, straight or twisted. The surface is light brown to dark brown. Neighbouring stems are often joined by compact mycelium that also grows through the substrate. Flesh: Light brown in the cap, reddish or dark brown in the stem. It is zoned. The taste and smell are bitterish; when drying it smells like the spice maggi. Spores: Whitish, spherical and slightly angular, with a surface covered in spines. Dimensions: 3–5 × 2.5–4 μm. Similar species: Phellodon niger (Polish: korkoząb czarniawy). It has darker fruiting bodies, from blue-black to grey-black; Phellodon confluens (Polish: korkoząb pozrastany).

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs on all continents of the Northern Hemisphere and on some islands; it has not been recorded in the Southern Hemisphere. In Poland it is a rare species. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is E – endangered species. It is also on lists of threatened species in Germany, Denmark, England and the Netherlands. It grows on the ground, in coniferous and mixed forests, also in urban forests, on needle litter and among bilberry undershrubs. It produces fruiting bodies from August to November. Saprotroph.
Phlebia radiata Fr. (Polish: żylak promienisty) is a species of fungus in the family Meruliaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: A tremelloid fungus. Fruiting bodies up to 8 mm thick, at first circular or oval, later spreading widely. They are spread out flat and entirely attached to the substrate, less often with a reflexed margin. The margin is ragged. As they grow, individual fruiting bodies fuse with neighbouring ones, covering a considerable area. The colour is pale flesh-pink or orange-reddish, with distinct veins or folds of the hymenophore radiating outwards. Hymenophore: In the form of radiating folds and veins. Pale pink, orange to red, darkening with age to brown or turning grey. Flesh: Gelatinous or fleshy-waxy. Spore print: White. Spores cylindrical, granular and smooth, measuring 4.5–6 × 1.5–2.5 μm. Similar species: Phlebia tremellosa (Polish: żylak trzęsakowaty) has a similar underside of the fruiting body, but unlike Phlebia radiata, which adheres closely to the substrate, it usually forms small caps or projecting lobes. The żylica olbrzymia is also similar.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Most localities of Phlebia radiata have been described in North America and Europe, but it also occurs in South America, Africa and New Zealand. In Poland it is fairly common. A tree-dwelling fungus, saprotroph. It occurs in forests, parks, gardens and orchards. It grows on stumps and on trunks and branches lying on the ground, mainly on the wood of deciduous trees: Alnus glutinosa, Betula pendula, Carpinus, Fagus, Populus tremula, Quercus petraea, Duercus sp., Salix caprea, Sorbus aucuparia, Tilia, less often on coniferous trees: on silver fir, Norway spruce and cultivated black pine.
Pholiota aurivella (Batsch) P. Kumm. (Polish: łuskwiak złotawy) is a species of fungus in the family pierścieniakowate.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 5–12 cm. In young individuals conical, later hemispherical, and finally flat. It is golden-yellow or rusty yellow with darker, adpressed patches. On young mushrooms there are remains of the partial veil at the cap margin, but they are fairly quickly washed away by rain. In wet weather and in young specimens the cap surface is sticky and even slimy. Gills: White when young, then olive and rusty brown with a serrated edge, adnexed to the stem or slightly notched with a tooth. Stem: Height 10–12 cm, thickness up to 1 cm. It is fibrous and the same colour as the cap, or slightly paler. Its ring consists of brown threads forming a woolly annulus, which later partly disappears. Below the ring it is covered with brown fibrils, above it is yellowish and downy. Flesh: Yellowish in the cap, slightly darker in the stem, odourless and not changing colour when damaged. It has a mild taste. Spore print: Rusty brown. Spores measuring 8 × 5–6 μm, ellipsoid, smooth. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been described in North America, Europe, Korea, Japan, Morocco and New Zealand. In Poland it is common throughout the country, both in the lowlands and in the mountains. A tree-dwelling fungus, saprotroph and parasite. It grows on dead and living deciduous trees; it has been found on the following tree species and genera: sycamore maple, horse chestnut, alder, silver birch, hornbeam, beech, walnut, poplar, acacia, white willow, elm, and only exceptionally on fir. It produces fruiting bodies from April to October.
Pholiota flammans (Batsch) P. Kumm (Polish: łuskwiak ognisty) is a species of fungus in the family pierścieniakowate.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 2–6 cm. In young individuals hemispherical, then hemispherically arched, finally flat-arched. It long retains an inrolled margin. The surface is dry, slightly slimy in wet weather, lemon-yellow to orange. It is entirely covered with large, uniformly coloured scales, which also hang from the cap margin. Gills: Crowded, lemon-yellow in young fruiting bodies, then darkening to olive, finally rusty brown. Stem: Height 3–8 cm, thickness up to 0.8 cm. Cylindrical, solid in young fruiting bodies, hollow in older ones. It is smooth only in a narrow zone under the cap; elsewhere it is entirely covered with spreading sulphur-coloured fibres. Flesh: Sulphur-yellow, rusting slightly only near the margins. The taste is bitterish, the smell somewhat radish-like. Microscopic features: Spore print brown. Spores yellowish, elliptical, smooth, without a germ pore, amyloid. Pleurocystidia of various shapes, up to 40 μm long; some are filled inside with uniform dark brown content, others stain under KOH like chrysocystidia. The numerous cheilocystidia, also of various shapes, are up to 20 μm long.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A species widespread in North America and Europe. It also occurs in Asia, where its occurrence is less well studied. In Asia it has been recorded in Japan, India and China. It grows in various types of forests and parks, on trunks and stumps of coniferous trees, especially pine and spruce. Fruiting bodies, produced from August to October, grow singly or in small groups.
Pholiota squarrosa (Vahl) P. Kumm. (Polish: łuskwiak nastroszony) is a species of fungus in the family pierścieniakowate.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 2–15 cm. In young individuals egg-shaped and closed, later hemispherical, and finally flat. It is ochre, ochre-brown to brown, darker in the middle. The surface is densely covered with spreading scales. The margin is inrolled for a long time. Gills: Yellowish when young, then rusty brown. They are crowded, slightly decurrent and attached to the stem. Stem: Height 4–8 cm, thickness up to 12 mm. Fibrous and the same colour as the cap. It has a ring.
