Only in young fruiting bodies is it white, soon becoming yellowish-greenish, finally black with a violet tinge, interspersed with thin, white fibres of capillitium. When mature the fruiting body splits, releasing the spores. Spores: Spherical, brown, with reticulate ornamentation, 8–13 μm in diameter. Similar species: Scleroderma bovista (Polish: tęgoskór brodawkowany) has at the base of the fruiting body a distinct, well-developed mycelium resembling a short root.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is widespread in North America, Europe and Asia, much rarer in South America, North Africa and Australia. In Poland it is common. It grows on the ground in sands and acid soils, at forest edges, in parks, also outside forests; on pastures, stony terrain, peat bogs and in thickets. It produces fruiting bodies from June to November.
Serpula himantioides (Fr.) P. Karst. (Polish: stroczek leśny) is a species of fungus in the family Serpulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Annual, spread out or spread out and reflexed. It attaches strongly to the substrate, covering large areas. A single fruiting body at first has a circular shape and reaches a diameter of 2–5 cm, but neighbouring fruiting bodies often merge with one another. The sterile margin is at first fluffy, cottony, up to 1.5 cm wide. As it dries it becomes leathery and projecting. The flesh of young fruiting bodies is spongy and elastic, that of older ones fibrous and leathery. It is 1–2 mm thick, yellow-rusty in colour, and darkens when damaged. The hymenophore is at first smooth, then successively warty, radially folded, finally coarsely maze-like. The colour is at first cream, then yellow-rusty, finally dark brown. The pores are very small, lilac in young fruiting bodies, yellow-rusty after drying. In the hymenium there are smooth-walled cystidia of spindle shape and measuring 50–80 × 5.5–8 μm. Young fruiting bodies have a pleasant, mushroomy smell, older ones an unpleasant one. No distinct taste. Microscopic features: Dimitic hyphal system. Skeletal hyphae with clamp connections, in the subhymenium thin-walled, 2–4 μm wide. Cystidia absent.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In Europe and North America it is widespread. In Europe its range extends from Portugal to about 66 degrees of latitude on the Scandinavian Peninsula. It has also been recorded in Zimbabwe in Africa, Japan, Australia and New Zealand. In Poland until recently it was considered an extinct species, but it does occur. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is R – a potentially threatened species because of its limited geographical range and small habitat areas.
Sparassis brevipes Krombh. (Polish: siedzuń dębowy) is a species

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Diameter 10–50 cm, white in youth, later straw-yellow, with fairly upright outer elements, coarsely leaf-like-wavy to fan-shaped, often zoned in colour on the surfaces. Flesh: White; odourless, with a mild taste. Spore print: Spores measuring 4.5–6 × 3.5–4.5 µm in diameter. Similar species: Sparassis brevipes resembles Sparassis crispa (Polish: siedzuń sosnowy) in colour and size, but is paler and has more broadly bent, more spread-out leaf-like ends of the branches.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In Poland it is a rare species. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is V – threatened with extinction. In the scientific literature 45 of its localities had been reported by 2020. More up-to-date localities are given by the online mushroom atlas. In 1995–2014 it was under strict protection, and since 2014 under partial protection. It is on lists of threatened species also in Germany, England and Norway. A tree-dwelling fungus. It produces fruiting bodies from August to October on the roots of beeches, oaks, firs, larches and spruces. The fruiting bodies grow from a hard, compact mycelium.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Height usually 5–20 cm, width 6–30 cm, but it can be larger, sometimes reaching even 6 kg (in 1711 in Turoszów a forester found two specimens, the larger of which weighed 20 kg and measured 2.55 metres). The shape is irregularly spherical; from a thick fleshy base it divides into leaf-like, variously fused branches with hymenium on both sides. The leaf-like lobes are strongly wrinkled, with teeth on the edges, so that in appearance it resembles a cauliflower. In young specimens the fruiting body is whitish, later yellowish, cream, ochre or yellow-brown. The branches of the fruiting body grow from a thick, blackish base of the stem, which often grows deep into the substrate. Flesh: Waxy, elastic, white. The smell is pleasant, the taste reminiscent of nuts. Spore print: Ochre. Spores 6–7 × 4–7 µm in diameter, short-ellipsoid, smooth, pale yellow. Similar species: A very similar species, Sparassis brevipes (Polish: siedzuń dębowy), also occurs in Poland. It has more faded, broader and more leaf-like ends of the branches.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In Poland it was regarded as a rare species. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographical range and small habitat areas. It is on lists of threatened species also in Belgium, Estonia, Lithuania, Norway and Latvia. Contrary to the findings of the red list, in Poland it is, however, fairly frequent. It occurs in coniferous and mixed forests. It grows on the roots of coniferous trees, both dead and living. It most often grows on pine roots, rarely on spruce. It can also attack Douglas firs (Pseudotsuga).
Sphaerobolus stellatus Tode (Polish: strzykacz gwiazdkowaty) is a species of fungus in the family Sphaerobolaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: 1 to 3 mm in diameter, spherical and elastic, coloured from whitish to straw-yellow. The gleba is contained in a smooth and sticky peridiole. During the ejection of the spores the outer membrane (exoperidium) suddenly opens into a star composed of 4 to 9 arms, which reveals the peridiole. The latter is thrown out (hence the Polish name “strzykacz”, meaning squirter) over a distance by the sudden tearing and turning outward of the inner layers, and thanks to its sticky layer it attaches itself to surrounding structures. Spores: Basidiospores ellipsoid-oblong, smooth, with thickened walls, uninucleate, hyaline, dextrinoid in Melzer's reagent, cyanophilic, with average dimensions of 6.8–9.2 × 4.7–7.9 µm, Q on average 1.53. Conidia elongated, thin-walled, binucleate or with more nuclei. Similar species: Nidularia deformis (Polish: gniazdnica kulista) is distinguished by larger basidia, an epiphragm and numerous peridioles on the basidia.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs on all continents except Antarctica and on many islands. In Poland Władysław Wojewoda in 2003 cited numerous localities, noting that because of its small size it is often overlooked. In the following years new localities were reported. A saprotrophic fungus growing on rotting wood, litter and dead plants. It occurs in forests, often in cultivated pine and spruce forests, in parks. It usually forms fruiting bodies from August to November.
Stereum hirsutum (Willd.) Pers. (Polish: skórnik szorstki) is a species of fungus in the family Stereaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting bodies: Annual, forming numerous clusters. A single fruiting body is 0.5–3 cm wide and 1–2 mm thick, spread out, spread out and reflexed, shelf-shaped, bracket-shaped, and wrinkled. Fruiting bodies growing in large numbers next to one another are arranged like roof tiles or fuse with one another. They attach to the substrate by their upper surface, and its sides bend outward. Growing on vertical trunks it forms small caps reflexed at the top. The upper surface is hairy, velvety, rough or bristly. The colour is whitish, ochre-yellow, grey-rusty-brown, and it is concentrically zoned and striped. The margin of the fruiting body is sharp and wavy. Hymenophore: Smooth, bright on young fruiting bodies, later orange-yellow or ochre, on older fruiting bodies fading and becoming light orange-brown. Context (flesh): Whitish (not changing colour when cut), hard, of leathery or corky consistency. It is covered with a thin cortex, visible already with a magnifying glass. Microscopic features: The hairs on the upper surface are made of colourless, or very weakly stained, hyphae 3.5–7 μm wide. Spore print white. They are thick-walled, sometimes almost solid.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Apart from Antarctica it occurs on all continents, and also on many islands. In Poland it is very common. It is one of the most frequently occurring fungi on dead wood. It occurs throughout the country. In the mountains it reaches the upper limit of the forest, and is also found on single trees growing above that limit, in the dwarf-pine zone. A saprotrophic fungus. It occurs in forests, thickets, parks, gardens and along roads. It produces fruiting bodies throughout the year. It develops in wood, mainly of deciduous trees.
Stereum rugosum Pers. (Polish: skórnik pomarszczony) is a species of fungus in the family Stereaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Perennial. Young specimens are more or less round, spread out. They adhere to the substrate entirely with their dorsal side, at most only their margins stand out slightly. A single fruiting body is 5–20 mm in diameter, but neighbouring fruiting bodies merge and form patches reaching even several metres in length. Older specimens, especially those growing on a vertical substrate, form projecting, elongated caps 1–2 cm wide. They are narrowly, deeply grooved and zoned and hairless, only the margin is brown-felted. The upper surface of these caps is at first whitish-hairy, later greyish-brown, and in old specimens dark brown-blackish. The flesh is leathery or corky-bast-like, woody in older fruiting bodies. The hymenial surface is uneven and wrinkled. It is yellowish, cream-yellowish to red-yellowish or grey-yellow, and in wet weather dark grey with spots. When rubbed it reddens. Older fruiting bodies, in which there are 10–20 layers of hymenium, are 2–4 mm thick. They are attached to the substrate in few places and can be easily detached. Microscopic features:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Widespread across the globe. Apart from Antarctica and South America it occurs on all continents and on many islands. In Central Europe it is common. Throughout Poland as well it is common. A tree-dwelling saprotroph. It develops on the wood of deciduous trees, on branches and trunks, mainly dead ones. It produces fruiting bodies throughout the year. It colonises stumps, logs and branches lying on the ground, and also still-standing dead trunks and branches. It occurs on hazel, alder, beech, oak and others.
Stereum subtomentosum Pouzar (Polish: skórnik aksamitny) is a species of fungus belonging to the family Stereaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body At first thin, round or funnel-shaped and adhering to the substrate, then connected to the substrate only by its side or a stem-like base, while the fan-shaped or spatula-shaped part of the fruiting body is free and forms a thin, small cap. It usually occurs in groups, and then the caps of neighbouring fruiting bodies overlap like roof tiles or grow in rows. A single cap reaches a width of 1–5 (exceptionally up to 10 cm) and a thickness of 0.5–1.2 mm. The surface is velvety or felty and concentrically zoned, the zones often being of different colours. The zones are hairless, wood-brown in colour. The upper surface is yellowish-grey, hazel or ochre, rarely chestnut-brown. Older specimens change colour to grey. In young fruiting bodies the cap margin is silkily fibrous, but not felty. In cross-section, under the cap skin a yellow-brown line about 0.1 mm thick is visible. Hymenial surface Smooth, sometimes only slightly knobbly, at the margins often radially veined (especially on young fruiting bodies). The colour is from pale beige through ochre to pale coffee.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In the Northern Hemisphere it is widespread. In the Southern Hemisphere its occurrence is known only in South Africa. Formerly it was rare in Poland. Gumińska and Wojewoda state that it occurred only in remnants of natural forests, e.g. in the Carpathians, in the Białowieża Forest, the Augustów Forest and in Kuyavia. In the last several decades, however, its abundance in Europe has clearly increased. In the scientific literature several dozen of its localities in Poland have been reported. A tree-dwelling saprotrophic fungus. It grows on dead wood of deciduous trees lying on the ground.
Strobilomyces strobilaceus (Scop.) Berk (Polish: szyszkowiec łuskowaty) is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter up to 15 cm, semicircular in young specimens, then convex to flattened in older ones. Covered with characteristic woolly tufts arranged like roof tiles. The tufts are thick, projecting and grey-brown with a darker tip. The cap surface is dry. Tubes: Up to 14 mm long, adnate or decurrent. The colour is from whitish in young specimens to grey-brown (sometimes with a reddish tinge) in older ones. Pores angular, relatively large, covered in young specimens with a whitish-grey veil. Its remains sometimes stay on the cap margin. Damaged tubes at first redden, then take on a black-violet colour. Stem: Thickness 1–3 cm, height up to 15 cm. Cylindrical, tapering slightly towards the cap, very hard. The colour is similar to the cap, covered with numerous cottony, grey-brown tufts. Under the cap there is a vanishing ring. A damaged stem takes on a reddish colour. Flesh: Fleshy, sometimes dry and springy, and woody in the stem. White in young specimens, through reddish to dark brown in older ones. When damaged it takes on a reddish colour. Taste and smell weak. Spore print:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs mainly in North America and Europe; localities have also been reported in Korea, Japan and West Africa. Since 2014 it has been under partial protection in Poland; formerly it was under strict protection. In the study Red List of plants and fungi of Poland it is classified in the category of rare fungi (R). It forms fruiting bodies from summer to autumn in coniferous, deciduous and mixed forests. It lives in mycorrhiza with beech, and in mountainous areas with spruce and fir. A rarely encountered fungus; it is more often met in the mountainous areas of southern Poland.
Strobilurus esculentus (Wulfen) Singer (Polish: szyszkówka świerkowa) is a species of fungus in the family Physalacriaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 1.5–2.5 (exceptionally up to 3.5 cm), the shape hemispherical to spread out, sometimes with a low umbo. The cap margin is not inrolled. The surface is coloured from grey-ochre through red-brown to dark brown, smooth and matt. Sometimes it may be wrinkled in places. When wet, the gills show through slightly at the cap margins. If the fruiting bodies develop under snow, they are white. Gills: Crowded, notched, whitish to light ash-grey in colour. Stem: Height 3–6 cm, thickness 1–2 mm, stiff, hard, tubular, with remains of mycelium at the base. The surface is shiny, brown-ochre, paler at the top. Flesh: Thin, whitish, odourless. The taste is mild. Microscopic features: Spore print pale cream. Spores ellipsoid, smooth, non-amyloid, measuring 5–6.5 × 3–4 μm. Pleurocystidia thick-walled, convex, with strongly incrusted tops and measuring 35–60 × 10–17 µm. Cheilocystidia also thick-walled and convex, but elongated and with only weakly incrusted tops. They measure 40–50 × 9–12 µm. Similar species: Several other species grow on cones: Strobilurus stephanocystis (Polish: szyszkówka tęporozwierkowa).

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: This species is known mainly in Europe. It is widespread here. Outside Europe its occurrence has been described only in Mexico in North America. In Poland it is common. A saprotrophic fungus. It occurs in forests, in cemeteries and in parks, on spruce cones lying in the litter, partly buried in the ground or hidden below the surface of the ground, exceptionally also on fir cones. It is common wherever spruces occur, so especially in mountain forests. Usually around one spruce cone there are a dozen or so fruiting bodies.
Stropharia aeruginosa (Curtis) Quél. (Polish: pierścieniak grynszpanowy, pierścieniak niebieskozielony, łysiczka niebieskozielona) is a species of fungus in the family Strophariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 3–8(10) cm, covered with a blue-green or bluish-green layer of slime, in which white scales can be seen. In drought the cap loses its slime, becomes shiny, smooth and of a faded colour. The shape of the cap in the initial phase of growth is convex, with time passing to bell-shaped, flat. The flesh is fairly compact, the skin can easily be pulled off the cap. Gills: Crowded and attached to the stem. In young fruiting bodies covered by a veil. The colour is at first whitish, later violet-blue, finally chocolate-brown. The gill edges are white and powdered. Stem: Up to 8 cm tall and 1 cm thick. The colour is light beige or light green, changing with time to brown; hollow inside. The ring is in the middle of the stem and disappears early. Below this ring the stem is covered with white fibrils or scales. Flesh: At first greenish-white, later cream. Taste and smell indistinct. Spore print: Spores violet-brown, elliptical-ovoid, 7–9 × 4–5.5 µm in diameter. The edge of the gills has hair-like cystidia. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America, in Europe and in Iran. In Poland it is common. Fruiting bodies appear from September to November, in deciduous and coniferous forests, in parks, sometimes along roads. It grows on the ground and on dead wood. It forms groups of mushrooms consisting of many individuals. It is fairly common. It most often grows under beeches, less often under firs.
Stropharia caerulea Kreisel (Polish: pierścieniak niebieskawy, pierścieniak białoniebieski, łysiczka niebieskawa) is a species of fungus in the family Strophariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 5–7 cm. Conical-arched in youth, later widened with a distinct umbo. The umbo is usually blunt, less often sharp. The cap skin is slimy, sky-blue or blue-green, and in older specimens it is coloured from sulphur-yellow to cream. The cap of pierścieniak białoniebieski (Stropharia caerulea) quickly loses its bluish colour. Gills: Adnate and decurrent with a tooth. At first they are flesh-olive in colour, later purple-brown, and their edges are white, fibrous or toothed. Stem: Height 3–7 cm, thickness 2–5 mm. Cylindrical and springy. At first it is blue-greenish, later becomes paler; at the base straw-yellow, at the top sky-blue. Finally it becomes whitish and covered with small flakes or fibrous-scaly. Flesh: Thin, fleshy. At first blue-green, then greenish-grey and dirty white, and cream at the base of the stem. The smell is sour. Spore print: Purple-brown. Spores ellipsoid, smooth, thick-walled and without a germ pore. Size 7–9 × 4.5–6 µm. Similar species: Most similar is Stropharia aeruginosa (Polish: pierścieniak grynszpanowy).

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America and Europe. It grows on the edge of coniferous, mixed and deciduous forests, also in clearings and pastures, in parks and gardens (especially in the vicinity of stinging nettle). It grows on the ground, in grass. Fruiting bodies appear from August to November. It is more often found outside forests, preferring soils rich in nitrogen.
Stropharia coronilla (Bull.) Quél. (Polish: pierścieniak koroniasty) is a species of fungus in the family Strophariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 2–4 cm, whitish, pale ochre or yellowish, sticky when wet. The shape of the cap is mostly semicircular. Gills: At first pale lilac, later purple-violet, with a paler edge. Stem: Whitish, with a closely adhering, narrow ring (or without). Similar species: Stropharia coronilla can be confused with dwarf Agaricus (Polish: pieczarki), which, however, have free gills.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North, Central and South America, Europe, Asia, Australia and New Zealand. In Poland it is not very frequent, but probably not threatened with extinction. It grows on the ground in fields, pastures, meadows, at road edges, in parks, among grasses, in thickets, on river banks under grey alder. It appears from May to October.
Stropharia rugosoannulata Farl. ex Murrill (Polish: pierścieniak uprawny) is a species of fungus in the family Strophariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 6–15, and even 20 cm, at first conical-convex, then convex, finally spread out. The margin is sharp, inrolled for a long time. The surface is smooth, bare, matt, dark wine-brown, then pales and becomes ochre-brown, finally cream; sometimes, however, from the very beginning it is cream-yellow with wine-red fibrils. It is dry and slimy; when wet only slightly sticky. Gills: Crowded, at first light grey, then grey-lilac to violet-black, with a paler edge. Stem: Height 7–15 cm, thickness 1.5–3 cm, cylindrical, sometimes with a widened base, white, yellowing with age. The ring is white, thick, sometimes its remains stay on the cap margin and on the stem. The surface is covered with long fibrils, but without scales. At the base with rhizomorphs. Spore print: Black-violet. Spores measuring 10–14 × 6.5–8 µm. Similar species: Stropharia hornemannii (Polish: pierścieniak okazały), which has scales on the stem, and the ring (if it remains) does not split, and the whole fruiting body is paler.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America, Europe, Asia and New Zealand. In Poland it is a synanthropic species and expansively increasing its range. In natural habitats it is probably not rare. Numerous localities are given by the online mushroom atlas. It is classified there among protected and threatened fungi. In natural habitats it is found in parks, allotment gardens, botanical gardens, in fields, less often in the forest. It appears in the months May – September. It grows on the ground, on rotten straw or garden waste.
Suillellus luridus (Schaeff.) Murrill (Polish: modroborowik ponury, borowik ponury) is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 5–20 cm, at first hemispherical, then flat-arched or cushion-shaped. The surface is smooth, sometimes suede-like, dry, coloured from cream to brown-olive. The skin is strongly fused with the flesh. It darkens when pressed. Tubes: Long, notched in a sinus shape at the stem, olive. Pores small, at first yellow, on older specimens dark orange, in very old ones olive. They turn blue after cutting. Stem: Height 5–15 cm, barrel-shaped in young specimens, club-shaped or cylindrical in older ones. The colour is from yellow to orange-reddish, wine-red at the base. A characteristic feature is the presence on the stem of a distinct, darker (rusty-reddish) network with elongated meshes. Flesh: Hard, yellow in the cap, reddish in the lower part of the stem. After cutting it turns strongly blue. The taste is mild, the smell weak. Spore print: Olive. Spores smooth, 6–7 × 9–16 μm in diameter. Similar species: Sutorius luridiformis (Polish: krasnoborowik ceglastopory) also turns blue, but on the stem it has no network, but small carmine-red scales.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North and Central America, Europe, Japan and Australia. In Poland it is moderately common. A ground-dwelling fungus, more often found on calcareous substrate. It occurs in deciduous, mixed and coniferous forests, especially under beeches and firs, also in parks under limes. It produces fruiting bodies from June to October.
Suillus bovinus (L.) Roussel (Polish: maślak sitarz) is a species of fungus in the family Suillaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 4–12 cm, at first hemispherical with a slightly wavy margin, later flat, becoming bent in older fruiting bodies. In youth the cap skin is covered with a delicate, pale, felty bloom, later slimy (especially when wet) and shiny, smooth, very hard to peel. The colour of the cap is cream, cream-ochre, orange-ochre, orange-brown, mostly with a paler rim at the margin. Tubes: Mature ones 4–10 mm long. Adnate to the stem, and even decurrent. Greyish-yellowish in young fruiting bodies, later yellow, grey-ochre, finally brownish. They separate from the cap flesh with difficulty. The pores of the tubes are very large and in appearance resemble the holes of a sieve. Hence also the species name. Pressed, they turn brown. Stem: Height 2–10 cm and width 0.8–2 cm. Cylindrical, solid, fibrous, without a ring. The colour of the cap or slightly paler, sometimes red-brown at the base. The mycelium at the base of the stem is coloured from whitish to violet-pink. Flesh:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In the Northern Hemisphere it is widespread, in the Southern Hemisphere it occurs only in New Zealand. In Poland it is a common species, the most frequently occurring of all the Suillus species. It occurs on dry, sandy soils accompanying Scots pine, with which it lives in mycorrhiza. Fruiting bodies appear from July to October. It often grows among heather.
Boletinus cavipes (Klotzsch) Kalchbr. (Polish: borowiczak dęty, borowiec dęty, maślak dęty) is a species of fungus in the family Suillaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 4–12 cm in diameter, at first semicircular or conical, with age flat with a small umbo in the middle. At first it has an inrolled margin, later sharp. Covered all over with small, darker fibrils and felty-scaly. The colour is from yellow-brown through red-brown to brown. Tubes: Short, slightly decurrent on the stem. Pores very large, radially elongated, coloured from yellow to yellow-olive. They do not change colour. In youth they are covered by a whitish veil. Stem: Height 4–10 cm, thickness 1–2 cm, cylindrical, thickened at the bottom, hollow. The same colour as the cap or paler. In the upper part with a whitish ring. Flesh: Yellowish and spongy in the cap, white, drier and more compact in the stem. It does not change colour when damaged. The smell is pleasant, the taste somewhat sour, in older specimens astringent, bitterish. Spore print: Olive-yellowish. Spores ellipsoid-spindle-shaped, measuring 7–19 × 3–4 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In the scientific literature more than 80 of its localities in Poland have been reported. It occurs more often in the mountains. In the study Red List of plants and fungi of Poland it is classified in the category of rare fungi (R). A ground-dwelling mycorrhizal fungus. It occurs exclusively under larches, with which it forms mycorrhiza.
Suillus granulatus (L.) Roussel (Polish: maślak ziarnisty) is a species of fungus in the family Suillaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: At first brown or rusty red, bare and slimy, in mature specimens yellow-ochre and dry. The skin is smooth, bare and easily separates from the flesh. Arched in youth with a sharp margin, mature ones cushion-shaped, 4–10 cm in diameter. Tubes: First pale yellow, later ochre, finally brown-yellow, adnate to the stem. Pores light yellow, small in youth, larger when mature. They exude white droplets of milky liquid, which after drying leave brown granules on the pores and the top of the stem. Stem: Height 4–8 cm, diameter 1–2 cm, cylindrical, solid, without a ring. The surface is pale yellow, in mature fruiting bodies brownish at the base, with brown granules at the top. These are dried droplets of milky liquid. Flesh: White-yellowish, brownish only at the base of the stem. The taste is mild, the smell pleasant. Spore print: Yellow-brown. Spores 7–9 × 2.5–3.5 µm in diameter, smooth, pale yellow. Similar species: Suillus luteus (Polish: maślak zwyczajny). It has larger fruiting bodies, a ring on the stem and a yellow-orange cap. It grows under pines.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is widespread. Apart from Antarctica it occurs on all continents, and also on many islands. In Poland it is common. Fruiting bodies grow from May to November, on the ground, under various species of two-needled pines (Scots pine, mountain pine, black pine, etc.). It prefers well-lit, sandy and grassy places. It is often found on the edge of forests.
Suillus grevillei (Klotzsch) Singer (Polish: maślak żółty) is a species of fungus in the family Suillaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Conical in young fruiting bodies, flattened and cushion-shaped in mature ones, 40–150 mm in diameter. The cap skin is smooth, bare, covered with slime, which dries in drought, and in wet weather is very slimy and shiny. The colour is golden-yellow, golden-orange, paler at the margin. The skin is very difficult to separate from the flesh; it can only partly be pulled off the margin of the cap of older fruiting bodies, but in young specimens this is almost impossible. Tubes: In young specimens they are covered by a yellow-white veil. 5–10 mm long. They are yellow, later olive-yellow, adnate. The pores are first round, later angular, yellow in youth, brown-yellow with age, when pressed they stain pink-brown, and then darken. Stem: Height 5–14 cm and diameter up to 2.5 cm, cylindrical or club-shaped, solid, with a ring at the top. Above the ring there is a lemon-yellow slimy annular zone, often with a network, and below the ring the stem is orange-brown. In older specimens the ring disappears, but a trace of it is clearly visible. Flesh: Yellow, in places sometimes turning pink, soft and juicy in the cap, hard, fibrous in the stem.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is fairly widespread; it occurs in Europe, North America, North Africa and Australia. In Poland it is common, especially in the mountains. A mycorrhizal fungus. It forms mycorrhiza with larches and occurs only under this tree. At the same time, among the three Suillus species growing under larches, it is the one most often encountered.
Suillus luteus (L.) Roussel (Polish: maślak zwyczajny) is a species of fungus in the family Suillaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 4–12 cm, dark brown, chocolate-brown, sometimes yellow-brown. On young mushrooms hemispherical, then flattened, broad. The skin is radially veined, sticky and shiny, dry in drought. It can easily be separated from the flesh. Tubes: Length 6–12 mm, lemon-yellow tubes, in young fruiting bodies covered by a white, membranous partial veil. In adult individuals the remains of this veil stay on the stem in the form of a white-violet, adnate ring. The pores of the tubes are at first roundish, angular on older specimens. Stem: Height 3–11 cm, thickness 1–2.5 cm, cylindrical, hard and solid. It is light yellow, with brown granules on the upper part. A very characteristic feature is the presence on the stem of a skin-like ring. By this it can be distinguished from the very similar Suillus granulatus (Polish: maślak ziarnisty), which does not have this ring. Flesh: At first hard, then soft. It is white-yellowish in colour and only at the bottom of the stem is slightly brown. The taste and smell are pleasant. Spore print: Rusty-ochre. Spores smooth, ellipsoid, measuring 7–11 × 2.5–4 μm. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is widespread. It occurs throughout the Northern Hemisphere in areas with a temperate climate, and also in South America, Australia and New Zealand. In Poland it is very common. A mycorrhizal fungus. It grows in coniferous forests, mainly under pines, because it lives together with their roots – the phenomenon of mycorrhiza. It often occurs in young pine stands. It occurs from May to autumn, but in a warm autumn and late winter fine specimens have been found in mid-December.
Suillus variegatus (Sw.) Richon & Roze (Polish: maślak pstry) is a species of fungus belonging to the family Suillaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 5–14 cm, semicircular with inrolled margins in young specimens, then cushion-shaped with a sharp margin. The skin in youth is coloured from yellow or yellow-grey through olive to dirty orange and is felty, then becomes ochre-brown to pale orange. Its surface is covered with small fibrils, which in older specimens sometimes disappear. It separates from the flesh fairly hard. Tubes: Fairly short, yellow or pale orange in youth, then dark olive. When pressed they first turn blue, then brown. The pores are roundish and of a similar colour to the tubes. Stem: Height 4–10 cm, thickness 2–4 cm. It is cylindrical, smooth and thickened at the bottom. It has a yellow or yellow-brownish colour with a slight reddish tinge. Flesh: Hard, pale yellow or pale orange, lemon-yellow under the surface of the stem. After cutting it turns slightly blue in places (slightly bluish). The taste is slight, the smell distinctive, somewhat reminiscent of conifer needles. Spore print: Olive-brown. Spores measuring 7.5–12 × 3–5 µm, smooth, spindle-shaped. Similar species: Suillus bovinus (Polish: maślak sitarz), but it has larger pores and lacks the characteristic smell

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is widespread in Central Europe, but also occurs in North America, South America and Japan. In Poland it is common. Fruiting bodies grow from summer to autumn, in coniferous forests, especially under pines, on heaths and in damp places.
Suillus viscidus (L.) Roussel (Polish: maślak lepki, maślak szary) is a species of fungus in the family Suillaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 4–12 cm, at first convex with an inrolled margin, later cushion-shaped, finally flatly spread out. The skin comes off easily, slimy, the surface coloured from grey-white through yellow-grey, olive-grey to red-grey. In dry weather the surface cracks into fibrous scales. In young fruiting bodies the margin is joined to the stem by a whitish-grey partial veil. Tubes: Long, adnate, often decurrent, grey-white in young fruiting bodies, dark grey in older ones. Pores large, angular, radially elongated, whitish in young fruiting bodies, dark blue in older ones, finally cinnamon-brownish. Stem: Height 4–10 cm, thickness up to 2.5 cm, cylindrical, fleshy, solid, club-like thickened at the base. The surface is yellow-grey, paler than the cap, netted above the ring, pitted below. The ring is thin, quickly vanishing. Flesh: Compact, later soft, whitish, greyish, yellowish in the stem. Weak smell, mild, fruity taste. Spore print: Tobacco-brown. Spores spindle-shaped, 8–14 × 3–5 µm in diameter. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs mainly in Europe, where it is fairly widespread. Apart from this, its occurrence has been reported only in the province of Quebec in Canada and in Japan. A ground-dwelling fungus, growing exclusively under larch. Fruiting bodies appear from July to October.
Tapinella atrotomentosa (Batsch) Šutara (Polish: ponurnik aksamitny) is a species of fungus in the family Tapinellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: It grows to large sizes – diameter up to 30 cm. In young specimens the margin is inrolled, the skin matt and suede-like, in older ones it becomes smooth. The colour is from olive to dark brown, sometimes also rusty brown. It often has an irregular shape. Gills: Crowded and clearly decurrent on the stem (especially in young specimens). The colour is at first white, with age ochre-yellow. They are often joined by cross-anastomoses. They turn brown in damaged places. Stem: Thickness about 2–4 cm, height about 3–7 cm. It is solid, hard, springy and covered with dark brown or black, velvety down. It is usually eccentric. Flesh: The colour is white or white-yellow, juicy, brittle. The taste is slightly bitterish, no smell. Spore print: Brownish or pale ochre. Spores broadly ellipsoid, with a smooth surface and almost colourless. Size: 5–7 × 4–4.5 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in Europe and North America. In Poland it is fairly frequent. Fruiting bodies grow from August to October, mainly in coniferous and mixed forests. It usually grows on dead roots and on rotten wood located in the ground. It occurs on various tree species, but most often on pines and spruces.
Tapinella panuoides (Fr.) E.-J. Gilbert (Polish: ponurnik bocznotrzonowy) is a species of basidiomycete fungus in the family Tapinellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter from 1–12 cm, but usually not exceeding 8 cm, shell-shaped or spatula-shaped, sometimes cup-shaped. Fruiting bodies attached laterally to the substrate or, less often, lateral on a short stalk. The cap skin is dry, velvety to suede-like, with age becoming almost smooth, with only the margin felty. The margin is inrolled, becoming increasingly wavy with age. Hymenophore: Gills crowded, with numerous connections resembling anastomoses, forked, usually wavy, decurrent. Ochre-yellow to yellow in colour, fading with age, easily detached from the cap. Stem: Most often there is no stem. Less often a rudimentary lateral and short one, in the colour of the cap, with gills running down onto it. Flesh: White or cream, and sometimes dirty yellow, soft and thin. It does not change colour when damaged. The taste is mild, the smell indistinct. Spore print: The colour of the spore print is yellowish, light brown or ochre-brown. Spores with a smooth surface, broadly elliptical, measuring 4–6×3–4 µm, dextrinoid. Mature spores usually with one droplet. No cystidia. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: On rotten, decayed wood in forests, parks, but also in houses, cellars, greenhouses, wells and mines. It colonises trunks of dead trees, boards, beams, wooden planters and other wooden objects. It grows on the wood of spruces and pines, sporadically on the wood of deciduous trees. It produces fruiting bodies from August to December, and in mild winters even until January, most often in tufts and small groups. It is not very frequent, but widespread. It is not a threatened species.
Thelephora caryophyllea (Schaeff.) Pers. (Polish: chropiatka lejkowata) is a species of fungus in the family Thelephoraceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Funnel-shaped, up to 5 cm in diameter and up to 4 cm tall. The upper part of the cap is often irregularly ragged and resembles a flower. The cap surface is brown or chocolate-coloured, only the margin is whitish. It is more or less zoned, sometimes covered with small scales or finely hairy. It fades after drying. It has a short, fairly thick and centrally set stem. The hymenium is smooth, running down onto the stem, brown or violet-brown, paler at the edges. The flesh is thin, brown, odourless. Microscopic features: Spores ellipsoid, more or less angular, covered with spines up to 1 μm long, less often up to 1.5 μm, sometimes they are bluntly ending warts. They are violet in colour and measure 6.5–8.5 × 5–7 μm. Basidia with 2–4 sterigmata. They are 7–8.5 μm long. Cystidia absent. Hyphae with brown walls and 3–6.5(8) μm thick, with septa. Similar species: A similar colour and also a funnel-shaped fruiting body is formed by Thelephora terrestris (Polish: chropiatka pospolita), but it does not have such ragged margins and is often a tiered fruiting body composed of several funnels.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs only in North America and Europe. In Poland it is a rare species. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is V – species vulnerable to extinction. It is on lists of threatened species also in Germany and Denmark. A mycorrhizal fungus. It grows on the ground in coniferous and mixed forests, especially under pines. It produces fruiting bodies from July to October.
Thelephora palmata (Scop.) Fr. (Polish: chropiatka cuchnąca) is a species of fungus in the family chropiatkowate.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Branched like a small shrub, up to 10 cm tall, without a distinct main stem. The branchlets are dense, with flattened tips bearing teeth. The surface is smooth, dark brownish, chocolate-brown or rusty-brown, often with a violet tinge. In youth the ends of the segments have whitish tips. Flesh: Black-brown, very compact and bast-like, with an unpleasant smell of garlic or rotten cabbage. Sometimes, however, there is no smell. After drying it becomes brittle. Microscopic features: Spores brown, irregularly angular, measuring 8–12 × 7–9 μm. The surface has short spines measuring 0.5–1.5 μm. Basidia measuring 70–100 × 9–12 μm with 2–4 sterigmata. Cystidia absent. Hyphae 3–9 μm wide with clamp connections, often with secondary septa. In the context the hyphae are condensed, often at the ends of the segments the hyphae are sterile. Similar species: Most similar is Thelephora anthocephala (Polish: chropiatka kwiatowata). It has similar, shrub-like fruiting bodies, but smaller, sometimes resembling the crown of a flower. They give off no smell. It occurs in deciduous forests.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Thelephora palmata is widespread. It occurs in North and Central America, Europe, Asia and Australia. In Poland it is fairly common, but it is on the red lists of threatened species in Germany and the Netherlands. It grows mostly in groups in coniferous and mixed forests, among mosses and needle litter, especially under pines. It appears from July to November.
Thelephora penicillata (Pers.) Fr. (Polish: chropiatka pędzelkowata) is a species of fungus in the family Thelephoraceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Short-lived, fan-shaped, resembling a rosette, formed low on the forest floor. It is from 4 to 15 cm wide, and the individual spines reach a length of 2 to 7 cm. The colour is violet-brown at the base and white or cream towards the branched and pointed tips. Older fruiting bodies turn brown from the centre. The smell is earthy, but weak, the taste mild, not characteristic. Microscopic features: Trama hyphae monomitic, usually 4–7 µm wide, with clamp connections. Spores angular-ellipsoid, 7–10 × 5–7 µm with irregular warts, violet-brown in mass.

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: Thelephora penicillata occurs in North America, Europe and Asia. Most localities have been reported in Europe. In Poland, W. Wojewoda in 2003 cited a dozen or so localities. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its category is V – a vulnerable species which will probably move to the category of endangered species in the near future if the threatening factors continue to operate. More up-to-date localities are given by the online mushroom atlas. A mycorrhizal fungus, but it can probably also live as a saprotroph, drawing nutrients from decomposing wood, leaves and needles.
Thelephora terrestris Ehrh. (Polish: chropiatka pospolita) is a species of fungus in the family Thelephoraceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting bodies: Perennial, of very varied shapes. They may be goblet-shaped, funnel-shaped, circular, semicircular, fan-shaped, kidney-shaped, shelf-shaped. They attach to the substrate by their side, or by means of a short stem. Sometimes they occur singly, but more often in groups. They may grow like roof tiles or in rows, and then sometimes fuse with one another. A single fruiting body is 3-5, exceptionally up to 10 cm wide and 2–3 mm thick. The margin is usually sharp, ciliate and ragged on older specimens. The upper surface is rough, uneven, wrinkled, coarse or hairy, and zoned, both concentrically and radially. The colour is from cinnamon to chocolate-brown, the margin is paler; at first white, with age becoming white-beige. Hymenophore: Smooth, slightly warty or radially wavy and wrinkled. Flesh: Chocolate-brown, elastic and soft in young fruiting bodies, bast-like and leathery in older ones. The taste is earthy, the smell weak, sourish. Spores: Elliptical or kidney-shaped, measuring about 8–10×7–8 μm, with a warty surface, without a germ pore. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs on all continents, except Antarctica and South America, also on many islands. In Poland it is fairly common. It grows in coniferous and deciduous forests. It produces fruiting bodies from July to November. It grows mainly in pine forests, often also in young stands and forest nurseries. It grows on soil, on stumps, on needles in forest litter, on twigs, on heaps of dead grasses and other plant remains. It also attacks trees cultivated in gardens and parks. It usually produces fruiting bodies at the root collar of attacked trees.
Trametes gibbosa (Pers.) Fr. (Polish: wrośniak garbaty) is a species of fungus in the family Polyporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Annual, but fairly durable, so that they are met throughout the year. Sometimes they overwinter. Young specimens are shaped like a misshapen tuber, after maturing they become bracket-shaped, semicircular or shell-shaped. They attach to the tree by their side and reach a width of 8-10, exceptionally up to 20 cm and a thickness of 1-4, exceptionally up to 8 cm. They differ from other Trametes species in a humped thickening at the point of attachment. The upper surface of the fruiting body has very varied colours, it is white, white-ochre, yellowish, white-hazel, grey, rusty-cinnamon, olive-celadon, bluish, and has concentric ridges of the same colour. The margin of the fruiting body is even, blunt, with time becoming wavy, sometimes brown-red. The fruiting body is often overgrown with algae, taking on a green colour, and usually only the margins are white. Only in young fruiting bodies is the upper surface velvety, later it becomes smooth and bare. Hymenophore: Tubular. The tubes are 1–5 mm long and have white pores. A characteristic feature of this species is that these pores are never round, but always elongated, pit-like. Sometimes near the hump they take the form of gills. Flesh:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is common in Asia and Europe. In North America it did not occur, but has spread in some regions as an introduced species. In Poland it is fairly common, especially frequently found in beech and hornbeam forests. It grows on trunks and dead wood of deciduous trees. It often occurs in groups. It occurs on the following deciduous trees: horse chestnut, silver birch, hornbeam, beech, poplar, oak, very rarely on fir.
Trametes hirsuta (Wulfen) Lloyd (Polish: wrośniak szorstki) is a species of fungus in the family Polyporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: It reaches a width of up to 10 cm and a thickness of up to 1 cm. It is flat, attaches to the tree by its side and is semicircular, fan-shaped or shell-shaped. The upper surface is coloured from whitish through greyish-yellow and rusty to hazel and has a characteristic concentric grooving. It is covered with fibrils giving it a shaggy or felty appearance. The margin is usually darker (brownish) and wavy or crenate. The fruiting body is often overgrown with algae, as a result of which it becomes green. Bluish or grey-black tinges never occur. Fruiting bodies often occur in groups in rows. They are very variable morphologically and in different environmental conditions this fungus forms many forms differing considerably in the morphology of the fruiting bodies. Hymenophore: Tubular, white on young specimens, then cream, finally greyish or rusty. The tubes form only one layer. They are 1–3 (exceptionally up to 5) mm long, the pores round or polygonal, white, on older fruiting bodies cream, 0.2–0.4 mm in diameter. Flesh: Whitish, elastic, 2–6 mm thick. It has a light smell of anise. Spore print: White or straw-yellow.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A cosmopolitan species. Apart from Antarctica it occurs on all continents, and also on many islands. In Central Europe it is one of the most common Trametes species. An annual fungus. It usually occurs in clusters. It attacks mainly deciduous trees (birch, beech, rowan, oak, willow), less often coniferous. A characteristic feature of this species is its occurrence on dry wood and in well-lit places.
Trametes ochracea (Pers.) Gilb. & Ryvarden (Polish: wrośniak strefowany, wrośniak wielobarwny) is a species of fungus in the family Polyporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Width 3–10 cm, thickness 0.5–1 cm. It attaches to the tree by its side or centrally. With lateral attachment it is bracket-shaped, with central attachment plate-shaped or rosette-shaped. The cap margin is sharp, thin and wavy. At the point of attachment the cap is distinctly thicker and usually has a small knob here. The surface is delicately velvety, felty, matt, without gloss, coloured from ochre-brown through light red-brown to chestnut or grey-coffee. The cap is distinctly concentrically zoned, though less contrasting than in Trametes versicolor (Polish: wrośniak różnobarwny). Hymenophore: Tubular. Tubes 1–4 mm long, pores roundish and angular, flattened in older fruiting bodies. They are 2.5–3.3 mm in diameter, coloured from white to cream. The tubes form only one layer, and their edge is toothed or serrated. Flesh: White, elastic, with a slightly sourish smell. Spore print: Cream. Spores colourless, non-amyloid, cylindrical and bent into a comma shape. One end is pointed. Dimensions: 5.5–7.5 × 2.5–3 μm. Similar species: Most similar and sometimes difficult to distinguish is Trametes versicolor.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs throughout the Northern Hemisphere; in Asia, Europe, North and Central America and the northern part of South America. In Poland it is widespread and common. It occurs in forests, gardens, parks and road edges. It colonises dead wood, both barked and unbarked. Fruiting bodies appear throughout the year. Its occurrence has been found mainly on deciduous trees and shrubs; on grey alder, silver birch, cherry, beech, poplar, plum, black locust, willow, lilac, elm, very rarely on coniferous (silver fir).
Trametes versicolor (L.) Lloyd (Polish: wrośniak różnobarwny) is a species of fungus in the family Polyporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Basidiocarp: Width 3–8 cm, thickness 2–5 mm. It attaches to the tree by its side or centrally. With lateral attachment it is bracket-shaped, with central attachment plate-shaped or rosette-shaped. Young individuals are almost uniformly light brown and felty and at this stage of development are hard to distinguish from other Trametes species. Older ones become bare, silkily shiny and – which is a characteristic feature of this species – have distinct concentric zones in different shades from brown through dark blue to black. The margin of the fruiting body is sharp and thin, the surface uneven, radially wrinkled and grooved, shortly hairy or rough, silkily shiny. On older fruiting bodies algae often develop, as a result of which they change colour to a more or less greenish one. Hymenophore: Polyporoid. Tubes 0.5–2 mm long. They form only one layer, their edges are toothed or serrated. They are cream in colour, light brown on older specimens. Pores round, with time angular, and irregular in older fruiting bodies, 0.15–0.4 mm in diameter. Context: White and very thin (2–5 mm), elastic and aromatic. Spore print: Straw-yellow. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A cosmopolitan species; apart from Antarctica it occurs on all continents, and also on many islands. It is probably one of the most frequently occurring fungus species of the order Polyporales in Europe. In Europe and in Poland it is very common, rarer only in riverside alluvial forests – there other species occur that are better adapted to life on the soft wood of these forests. A tree-dwelling fungus, a saprotroph growing on trunks and stumps of trees, often already soon after the tree is felled or dies. It usually grows in groups, with neighbouring fruiting bodies overlapping like roof tiles.
Trichaptum abietinum (Pers. ex J.F. Gmel.) Ryvarden (Polish: niszczyk iglastodrzewny) is a species of fungus in the order Hymenochaetales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Annual. Width from a few to a dozen or so cm. Thin, of variable shape. Usually spread out and reflexed, but sometimes shelf-shaped, hemispherical or entirely spread out. The margin is thin and sharp. It attaches to the substrate by its upper surface, which is uneven, felty and coloured from whitish through white-grey, greyish to greyish-yellowish. Hymenophore: Tubular. The pores in youth are beautifully violet, especially near the margin, often running far down onto the wood. Flesh: Thin, two-layered, elastic, leathery-waxy. Microscopic features: Basidia thickened, measuring 13–15 × 5–6 μm with 4 sterigmata. Spores cylindrical and slightly bent, smooth, colourless, non-amyloid. They measure 6–7.5 × 2–2.5 μm. Cystidia are numerous, up to 47 μm in diameter, usually incrusted, embedded in the hymenium, or projecting above it by up to 15 μm. Hyphae colourless, rarely branched, with clamp connections. They are 2–4 μm thick. Similar species: Trichaptum fuscoviolaceum (Polish: niszczyk ząbkowaty), also occurring on the wood of coniferous trees, but differing in its gill-like-toothed hymenophore.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs on all continents except Antarctica and Africa, but is most numerously recorded in the Northern Hemisphere in the temperate climate zone. It forms fruiting bodies throughout the year. It grows in forests on the wood of coniferous trees. It colonises pine, spruce, fir, larch, and also many exotic coniferous tree species cultivated in Poland. It occurs throughout Poland and is common.
Trichaptum biforme (Fr.) Ryvarden (Polish: niszczyk liściastodrzewny) is a species of fungus in the order Hymenochaetales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting bodies: Sessile (without a stem), up to 6 cm in diameter and up to 3 mm thick, more or less semicircular, irregularly hoof-shaped or kidney-shaped, sometimes spread out and reflexed. The surface is hairy, finely hairy or fairly smooth, with zones coloured from whitish to greyish-white. The margin is pale lilac in places. Fruiting bodies are usually in large and dense clusters arranged like roof tiles. The hymenophore is tubular. Pores 3–5 per mm, coloured from violet to lilac, most strongly coloured at the margin, with age fading to tawny or brownish, as they mature turning into teeth or spines. They do not turn blue when touched. The flesh is whitish, hard and leathery, in reaction with KOH negative to pale yellow. Microscopic features: Dimitic hyphal system. Spores 6–8 × 2–2.5 µm, smooth, cylindrical to slightly sausage-shaped, hyaline in KOH, non-amyloid. Cystidia numerous, measuring up to 35 × 5 µm, with incrusted tips, more or less spindle-shaped. Similar species: Trichaptum fuscoviolaceum (Polish: niszczyk ząbkowaty), occurring on the wood of coniferous trees, also differs in its gill-like-toothed hymenophore.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A cosmopolitan species, occurring on many islands and all continents except Antarctica. W. Wojewoda, in his 2003 list of large basidiomycetous fungi of Poland, cited numerous localities, but according to him it is a rare species in Poland. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is R – a rare species, with a limited geographical range, with small habitat areas or occurring over a vast area but in great dispersion. The most up-to-date localities are given by the online mushroom atlas.
Trichaptum fuscoviolaceum (Ehrenb.) Ryv. (Polish: niszczyk ząbkowaty) is a species of fungus in the order Hymenochaetales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting bodies: Annual and usually occurring in groups. A single fruiting body is 1.5–6 cm wide, 1–4 mm thick, semicircular, fan-shaped, spread out or spread out and reflexed. The margin is sharp and thin, inrolled in older specimens. It has no stem, and attaches to the substrate by its side or base. Fruiting bodies growing in numbers next to one another fuse at their bases, sometimes covering a large area. In young specimens the surface is strongly felty-hairy, woolly, or at least velvety, in older ones bare. The colour is white, white-grey, green-grey and concentrically zoned and grooved. The cap margin is at first violet, later yellow-brown. Hymenophore: Tubular-reticulate-gill-like. It takes the form of a net-like structure at the margin passing into radiating gills. The openings of the hymenophore are spatula-shaped and toothed. At first it is cream-violet or violet, later grey-yellow-brown. It is covered with a grey-violet bloom. Flesh: It forms two layers, the upper one felty, white, the lower skin-like, yellow-brown. In young fruiting bodies it is elastic, in older ones gradually hardening, finally stiff. Microscopic features:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in the Northern Hemisphere: in North America, Europe and Asia. In Central Europe it is frequent, in Poland too it is common and occurs throughout the country. In Denmark and the Netherlands it is rare, and is on the red lists of threatened species there. It develops in coniferous and mixed forests, in parks, also sometimes in timber yards. It grows exclusively on coniferous trees; on dead trunks lying on the ground, on stumps and logs, mainly on pine, less often fir and spruce.
Tricholoma columbetta (Fr.) P. Kumm. (Polish: gąska gołębia) is a species of fungus in the family Tricholomataceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter from 5 to 10 cm, young – conical, later flat, with a broad blunt umbo, the margin at first inrolled, later sharp, wavy and finally bent. The skin is silkily glossy, radially fibrous, sticky in wet conditions, whitish, often with ochre, greenish or reddish spots. Gills: At first narrow and crowded, later up to 10 mm wide, with irregularly toothed edges, whitish to whitish-cream. Stem: Height from 5 to 10 cm, diameter up to 3 cm, cylindrical, narrowed at the base, whitish, often with blue-green spots at the bottom. Flesh: Juicy, compact, whitish. The smell is indistinctly earthy-mealy. The taste is slightly mealy. Microscopic features: Spore print white. Spores ovoid, 5.5-7 × 4-5.5 µm in diameter, smooth, with one oily droplet. Basidia thickened, cylindrical, 4-spored, measuring 29-42 × 7-8 µm. Hyphae in the gills thin, without clamp connections. Skin hyphae thin, with rounded cells without pigment. Similar species: There are several species of white Tricholoma, but this one is easy to distinguish if certain characteristic features of structure and habitat are taken into account.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been described in North America, Europe and Costa Rica. In Poland it is a rare species. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographical range and small habitat areas. It is on lists of threatened species also in Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands and Lithuania. A ground-dwelling fungus. It appears from August to October in light deciduous forests (under beeches, birches or oaks), on soils poor in calcium, though not very acid; dispersed.
Tricholoma equestre (L.) P. Kumm. (Polish: gąska zielonka) is a species of fungus in the family Tricholomataceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 4–10 cm, yellow-green or yellow-brown, darker in the middle, smooth, in a young fruiting body conical-convex, later flat, often variously bent. The skin is bare or finely scaly, greasy and therefore often with grains of sand, slimy in damp conditions. Gills: From pale yellowish to sulphur-yellow, moderately crowded, thin, notched with a tooth, but broadly adnate at the base. Stem: It reaches a length of 3 to 9 cm and a thickness of up to 3 cm. It is cylindrical, solid. The surface at first with longitudinal fibres, later smooth, yellow or yellowish-greenish. Flesh: Hard, brittle, white, does not change colour after cutting. The taste is sweetish-nutty, it smells like freshly ground flour. Spore print: White. Spores 6–8 × 3.5–5 µm in diameter, ovoid, smooth, colourless. Similar species: Tricholoma frondosae (Polish: gąska liściowata), Tricholoma sejunctum (Polish: gąska zielonożółta), which has a more olive-grey cap and occurs mainly in deciduous forests. Muchomor differs in having a volva at the base of the stem, a tall stem and free gills.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Tricholoma equestre is widespread in North America and Europe, but has also been reported from some places in Asia (Japan), Central America (Costa Rica) and Africa. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is I – a species of indeterminate threat. It is on lists of threatened species also in Germany, the Netherlands and Slovakia. In countries where it is a threatened species – harvesting of this species is prohibited. A ground-dwelling mycorrhizal fungus.
Tricholoma fulvum (DC.) Bigeard & H. Guill. (Polish: gąska żółtobrunatna) is a species of fungus in the family Tricholomataceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 4–8 cm, at first hemispherical to conical-convex, later flat, with a blunt broad umbo, sometimes shallowly concave in the middle, sticky in wet conditions, shiny in drought, with delicate, embedded, radial fibrils, smooth, red-brown, brown, yellow-brown, with a darker centre. Gills: Width from 6 to 10 mm, moderately crowded, light yellow to brownish-yellow, on the smooth edge with red-brown spots. Stem: Height from 5 to 11 cm, diameter from 1 to 1.8 cm, cylindrical, young – solid, later tubular, with longitudinal brown fibrils on a yellowish background, paler in the upper part, yellowing when scraped. Flesh: Compact, fairly thick in the middle of the cap, white to yellowish. The smell is slightly mealy, the taste mealy and bitterish. Spore print: White. Spores smooth, elliptical, non-amyloid, measuring 5-7.5 × 6-4 µm. Similar species: There are many similar brown Tricholoma species, among them: Tricholoma batschii (Polish: gąska czerwonobrązowa) with cream-white gills and a stem wedge-shaped narrowed at the base, Tricholoma ustale (Polish: gąska bukowa), with a smooth and shiny cap and rusty gills

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Tricholoma fulvum is widespread in North America and in Europe; from Asia its occurrence has been confirmed only in Japan. In Poland many localities have been reported. A ground-dwelling fungus. Fruiting bodies appear from July to October (November), in mixed forests under birches, rarely in single-species spruce forests; it likes acid soils. It is fairly common. It grows mainly under birch and spruce.
Tricholoma imbricatum (Fr.) P.Kumm. (Polish: gąska dachówkowata) is a species of fungus in the family Tricholomataceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 3–8(10) cm, young almost bell-shaped, with an inrolled margin, later slightly flattened to completely flat, at first smooth-fibrous, then over the whole surface, except the top, scaly, red-brown to brown, rarely also with an olive-yellow background. The skin is dry, cracking into tiny scales. Gills: Crowded, rounded at the stem or notched with a tooth, at first dirty white, later spotted red-brownish. When damaged they change colour to brown. Stem: Length 6–15 cm and thickness 1–1.5 cm, cylindrical, at first solid, later hollow. White at the top, otherwise pale brown with small fibrils. The base of the stem narrowed or rooting. The annular zone invisible. Flesh: White, rusty-brownish at the base of the stem. It is odourless, or has a weak mushroomy-herbal smell. The taste is mild or bitterish. Spore print: White. Microscopic features: Spores short-ellipsoid, smooth, colourless, 5–5.5 × 3.5–4 µm in diameter. Similar species: Many similar Tricholoma species grow in Poland.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The most numerous localities of this species have been described in North America and Europe, but it also occurs in Japan, Australia and Costa Rica in Central America. In Poland it is fairly rare. A ground-dwelling fungus. It grows from September to December in coniferous forests, above all under pines, less often under spruces. Sometimes it grows in large groups and forms fairy rings. It likes sandy soils. It is resistant to rot – its fruiting bodies can persist in the forest for even several weeks.
Tricholoma portentosum (Fr.) Quel. (Polish: gąska niekształtna) is a species of fungus in the family Tricholomataceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 3–10 cm, the surface grey, pale grey, dark grey, often with an olive, yellowish or violet tinge and with characteristic blackish, embedded radial fibrils. At first the fruiting body is conical-convex, later flattened, with inrolled margins, often with a blunt umbo in the middle, usually with wavy margins. In damp conditions slightly slimy. Gills: At first white, then greyish, moderately crowded, thin, notched with a tooth. Stem: Height 5–10 cm, thickness 2 cm. It is cylindrical, solid, smooth, shiny. The surface is whitish with a yellowish or greyish tinge, in old age yellow-greenish in places. Flesh: White, only under the cap skin bluish-grey. It does not change colour when pressed. The taste is mild – sweetish and nutty, the smell mealy. Spore print: White. Spores 5–6 × 4–5 µm in diameter, ovoid, smooth, colourless. Similar species: There are several Tricholoma species of similar, grey-black colouring: Tricholoma virgatum (Polish: gąska pieprzna). It has a sharply conical cap, without fibrils and is pungent in taste; Tricholoma atrosquamosum (Polish: gąska czarnołuskowa) has blackish scales on the cap,

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North and Central America, Europe, Africa and Asia. In Europe it is widespread. In Poland a common species. A ground-dwelling fungus. It produces fruiting bodies from October to December in pine forests with a great deal of lichens or mosses, likes sandy soils, almost always in groups, sometimes together with Tricholoma equestre; in places frequent.
Tricholoma saponaceum (Fr.) P. Kumm. (Polish: gąska mydlana) is a species of fungus in the family gąskowate.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 5–10 cm, bell-shaped or hemispherical in youth, later flat-arched, but for a long time with an inrolled margin, finally becomes flat and bent with concave hollows. It is fleshy, smooth and shiny, in dry weather it has a cracked skin, in wet weather it is sticky. It is characterised by enormous variability of colour among individual specimens. Most often the cap skin is grey-green, but it may be from white to black-brown. In dark-coloured specimens the margin is distinctly paler. Several varieties differing considerably in colouring are distinguished. Gills: Widely spaced, slightly thickened, notched with a tooth. At first they are white, later yellow-grey, blackening when damaged. Stem: Height 6–10 cm, thickness 1–2.5 cm. It is cylindrical or spindle-shaped, pointed at the bottom, usually smooth, bare or scaly, sometimes with ochre spots. Coloured like the cap, but in a paler shade. Flesh: Whitish, fleshy, flushed red at the base of the stem. After some time from harvesting reddening, with a soapy smell and a (sometimes) bitterish-mealy taste. Microscopic features: Spore print white.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Tricholoma saponaceum occurs on all continents except Antarctica. In Poland it is common. A ground-dwelling fungus. It appears from September to November, in coniferous and mixed forests. Sometimes it occurs in groups. It grows under firs or pines.
Tricholoma scalpturatum (Fr.) Quél. (Polish: gąska żółknąca) is a species of fungus in the family Tricholomataceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 2.5–8 cm, at first arched, but quickly becomes flat-spread out. In the middle it has a blunt umbo. The margin stays inrolled for a long time. The surface is covered with radial fibrils and scales. The colour is at first grey-brown with a faint violet tinge, later becomes paler, cream. The scales are coloured from dark grey-brown to black-brown with a reddish tinge. Older specimens turn yellow. Gills: Decurrent on the stem with a tooth, broad. The colour is at first white, with age they turn yellow. Stem: Height 3–6 cm, thickness 0.6–1.2 cm, cylindrical with a thickened base, solid. The surface is longitudinally fibrous and silkily shiny, whitish or slightly grey, yellowing in older specimens. Flesh: White, yellowing with age. Taste and smell weak, mealy. Similar species: A characteristic feature of this species is yellowing with age, and after damage to various parts of the fruiting body, especially the gills. This feature makes it possible to distinguish Tricholoma scalpturatum from the very similar Tricholoma pardinum (Polish: gąska tygrysia), which does not yellow. Also similar is Tricholoma cingulatum (Polish: gąska wierzbowa), but it occurs exclusively under willows and has a ring on the stem.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in Europe and North America. In Poland many localities have been reported. A ground-dwelling fungus. It occurs in coniferous and deciduous forests, in parks, thickets and at road edges. It produces fruiting bodies from July to October. It prefers alkaline soils.
Tricholoma sulphureum (Bull.) P. Kumm. (Polish: gąska siarkowa) is a species of fungus in the family Tricholomataceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 3–8 cm, in a young fruiting body conical-convex, later flat. The margin is sharp, the surface bare, sometimes finely scaly, slimy in wet weather. The colour is sulphur-yellow, olive-yellow, and in places red-brown. In the middle it is darker and very delicately covered with purple flakes. Gills: Bright yellow, rather thick, notched with a tooth. They are distant, which is an important feature making it possible to distinguish Tricholoma sulphureum from the similar Tricholoma equestre (Polish: gąska zielonka), which has more crowded gills. Stem: Height 4–10 cm, thickness up to 2 cm, the shape cylindrical or club-shaped. It is at first solid, later hollow, sulphur-yellow, covered with rusty fibrils. At the base it is whitish and hairy. Flesh: Yellow. The smell is unpleasant, like carbide or town gas. Spore print: White. Spores fairly large, ovoid, smooth, colourless, 9–12 × 5–7 µm in diameter. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Tricholoma sulphureum occurs in Europe and North America, and has also been found in China. In Central Europe it is widespread, but occurs in a dispersed manner. In Poland it is fairly common. A ground-dwelling mycorrhizal fungus. It grows in deciduous and mixed forests, on the ground, among grasses and fallen branches, with no particular requirements as to soil reaction. It often occurs under pines. It produces fruiting bodies from August to November.
Tricholomopsis decora (Fr.) Singer (Polish: rycerzyk oliwkowożółty) is a species of fungus in the order Agaricales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 3–6 cm, at first arched, later flat with a depressed centre. The surface is golden-yellow, covered with scales coloured from olive-brown to olive-black. Most of the scales are in the middle of the cap. Gills: Moderately crowded, 3–8 mm wide, notched with a tooth at the stem. They are intensely yellow, with evenly frosted edges. Stem: Height 5–8 cm, thickness 0.7–1.2 cm. It is cylindrical, usually curved, at first solid, with time hollow inside. The surface is scaly or fibrous, yellow, only in the uppermost part under the gills whitish in young fruiting bodies. Flesh: Thin, springy, yellow. It does not change colour when damaged. The taste is somewhat bitter, the smell mild and weak. In reaction with KOH it changes colour to pink or red. Spore print: White. Spores elliptical, smooth, non-amyloid, measuring 6–7.5 × 4.5–5 μm. Pleurocystidia sparse and barely projecting above the basidia, cheilocystidia numerous. Similar species: Tricholomopsis ornata (Polish: rycerzyk czerwonołuskowy), which has red-brown or reddish scales. Tricholomopsis rutilans (Polish: rycerzyk czerwonozłoty) is larger, has reddish tinges on the cap and red-violet scales.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America and Europe. In Europe it occurs mainly in the mountains, at scattered localities; outside the mountains it is found very rarely. In Poland it is a rare species. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographical range and small habitat areas. It is on lists of threatened species also in Denmark and the Netherlands. Saprotroph. It grows in coniferous and mixed forests on rotting wood of spruces and pines. It produces fruiting bodies from June to October.
Tricholomopsis rutilans (Schaeff.) Singer (Polish: rycerzyk czerwonozłoty) is a species of fungus in the order Agaricales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 3–15 cm, in young specimens semicircular, arched with an inrolled margin, in older ones spread out, sometimes with a blunt umbo. The skin is delicately felty, the yellow background covered with lilac-red scales. This species has a very variable cap colouring; in young specimens the cap may be entirely purple-violet, and in older ones uniformly yellow. A record specimen was found in Italy on the trunk of a cork oak – its cap was 56 cm in diameter. Gills: Fairly crowded, notched with a tooth at the stem or broadly adnate and somewhat lobed. They are always yellowish in colour, but in younger specimens they are paler, darkening with age. Stem: Height 5–12 cm, thickness 1–3 cm. It is cylindrical, the colour of the cap, sometimes only yellow, set off whitish or yellowish right under the cap, soon becoming hollow. Flesh: Yellow. The smell and taste are somewhat insipid. Spore print: White, non-amyloid. Spores smooth, elliptical, measuring 6.5–8 × 4.5–5.5 μm, without a germ pore.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North and Central America, Europe, Asia and Australia. In Poland it is common. It produces fruiting bodies from July to November, singly or in clumps on tree trunks. Sometimes it occurs in groups. It grows at the base of trunks or on dead wood. Sometimes it seems to grow on the ground, but in reality the mycelium growing from the base of its stem grows on tree roots. It grows on various tree species, both deciduous and coniferous, but it has been observed that in Central Europe it grows mainly on coniferous trees, while in Southern Europe on deciduous trees.
Tubaria conspersa (Pers.) Fayod (Polish: trąbka kłaczkowata) is a species of fungus in the family Tubariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 8–25 mm, at first hemispherical, then weakly convex, sometimes with a slight depression in the middle. The margin is at first bent, then straight, finally slightly raised, indistinctly striate, sometimes with hanging flocks. It is hygrophanous. When wet it is bright cinnamon-brown, when dry ochre or grey-ochre. The surface is at first delicately felty, then scaly. Gills: Adnate and slightly decurrent, broad, distant, light cinnamon-brown. Stem: Height 2–3.5 cm, thickness 1.5–3 mm, cylindrical, sometimes thickened at the base. The surface is bare with a few scales, at the base with white hyphae of mycelium. Flesh: Very thin, elastic, whitish-ochre-brown, fleshy in the cap, fibrous in the stem. It does not change colour when damaged. The taste is mild, the smell mushroomy, weak. Microscopic features: Spore print ochre-brown. Cheilocystidia of a shape from cylindrical to club-shaped, strongly elongated, sometimes irregularly bent.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of Tubaria conspersa is known in North America and in Europe. In Europe it is widespread. In the scientific literature, numerous localities in Poland had been reported by 2003. Numerous localities are also given by the online mushroom atlas. It is described there as a common species, nevertheless it has been placed on the list of threatened species worth protecting. Saprotroph. It occurs on the ground in deciduous and mixed forests. Fruiting bodies usually appear from September to November.
Tubaria furfuracea (Pers.) Gillet (Polish: trąbka otrębiasta) is a species of fungus in the family Tubariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 1–4 cm, at first convex, but quickly becomes spread out, sometimes with a blunt umbo. In young fruiting bodies there are fibrils at the margins that are remains of the veil. It is hygrophanous; when wet the surface is coloured from yellow-brown to red-brown and the cap is translucently striate from the margins to half its diameter, when dry it is coloured from brown-ochre to light ochre and is not striate. In older specimens the cap margin is bent outward. Gills: Broad and broadly decurrent, coloured from light ochre to red-brown. Stem: Height 2–4 cm, thickness about 0.4 cm, cylindrical. The surface is light ochre-brown with remains of the veil in the form of whitish scales. In young fruiting bodies there is a fibrillose, but quickly vanishing annular zone. Flesh: Thin and the same colour as the cap. It has an indistinct taste and a weak mushroomy or radish-like smell. Spore print: Light orange-brown. Spores oval or ellipsoid, smooth, measuring 7–8 × 4.5–5 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America and in Europe, commonly in Central Europe. In Poland it is common. It grows in forests, parks and gardens on dead wood, on bark, twigs, also on wood buried in the ground, less often on stumps. Fruiting bodies appear from March to December. It appears on the wood of both deciduous and coniferous trees.
Tulostoma brumale Pers. (Polish: berłóweczka zimowa, pałeczka zimowa) is a species of fungus in the family Agaricaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: The young fruiting body is spherical or egg-shaped, and forms underground (hypogeically). During maturation a stem develops that pushes up above the ground, and at its top a spherical head up to 1.3 cm in diameter forms. The outer covering (exoperidium) is membranous, whitish and quickly falls off. Only on the lower part of the head do its remains often persist in the form of hanging fringes.
