The inner covering (endoperidium) is stiff, parchment-like, smooth, whitish, with age ochre-white with rusty spots. It opens at the top with a short tubular, slightly projecting mouth. The zone around the mouth is darker in colour. The stem is 1.5 to 7 cm long and up to 0.4 cm thick, tawny-rusty, at first fibrous, then bare. It is covered with delicate scales more or less adhering to the stem, becoming smooth with age. The gleba is light brown. Microscopic features: Capillitium transparent and colourless, thick-walled, with a narrow lumen, rarely septate and often covered with crystals. Spores spherical, pale yellowish, finely warted, up to 6 µm in diameter. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in the Northern Hemisphere. In Poland it is rare. Newer localities are given by the online mushroom atlas. In Poland it was a strictly protected species; on 9 October 2014 it was removed from the list of protected fungus species. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is R – rare species. It is on lists of threatened species also in Germany, Austria, Belgium, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Norway, Finland and Sweden. A ground-dwelling fungus. It grows singly or in groups in warm grasslands among grasses and mosses, on dry, sandy or calcareous soils.
Tylopilus felleus (Bull.) P. Karst. (Polish: goryczak żółciowy) is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter generally up to 12 cm, semicircular in young specimens, then convex, to spread out in older ones. The surface is first downy, suede-like, then smooth. The colour is from light brown to flesh-brown. Tubes: Long, with pores extending beyond the cap margin. In young specimens they are white, later pale pink, and damaged ones take on a dirty wine colour. They can be easily separated from the flesh. Stem: Thickness 2–4 cm, height up to 14 cm. Solid, barrel-shaped in young specimens, club-shaped in older ones, paler than the cap, covered with a distinct brown network with wide meshes. Flesh: White, elastic, does not change colour after damage. Hard in youth, spongy in older specimens. It has a pleasant smell, but is very bitter. Spore print: Pink. Spores spindle-shaped or ellipsoid, measuring 10–15 × 4–6 μm. Similar species: Young specimens are quite often confused with Boletus edulis (Polish: borowik szlachetny) or Leccinum scabrum (Polish: koźlarz babka). A simple way to distinguish these species is to touch a broken-off fragment of the cap with the tongue. The taste of bile leaves no doubt that it is Tylopilus felleus.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America, Europe and Asia (in the latter its occurrence has been described only in Japan and Korea). In some regions it occurs fairly numerously. It grows on the ground, sometimes also on trunks and stumps, since its mycelium can also develop on rotting wood. It produces fruiting bodies from June to the end of October in coniferous forests, and likes acid soils. It forms mycorrhiza with pine.
Verpa bohemica (Krombh.) J. Schröt. (Polish: naparstniczka czeska) is a species of fungus in the family Morchellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Made up of a head and a stalk. It reaches a height of up to 10–20 cm. Head: 2–5 cm tall, 2–4 cm in diameter and conical to bell-shaped in shape, attached only at the top, all the rest is free. The surface is ribbed; between low, thin, vertical, wavy and in places crosswise-connected ribs there are alveoles. The colour is from yellow-brown to dark brown. Stem: Height 7–20 cm, thickness 1–2.5 cm, cylindrical, sometimes flattened and bent, at first cottony, then hollow, brittle. The surface is at first whitish with whitish fibrils, then bare, cream-yellowish with ochre-orange spots. Flesh: Thin, waxy, white. The taste is mild, the smell mushroomy. Microscopic features: Asci two-spored, spores strongly elongated, ellipsoid, yellowish, very large, 50-80(100) with 15-25 µm. Similar species: Morchella semilibera (Polish: smardz półwolny) is distinguished by having the head attached for 1/3 to 1/2 of its length. Verpa conica (Polish: naparstniczka stożkowata) has smaller fruiting bodies, and the surface of the head is not folded.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Verpa bohemica is widespread in the Northern Hemisphere. In Poland it also occurs over the whole area. By 2020, 120 of its localities had been reported. More up-to-date localities are given by the online mushroom atlas. It is on the list of threatened species worth protecting there. In the study Red List of plants and fungi of Poland it is classified in the category of species vulnerable to extinction (V), which will most probably move in the near future to the category of endangered species if the threatening factors do not disappear.
Volvariella bombycina (Schaeff.) Singer (Polish: pochwiak jedwabnikowy) is a species of fungus in the family Volvariellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap Diameter 8–20 cm, white or yellowish. Ovoid-bell-shaped in youth, then convex, with age almost flat. Whitish in colour and delicately yellowish in the central part in older fruiting bodies. The cap margin is not inrolled. The surface is dry, covered with delicate, silky, cream or light brown fibrillose scales, hanging from the cap margin. Hymenophore Gills white, with age taking on a flesh-pink colour, broad, mixed, bulging. Crowded and not attached to the stem (free). Stem Solid, 6–20 cm long and 0.7–2 cm in diameter. More or less equal, but usually tapering slightly towards the top. Often curved in order to set the cap in a horizontal position, because of lateral growth on wood. The surface is dry, white or yellowish, smooth and without a ring. The base of the stem is surrounded by a thick volva, reaching up to half its height. It is at first whitish, with age turns yellow and brown, smooth, matt. Flesh Compact, but delicate, soft, white, does not discolour after damage. With a light smell of radish. The taste is mild, pleasant. Spore print: Pink. Spores 6.5–9 × 4.5–7 μm, elliptical and smooth. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Not very frequent. Fruiting bodies grow from June to October on living and dead trunks, logs and roots of deciduous trees. Very often in hollows and cracks, even high above the ground. It likes warmth. In principle it occurs singly, but is sometimes found in groups. It can be met in gardens, parks, along roads, on trees of the genera: maple, poplar, willow, lime, beech, oak. It has also been observed on species such as: horse chestnut, European ash, walnut or black locust. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland.
Volvopluteus gloiocephalus (DC.) Vizzini, Contu & Justo (Polish: pochwiakowiec okazały, pochwiak okazały) is a species of fungus in the family Pluteaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: It reaches a diameter of 5–12(15) cm. Whitish, ivory-coloured with a grey, grey-brownish centre. Ovoid when young, then spread out with a bulge in the centre. The skin is bare, rarely with white remains of the veil, slimy in wet weather. Stem: Dirty whitish. Of equal thickness, long, slender, deeply embedded in the soil. Without a ring, dry and smooth. The base with a skin-like, white volva. Gills: White, with age salmon-pink. Fairly broad and crowded, free. Flesh: White, soft. The smell is reminiscent of radish, the taste mild. Microscopic features: Spore print salmon-pink. Spores measuring 14–18.5 × 8–10 µm. They are ellipsoid or slightly ovoid and elongated. The club-shaped or spindle-shaped cheilocystidia measure 45–150 × 12–15 µm. Sometimes they have a papilla at the top. Pleurocystidia of similar shape and size are numerous. Similar species: Volvariella species are distinguished by the pink colour of the spore print (and of mature gills) from muchomory, which are characterised by a white spore print and gills of the same colour when mature. In addition muchomory have a ring, which is absent in pochwiaki (Volvariella).

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in a dispersed manner in Europe, and also in many places in the world. In the scientific literature numerous localities of this species in Poland have been reported. It is not, however, a frequently encountered fungus. Fruiting bodies usually grow in groups, from May to October, in cultivated fields, meadows, parks, gardens, on fertilised soil. It is easiest to find in autumn in winter-cereal sowings – the projecting caps are visible from a great distance. Saprotroph.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 3–10 cm, at first convex or hemispherical, later slowly flattens and sometimes sinks slightly in the middle. The skin is dry, matt, finely downy, brown, yellow-brown, often with an olive tinge, ochre-grey, red-brown or dark brown. In drought it cracks into patches and the flesh in the crust, from whitish to reddish, shows. Tubes: At first pale yellow, later green-yellowish or olive-greenish. They turn blue under pressure. The pores are the same colour as the tubes, wide and angular, sometimes spotted brown, turning blue under pressure. Stem: Height 4–8 cm, thickness 1–2 cm, mostly cylindrical, tapering towards the base, often slightly bent. Yellow under the cap, otherwise mostly coloured red or brown, often with longitudinal fibrils. Flesh: Hard in young specimens, later delicate, soft, watery and quickly decomposing. It is often attacked by mould. In the cap it is yellow, when damaged at first turns blue and later reddens, in the stem of adult specimens it is brown-red. It has a weak smell and a somewhat sourish taste. Spore print: Brownish-olive or olive.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is common throughout the Northern Hemisphere in the temperate climate zone. In Poland it is very common. A ground-dwelling mycorrhizal fungus. It occurs in coniferous and deciduous forests and parks. It grows on the ground under beech, Scots pine, scarlet oak, sessile oak and pedunculate oak. Fruiting bodies appear from June to November.
Xerocomellus cisalpinus (Simonini, H. Ladurner & Peintner) Klofac (Polish: suchogrzybek zmienny) is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter up to 7 cm, at first hemispherical, then convex. The surface is ochre, pale brown, grey-brown, olive-brown, dark brown to blackish-brown, sometimes with a reddish tinge, and may also be entirely red. When dry it is velvety, but cracks very quickly and a pinkish flesh shows through the cracks. Tubes: At first lemon-yellow, later pale yellow with an olive tinge, turning blue when crushed. Pores the colour of the tubes. Stem: Height 4.5–8 cm, thickness 1–1.5 cm, cylindrical or slightly club-shaped, often curved and usually tapering at the base. The surface is light yellow at the top, gradually becoming bright red towards the bottom. It turns blue when damaged. The mycelium at the base of the stem is white. Flesh: In the cap coloured from cream to yellowish, in the stem brownish, turning blue when damaged, especially in the stem. Smell and taste indistinct. Microscopic features: Spores 10.5–16 × 4–5.5 μm, striate. The cap skin is made of palisade-arranged and septate hyphae. They consist mainly of cylindrical, incrusted cells. Similar species: It may be hard to distinguish from Xerocomellus chrysenteron (Polish: suchogrzybek złotopory).

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of Xerocomellus cisalpinus is known in many countries of Europe, in the Republic of South Africa and in New Zealand. Its distribution is not exactly known, because it is a recently separated fungus species and is often confused with Xerocomellus chrysenteron. Its current localities are given by the online mushroom atlas. A ground-dwelling ectomycorrhizal fungus living in symbiosis with deciduous trees, mainly oaks, but also with beech, pine and cedar. It occurs in deciduous and mixed forests.
Xerocomellus pruinatus (Fr.) Šutara (Polish: suchogrzybek oprószony, podgrzybek oprószony, borowik oprószony) is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 3–10 cm, flat-arched or cushion-shaped. The skin is velvety, dry and uniformly coloured red-brown or dark brown. Damaged places change colour to red-brown. A characteristic feature of this species, distinguishing it from other similar ones, is that its cap does not crack into patches in old age and in dry weather. Tubes: In young specimens pale ochre, later pale yellow, turning blue when damaged. The pores are at first whitish, later yellow or yellow-green. Stem: Height 5–10 cm, thickness 1–2 cm, cylindrical, solid and hard. The skin is longitudinally fibrous, on a yellow background with red-brown colouring, except for the upper part under the cap, where it is always yellow. Flesh: Yellow, juicy and fairly hard, fibrous in the stem. When damaged it turns slightly blue, the taste is fruity, the smell pleasant. Microscopic features: Spore print brown. Spores smooth and thick-walled, brown or olive-green in colour, slightly spindle-shaped, without a droplet in the middle. Size: 11.5–14 × 4.5–5.5 µm. Basidia with four sterigmata.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Its localities have been reported only in Europe. In Poland many localities have been reported. Current localities are also given by the online mushroom atlas. It is on the list of threatened species worth protecting there. A ground-dwelling mycorrhizal fungus. It grows in various types of coniferous and deciduous forests. Fruiting bodies appear from September to November, most abundantly after cooling.
Xerocomus ferrugineus (Schaeff.) Alessio (Polish: podgrzybek grubosiatkowany, podgrzybek żeberkowany) is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 3–10 cm, hemispherical in young specimens, later becomes arched, finally flat and slightly depressed in the middle. The skin is felty, dry and uniformly coloured yellowish-olive, olive-brown, red-brown to dark brown. Damaged places change colour to red-brown. Tubes: In young specimens intensely yellow or golden-yellow and the pores round, later brown-yellow or yellow-greenish, and the pores angular. The colour of the pores is the same as that of the tubes. Stem: Height 3–10 cm, thickness 0.5–2.5 cm, cylindrical, solid and compact. The skin is smooth, coloured from cream through light brown to pale red-brown. The mycelial hyphae at the base of the stem are lemon-yellow. Flesh: Whitish or yellowish with an indeterminate taste. Dried fruiting bodies give off an unpleasant smell of urine. Similar species: Boletus subtomentosus (Polish: podgrzybek zajączek). It sometimes has similar colour varieties, but its pores turn blue when pressed, the flesh after cutting has a similar colour in the cap, but the stem is pinkish in the lower half. It also has a different colour of mycelial hyphae – white.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs only in Europe. It is absent in Scandinavia, but is present in Iceland. It grows mainly in mountain coniferous forests and under beeches, especially on sandy soils. A mycorrhizal fungus.
Xerocomus subtomentosus (L.) Quél. (Polish: podgrzybek zajączek) is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 3–10 cm, semicircular in young specimens, more flattened in older specimens. The margin is inrolled for a long time. The skin is velvety or felty, matt and cannot be peeled off. In dry weather it is cracked into patches. The colour is most often olive-brown, sometimes yellow-brown or grey-brown. It forms several colour forms, e.g. with a light yellow cap (X. subtomentosus var. luteolus) or brown-reddish (X. subtomentosus var. rubrotinctus). Tubes: 5–20 mm long, yellow, darkening with age to green-yellow and olive-brown, at first adnate and slightly decurrent, then free. Pores large, angular, irregular, light yellow then greenish-yellow, damaged ones do not change colour, in older fruiting bodies they may turn grey. Stem: Height 5–13 cm, thickness 1–3 cm, slender, cylindrical, solid, narrowed at the bottom, crenate at the top. The colour is from yellow through yellow-brown to red-brown. There may be longitudinal, darker streaks or a network with very elongated meshes. The mycelial hyphae at the base of the stem are white, which is an important identification feature. Flesh: White or cream with a yellow tinge, darker above the tubes.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In the Northern Hemisphere it is widespread, especially in areas with a temperate climate; in the Southern Hemisphere it does not occur; from equatorial regions its localities have been reported only in Colombia in South America. In Poland it is common. A ground-dwelling fungus occurring in coniferous and deciduous forests, in thickets, less often in parks.
Xeromphalina campanella (Batsch) Kühner & Maire (Polish: pępowniczka dzwonkowata) is a species of fungus in the family Xeromphalinaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 0.5–2 cm, at first bell-shaped-convex, later depressed. The margin is striate. The surface is coloured from yellow to brown, dry and smooth. Gills: Arched and decurrent on the stem, sometimes joined by anastomoses. They are the same colour as the cap, or slightly paler. Stem: Height up to 1–1.5 cm, thickness 0.1 cm. At first solid, later hollow. It is red-brownish, and at the base it is covered with brown hyphae of mycelium. Flesh: White. In the cap very thin. It does not change colour when pressed. The taste and smell are mild. Spore print: White. Microscopic features: Spores 5.5–7 × 3–4.5 µm, smooth, ellipsoid, weakly to moderately amyloid. Pleurocystidia and cheilocystidia spindle-shaped, measuring up to about 55 × 15 µm. Caulocystidia club-shaped to spindle-shaped, up to 75 × 15 µm, thin-walled, hyaline in KOH. Clamp connections present. Similar species: Xeromphalina campanella is hard to confuse with other species, thanks to its tufted growth on stumps of coniferous trees. Numerous Galerina species are similar in habit and cap colouring, but they do not have a dark brown stem, only a light brown one, and moreover they have a dark spore print.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North and Central America and in Europe and Asia. In Asia its distribution is poorly known, it is mentioned only from Japan and Korea. In Central Europe it occurs mainly in the mountains and foothills, in the lowlands it is rare, whereas on the Scandinavian Peninsula it is frequent also in the lowlands. In Poland it is common. A tree-dwelling saprotrophic fungus. It grows in various types of forests, sometimes also in parks, on dead trunks and stumps of coniferous trees, especially fir, spruce and pine. It produces fruiting bodies almost throughout the year (in favourable weather also in winter).
